evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: An agent skill that builds award-caliber websites from one line

evidence.heading: /awwwards
evidence.text:
**An agent skill that builds award-caliber websites from one line.**


  
  
  
  
  
  
  



  


[Demo](#demo) · [Install](#install) · [Usage](#usage) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Limits](#limits) · [/jury](#jury)



```
> make me a portfolio, my name is Julio
```

That's the whole brief. The agent works as creative director, designer and creative developer
in one, then hands back a site it has already checked in a real browser.

evidence.heading: Quick start
evidence.text:
```bash
npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g   # optional: interactive isometric explainer figures
npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g
```

Open a **new** agent session, then type `/awwwards` or just ask for a website.

The same repo has [/jury](#jury), which scores any site the way an Awwwards jury would: yours,
one /awwwards built, or a competitor's.

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
Install with the [skills CLI](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills). It runs through `npx`, so
there's nothing to install first, and it detects your agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor,
Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Copilot and more) and lets you pick.

```bash
npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g
```

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g -a claude-code` | Claude Code only (use `codex`, `cursor`… for others) |
| `npx skills add juliobsz/skills` | This project only, instead of your user folder |
| `npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g --skill jury` | One skill only (`awwwards` or `jury`) |
| `npx skills add juliobsz/skills -g --copy` | Copy the files instead of linking them |
| `npx skills update -g` | Update to the latest version |
| `npx skills remove awwwards jury -g` | Uninstall |

The CLI collects anonymous usage data. Set `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` to turn
it off.


Claude Code plugin

If you prefer Claude Code's plugin system, which updates the skill for you:

```
/plugin install awwwards --marketplace juliobsz/skills
/plugin install jury --marketplace juliobsz/skills
```

On Claude Code before 2.1.275, run `/plugin marketplace add juliobsz/skills` and then
`/plugin install awwwards@juliobsz` (or `jury@juliobsz`). The skills then run as
`/awwwards:awwwards` and `/jury:jury`. Use the plugin or the skills CLI, not both, or each
skill shows up twice.



Google Antigravity (CLI, IDE & 2.0)

For Google Antigravity across all surfaces (CLI `agy`, Antigravity IDE, Antigravity 2.0):

- **Workspace**: If working inside this repository, `.agents/skills.json` automatically registers `awwwards` and `jury`. In your own project, copy them into your `.agents/skills/` directory:
  ```bash
  mkdir -p .agents/skills
  cp -r <path-to-repo>/awwwards <p

evidence.heading: Requirements
evidence.text:
- **Node 22.20+** for the skills CLI. The helper scripts need Node 20+.
- **Playwright** in the site's project for screenshots and the OG image, and **axe-core** for
  the accessibility pass. `/awwwards` installs both as dev dependencies when it needs them.
  `/jury` leaves the project it reviews alone and installs them once into `~/.cache/jury`.
  Both use a Chromium you already have when they can.
- **A model that can read images**, so the QA loop can look at its own screenshots.
- **A Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare account** only if you want it to deploy.


Troubleshooting

- **`/awwwards` or `/jury` isn't found.** Start a new session; agents read their skills folder
  at startup. Then run `npx skills list -g` to see where it was installed.
- **It shows up twice.** You installed it two ways (for example the skills CLI and the plugin).
  Remove one with `npx skills remove awwwards -g` or `/plugin uninstall awwwards@juliobsz`.
- **Installed into the wrong agent.** Name the target with `-a`, for example `-a codex`.
- **Screenshots fail with "Playwright not found".** Run `npm i -D playwright` in the site's
  project. If it reports no Chromium, run `npx playwright install chromium` once.

evidence.heading: Usage
evidence.text:
Ask in one line and let the agent decide. It writes its assumptions down instead of running a
questionnaire.

```
make me a portfolio, my name is Ana
a site for my architecture studio in Lisbon, we do small houses
launch page for a mechanical keyboard called Kestrel, it should feel insane
redesign this landing page so it could win site of the day
```

Better input gives a better site. Your real name, what you do, where you are and two or three
real projects let the concept come from your story instead of a placeholder.

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Brief** | Infers who it's for, the audience and the site's job. Missing facts become written assumptions |
| **Concept** | Three concepts from different territories (your name, your craft's materials, your place, how you work, a formal system), scored on originality and fit. The winner becomes a one-line idea with a signature moment |
| **Art direction** | Palette by role, type pairing from a curated free-font library, grid, rhythm and motion language, all written to `DESIGN.md`. Then a "genericness test" kills anything an average model would have produced |
| **Build** | Semantic HTML that looks finished with motion off. Then reveals, page transitions, a loader that tracks real loading, and the signature moment |
| **QA loop** | Production build, a crawling audit (SEO, metadata, accessibility, weight, placeholder copy, AI-copy tells) and real-browser screenshots on desktop, mobile, reduced motion and mid-transition. It also measures LCP and CLS on a throttled phone, runs axe and tabs through every page. The agent reads every frame, a fresh critic subagent that never saw the plan scores the site against the rubric, and the agent fixes things until every category hits 8/10 |
| **Ship** | OG image, favicon, sitemap, robots, then deploy to Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare (only after you confirm) |

evidence.heading: Limits
evidence.text:
- **It takes a while.** A full run is concept, design system, build and several rounds of
  screenshots and fixes. Expect a long session and heavy token use, not a quick snippet.
- **Results depend on the model.** It was built and tested with Claude Code, Antigravity and Codex. The
  concept and the visual QA are only as good as the model doing them.
- **Content is yours to finish.** Without real projects, photos and copy, the site ships with
  clearly marked placeholders that you replace.
- **8/10 is its own score.** The rubric keeps it honest, but you're the final judge.

github_projects.description: Manage your real AI agents, using Minecraft as your interface!
github_projects.description_zh: 管理你的真实 AI 智能体，使用 Minecraft 作为你的界面！

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Manage your real AI agents, using Minecraft as your interface!

evidence.heading: AgentCraft
evidence.text:
**A team of Claude agents doing real work on your code, inside a Minecraft studio you can walk around in.**

*Powered by Claude*

[](LICENSE)
[](https://www.minecraft.net)
[](https://fabricmc.net)
[](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview)
[](foreman/test)







Multi-agent coding usually means a wall of terminal text. AgentCraft turns it into a place.

You type a goal. A lead agent reads your repo, writes a plan and pins tasks to a wall. Workers walk to
their desks, sit down and start coding in their own git worktrees while their monitors stream every
file they read and every line they change. When a call is genuinely yours, an agent walks over to
you with a question. When work is ready, you review the real diff and press **Merge**. Nothing
touches your branch without that click, and nothing is ever pushed.

Close the game and the agents keep working. Open it again and the studio catches up.

evidence.heading: How a goal plays out
evidence.text:
**1. You give a goal.** Press <kbd>`</kbd> and type it. `@juniper` messages a specific agent, with
Tab completion.






**2. The lead plans.** Marlow splits the goal into tasks with dependencies. They land on the Task
Wall, and the plan goes into the shared library.








**3. The team builds.** Each worker codes in its own worktree. Monitors stream the live log: tool
calls, test runs, red and green diffs.






**4. They come to you.** A clay <kbd>!</kbd> appears, the bell rings, the agent walks to the
podium. Press <kbd>J</kbd> to answer.








**5. You review and merge.** A real code review screen: file list, line numbers, collapsed context,
the worker's summary and the reviewer's notes.






**6. Memory stays shared.** The lead's plan, decisions and repo conventions live in a library every
agent reads, and you can too.

evidence.heading: Meet the team
evidence.text:
Six hand-pixelled characters, each with their own silhouette and colour. **Marlow** leads: he plans,
splits work and reviews. **Juniper, Kit, Wren, Rowan and Tove** build. They walk the studio with
real pathfinding, sit at their desks while they type, show what they are doing with small particles
and nameplates, talk in speech bubbles, and come find you when they need a decision.

evidence.heading: The studio
evidence.text:
The Goal Atrium. Progress ring, task counts, and how many decisions need you.
The studio floor. Desks, status lamps, the library and the lounge.





Everything is information you can read at a glance. Far away, the lamps and the cupola beacon tell
you who is working, who is stuck and who is waiting on you. Closer, nameplates and cards tell you
what. Up close, monitors and screens tell you exactly how.

evidence.heading: Proven with real agents
evidence.text:
This is not a mockup. These screenshots come from a real run with Claude agents on a sample repo,
driven entirely through the game: a goal typed into the console, questions and permission prompts
answered in game, merges reviewed in the diff screen, including a merge conflict sent back to the
worker and resolved. The game was restarted mid run and the Foreman was taken offline and brought
back. Six features landed in the repo with its tests passing.








Marlow asks which default export format to use.
A worker's monitor streaming its live log.
Back online after a Foreman restart, the team resumes.

evidence.heading: Quick start
evidence.text:
**You need:** Windows 10 or 11, macOS, or Linux, Java 25, Node 22+, git, and a copy of
Minecraft: Java Edition.

**For the real agents** you need Claude API access, either of these:

- `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`: create a key at [console.anthropic.com](https://console.anthropic.com), then
  `setx ANTHROPIC_API_KEY sk-ant-...` and open a new terminal.
- A cloud provider supported by the Agent SDK: Amazon Bedrock (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1`), Google
  Vertex AI (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1`) or Microsoft Foundry (`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY=1`), with that
  provider's usual credentials.

Then:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/blendi-remade/agentcraft
cd agentcraft

tools\launch.ps1 -Backend sim                    # try it first: a simulated team, no API usage
tools\launch.ps1 -Repo C:\path\to\your\repo      # real agents on your repo
tools\stop.ps1                                   # stop everything launch.ps1 started
```

On macOS, install Java 25 with `brew install openjdk@25`. On Linux, install your distribution's
Java 25 JDK (on Arch: `pacman -S jdk25-openjdk`) or point `JAVA_HOME` at one. Then run from the
checkout (the script selects that JDK without changing your system Java):

```sh
node tools/unix.mjs launch --backend sim                 # try the studio without API usage
node tools/unix.mjs stop --profile sim
node tools/unix.mjs launch --repo /path/to/your/repo --use-claude-login
node tools/unix.mjs stop
```

This launcher installs npm dependencies on first run, downloads Minecraft and Fabric
through Gradle, starts the Foreman and game in the background, and waits for the studio world.
Use `--dev` for a muted client that does not take focus; `--no-game` starts only the Foreman,
which is also how you pair it with your own launcher instance (Prism and the like).
S

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph game ["Minecraft (Fabric mod)"]
        HQ["HQ, agents, monitors,Task Wall, podium"]
        UI["Console, decisions,diff review, library"]
    end
    subgraph foreman ["Foreman (Node + TypeScript)"]
        Team["Lead + workers(Claude Agent SDK)"]
        State["Task graph, messages,memory, decisions"]
        Git["Worktrees, diffs,approved merges"]
    end
    Repo[("Your git repo")]
    game <-->|"WebSocket, localhost only"| foreman
    Team --> Git --> Repo
```

- **The Foreman** (`foreman/`) runs the agents and owns all the state: tasks and their
  dependencies, messages, shared memory, decisions and worktrees. Everything is saved to disk and
  Claude sessions resume by id, so it survives restarts and crashes.
- **The mod** (`mod/`) is the window and the controls. It draws what the Foreman knows and sends
  back what you decide. If the game closes, no work is lost.
- **The sim backend** is a scripted team that exercises every feature with real git edits. It powers
  the demo, the screenshot QA and development, without any API usage.


More on the Foreman



- **Team:** a lead (Opus by default) that plans and reviews, and up to three workers at once (Sonnet
  by default). Pick the team with `--workers`.
- **Task graph:** tasks only start when the tasks they depend on are done, and move through todo,
  doing, review and done, with blocked on the side.
- **CI loop:** your tests run after each task. A failure goes back to the worker once, then to review
  with the failure noted.
- **Merge conflicts:** when parallel work collides, the branch goes back to its worker, who merges
  your branch in, resolves it and sends a fresh review.
- **Messages:** agents message each other and you, and a message to a busy agent reaches it mid task.

evidence.heading: What to ask a web browsing agent
evidence.text:
Anything that needs real web automation: a browser rather than an API, and a
person's judgement about what is on the page.

> Go to `<paste the URL>`. One way, Milan to Lisbon, economy, one checked bag,
> one adult. Check every date from the 12th to the 16th of next month, one at a
> time, and read the cheapest fare for each day. The date field is a calendar
> widget, so click the days rather than typing them. If a date has no
> availability, say so. Do not guess a number.

It drives the page the way a person would: the pointer moves, keys are pressed.

evidence.heading: Options: proxy, profile, seed
evidence.text:
- **`--openrouter-key`** Your key, or the `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` variable.
- **`--model`** An OpenRouter model id, or `INVISIBLE_MCP_MODEL`. Defaults to `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`.
- **`--proxy`** Optional. `http://user:pass@proxy.example.com:8080` or
  `socks5://proxy.example.com:1080`. Host and port are both required. The
  timezone, locale and egress follow it.
- **`--binary`** An engine binary you already have. It must be the build the seal
  pins, or startup refuses: this skips the download, not the version check.
- **`--seed`** An integer. Same seed, same browser identity, every run.
- **`--profile-dir`** A directory to keep the profile in, so logins and cookies
  survive restarts.
- **`--headed`** Show the browser window. The interface shows you the page anyway.
- **`--host`, `--port`** `127.0.0.1` and `8765`. Changing the host
  exposes an interface that has no authentication.

evidence.heading: A `.env` beside the command
evidence.text:
Rather than retyping the key and the binary path, put them in a `.env` in the
directory you run from:

```
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
STEALTHFOX_BINARY=/path/to/firefox
```

It is read at startup, and on the way in it **never overrides** something
already set, so the order is `--flag` > the environment > `.env` > the default.
Only the directory you are in is read - there is no search upwards, so running
from a subfolder cannot silently pick up a different key. The startup line names
the variables it applied and never prints their values.

Passing `--openrouter-key` puts the key in your shell history, and on Linux in
the process list. `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in the environment or in a `.env` avoids
both.

evidence.text:
*The LLM is the brain. The harness is the body.*

*Version 1.1, October 2026.*

> AI usage disclosure: I drafted every chapter myself, from what I learned
> building
> [WSO2 MI Copilot](https://mi.docs.wso2.com/en/latest/develop/mi-for-vscode/wso2-integrator-copilot/overview/),
> [WSO2 BI Copilot](https://wso2.com/integration-platform/docs/saas/editor/copilot)
> and [One Code](https://github.com/IsuruMaduranga/one-code). I used Claude
> Code and One Code to reorder each chapter so it leads with the answer (the
> Minto pyramid), to polish the English, to generate the diagrams, and to
> write the code that draws the charts.

A blog series about building AI agents from first principles, published as a
book.

**📖 Read it online: <https://isuruwijesiri.com/harness-engineering-101/>**

An LLM API is stateless. Every turn, you send the entire conversation as a JSON
array and get text back. A *harness* is the program that builds, maintains, and
protects that array. Everything the field calls "agents" is a set of patches to
that one loop, and each patch exists because something concrete broke. This
series develops that one idea across 16 chapters, growing a ~300-line toy agent
in plain Python as it goes.

I use the same ideas in [One Code](https://github.com/IsuruMaduranga/one-code),
an open-source coding agent built on [pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi).

The rendered book reads best online at the link above. If you'd rather read
the source here on GitHub, follow the chapters in order below. The full
introduction is on the [book's landing page](src/README.md).

summary.text: Harness Engineering 101 是一系列关于从第一原理构建 AI agent 的博客文章合集，以书籍形式发布；核心观点是 LLM 是大脑，harness 是那个构建、维护并保护对话 JSON 数组的程序。

value.text: 将 agent 开发中看似神秘的「框架」拆解为可理解的补丁序列，帮助开发者摆脱对现成框架的依赖，真正理解为什么需要工具、缓存、子 agent、护栏等组件；书中每章都遵循「失败 → 最小补丁 → 代价」的结构，便于学以致用。

audience.text: 对 AI Agent 原理感兴趣的开发者、工程师与技术决策者；希望从第一原理理解「LLM + 编排程序」如何构成 agent 的学习者；适合具备基础 Python 与 LLM API 使用经验的人群。

outcome.text: 读者将理解 AI agent 的核心架构——如何在无状态 LLM API 上构建有状态的程序，如何管理上下文预算，如何注入工具与护栏，并能亲手实现一个可运行的玩具 harness。

mechanism.text: 以「LLM 是大脑，harness 是身体」为核心隐喻，将 agent 拆解为对 JSON 数组（对话历史）的构建、维护与保护循环；每个章节针对一个具体失败场景（如工具无法触及世界、上下文窗口填满、循环同步阻塞）提出最小补丁（工具映射、上下文预算、子 agent 分叉、后台工作与时间注入），逐步生长出完整的 agent 编排层。

inspiration.text: 可尝试从零设计一个面向特定场景（如自动化客服或代码审查）的 agent harness，先写出最小的 JSON 数组循环，再按失败驱动逐步添加工具、缓存、子 agent 与护栏，最终形成可复用的框架。

limitations.text: 内容为作者学习心得的总结，非官方文档；玩具 agent 仅 ~300 行，不能覆盖生产级 agent 的全部复杂度（如分布式追踪、多模型路由、细粒度权限控制）；书中未涉及具体 LLM 供应商的 API 细节。

how_to.text: 入口：在线阅读 https://isuruwijesiri.com/harness-engineering-101/ 或在 GitHub 按章节顺序阅读 src/ 目录下的 Markdown。
前提：无需安装任何软件，只需浏览器或 Markdown 阅读器；若想动手实践，需具备 Python 基础与 LLM API 调用经验。

操作：读完 Epilogue 后，可尝试在本地复现书中逐步生长的 ~300 行 Python 玩具 agent，并自行添加一个新补丁（如记忆持久化或工具重试）。

|---|---:|---:|
| Median tokens per question | **436** | 107,122 (245×) |
| Relevant record returned | **99.0%** top 5 · 98.5% rank 1 | 96.0% within a 30K-char output |
| Worst case (1,200 questions) | **602 tokens** | 9.7M tokens |
| Median latency | **33 ms** | 92 ms |

Measured on a synthetic maintenance log (one example dataset; nothing in
Leviathan is specific to it). Methodology, all six scales and caveats:
[docs/BENCHMARKS.md](docs/BENCHMARKS.md).

evidence.heading: Quickstart
evidence.text:
```bash
cargo install leviathan-index       # or: cargo install --git https://github.com/elstongun/leviathan
cd examples/tickets && leviathan index
leviathan search -g acme "sso login loop after password reset"
```

```text
leviathan search · customer C-ACME "Acme Corp" (7 tickets) · query "sso login loop after password reset" · shown 3 of 3 · 24 tickets indexed
[1] T-1001 · 2024-01-08 09:12 · rel 16.9
  Login loops back to sign-in page after password reset
  status: closed · priority: high
  resolution: Cleared stale session cookies on password reset; shipped in 4.2.1. Workaround: clear site data.
  match: Users who reset their password get redirected to the sign-in page again in an endless loop.
...
```

- `-g` accepts a key, name or partial name. Ambiguous or unknown groups list candidates and exit 3, never guess.
- No match in the group falls back to other groups, labeled `OTHER CUSTOMER`.
- Combine `--where field=value`, `--since`/`--until`, `"phrases"` and `-exclusions`.

Prebuilt binaries are on [Releases](https://github.com/elstongun/leviathan/releases). No runtime dependencies; the index is one SQLite file.

evidence.heading: Map your data
evidence.text:
Fields are paths (`a.b`, `items[].name`); only `id` is required.

| Field | Enables |
|---|---|
| `id` | `get`, `upsert`, `delete`, citations |
| `title` / `text` | Card headline (weighted 2×) / searched text (default: all strings) |
| `group` / `group_name` | `-g` scoped search, name resolution, labeled fallback |
| `date` | `--since`, `--until`, `recent` |
| `filters` / `display` | `--where` facets / fields shown on cards |
| `empty_values` / `rank.boost` | Placeholders treated as missing / favor complete records |

```bash
leviathan init ./export                       # infer a commented leviathan.toml
leviathan index tickets.csv --id "Ticket ID" --group customer_id --date created_at   # or flags
leviathan index -c tickets.toml               # or a config your agent wrote from the schema
leviathan describe                            # fields, groups, filter values, example calls
```

Any database works through its own CLI; Leviathan never holds credentials:

```bash
psql "$DATABASE_URL" -At -c "SELECT row_to_json(t) FROM tickets t" | leviathan index - -c tickets.toml
leviathan index app.db --sql "SELECT * FROM tickets" -c tickets.toml
duckdb -json -c "SELECT * FROM 'events/*.parquet'" | leviathan index - -c events.toml
```

Builds are atomic and skipped when nothing changed; `upsert` and `delete` keep an index fresh. Full reference: [docs/CONFIG.md](docs/CONFIG.md).

evidence.heading: Plug it into your agent
evidence.text:
**CLI + skill (recommended):** any agent with a shell can call it. Copy
[`skills/leviathan`](skills/leviathan/SKILL.md) into `~/.claude/skills/` or
paste it into `AGENTS.md` / `.cursor/rules`. Costs 0 tokens until used.
[`skills/leviathan-memory`](skills/leviathan-memory/SKILL.md) does the same
for memory.

**MCP (optional):** `leviathan mcp` serves four read-only stdio tools
(`search`, `resolve_group`, `get`, `describe`) whose descriptions include a
summary of your dataset (~640 tokens per session). `leviathan wrap <agent>`
prints the config for 24 agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code /
Copilot, Gemini CLI, Windsurf, Cline, Zed, JetBrains and more) and
`--apply` writes it; `leviathan wrap` lists them all
([docs/AGENTS.md](docs/AGENTS.md)).

**Remote (optional):** `leviathan serve --http` serves the same tools as
Streamable HTTP MCP, REST and OpenAPI, with a bearer token or OAuth 2.1, so
claude.ai, ChatGPT, the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs and agent frameworks can
connect ([docs/REMOTE.md](docs/REMOTE.md)).

evidence.heading: Memory
evidence.text:
Optional read/write memory for agents, in its own SQLite file. The agent
`remember`s one claim at a time; anything that can change has a `key`, so the
next write replaces the old value instead of contradicting it. Sessions start
with a short briefing, and `recall` returns only what fits a token budget.

```bash
leviathan wrap claude --memory --hooks --rules --apply   # tools, session-start briefing, always-on rule
leviathan memory remember "Prefers pnpm over npm" --kind preference -s josh -k package_manager
leviathan memory recall package manager
leviathan memory import ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md   # bring an existing markdown memory
```


  


| After 300 sessions | Leviathan memory | MEMORY.md, whole file | MEMORY.md, first 200 lines |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Tokens at session start | **736** | 33,313 | 2,588 |
| Answer in context | **100%** | 100% | 18% |
| Stale value in context | **0%** | 73.8% | 36.4% |

Writes are explicit (no model runs inside Leviathan), secrets are refused,
and history stays queryable (`as_of`, `history`). Guide, formats and
benchmark: [docs/MEMORY.md](docs/MEMORY.md).

evidence.heading: Commands
evidence.text:
| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `init` / `index` / `upsert` / `delete` | Propose a mapping / build / update / remove records |
| `search [-g G] [words]` | Ranked records (`--scope`, `--where`, `--since`, `--until`, `-n`, `--offset`) |
| `recent [-g G]` · `resolve <g>` · `get <id…>` · `describe` | Newest · group candidates · full records · index summary |
| `memory remember` / `recall` / `forget` / `briefing` | Write / ranked read / retire / session-start briefing (`--memory=PATH`) |
| `memory list` / `history` / `stats` / `import` / `export` / `prune` | Browse / slot versions / counts / markdown or JSONL in / backup / clean up |
| `mcp [--memory] [--remote URL]` · `serve --http ADDR` | stdio MCP server or bridge · HTTP MCP + REST server |
| `wrap [agent]` | Agent config (`--memory`, `--hooks`, `--rules`, `--apply`); no agent lists targets |

Global: `--index PATH`, `--json`, `--max-chars N`. Exit codes: `0` ok (zero hits included), `1` error, `2` bad request, `3` group unknown/ambiguous.

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
Records stream into one SQLite file with an FTS5 index. A search resolves the
group (exact → name → contains → fuzzy), runs one FTS5 match where group and
filter values are indexed tokens (no post-filtering), ranks by BM25 × boosts,
and decodes only the top N into capped cards. A record's own group name is
excluded from scoped matching, placeholders count as missing, and every
answer reports `shown N of M` so agents can tell "no match" from "no data".

github_projects.name: Papermorph
github_projects.description: An AI skill that turns books into animated, narrated, interactive web experiences
github_projects.description_zh: 一个将书籍转化为动画、旁白和互动网页体验的 AI 技能

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: An AI skill that turns books into animated, narrated, interactive web experiences

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text:
A Claude Code Skill that turns textbooks into narrated, interactive web lessons,and stories into paper-puppet films.



  Open the live bookshelf →
  ·
  Read the Skill

evidence.heading: What you can make
evidence.text:
| You give it | You get | On the shelf |
|---|---|---|
| A textbook PDF (maths) | Lessons where formulas and diagrams change step by step as the narration explains, with quick checks and chapter practice that grade the maths, not the string | [Elementary Algebra](https://papermorph.diamonddoge.org/elementary-algebra/) (68 chapters), [Elementary Mathematics](https://papermorph.diamonddoge.org/math-notebook/) (23) |
| A textbook PDF (science) | Illustrated scenes with acting characters and camera work, plus the same quizzes | [Elementary Physics](https://papermorph.diamonddoge.org/science/) (9 chapters and a sample) |
| A story, a joke or a fairy tale | A short film of paper puppets in front of sets drawn in code or painted by an image model, with voices, subtitles, sound effects and music | [Joke Collection](https://papermorph.diamonddoge.org/joke-collection/) (7 episodes), [Little Red Riding Hood](https://papermorph.diamonddoge.org/little-red-riding-hood/) |


  
  


Everything is a static web page: no server, no database, no account. A book is a folder you can host anywhere.

evidence.heading: Get started
evidence.text:
Install the Skill in your project:

```bash
npx skills add DozenTwelve/Papermorph --skill papermorph --agent claude-code
```

Then, in Claude Code:

```text
/papermorph
```

It finds the PDF in your project (or asks for your story), tells you what kind of book it is, suggests a chapter to try first and how much animation it needs, and offers a recommended option at every step. Your choices are saved in `style.json`, so every later chapter is made to the same style.

You need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), ffmpeg, and Playwright's browsers (`uv run --with playwright playwright install chromium firefox`). Narration uses Edge TTS (online) or Kokoro (local). Painted sets for picture books need an image-model API key; everything else runs without one.

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
**Textbooks:** the PDF is split into chapters → each chapter gets a beat plan and narration → the narration is voiced, and every word gets a time → the picture is laid out as a storyboard first, then animated in time with those words → quizzes go between the steps → the model watches its own output (contact sheets, overlap and blank-frame checks, end-to-end tests) and fixes what it sees.

**Picture books:** your telling becomes a script and a shot list → puppets and sets are built (or painted) once and reused across episodes → voices, mouth shapes, sound effects and music are made and joined per scene → scenes are filmed in parallel → review rounds (a director, picture reviewers and a sound reviewer) send scenes back until they hold up next to approved episodes.

Large chapters can be made by a team of subagents, each step on the model that suits it ([team.md](.claude/skills/papermorph/references/team.md)).

evidence.heading: The player
evidence.text:
Every book plays in the same player: pause anywhere, step back and forth, click a step to jump there, speed control, captions, keyboard shortcuts, and progress saved per book. Interface text follows the book's language (`<html lang>`: English, Russian, Chinese and Japanese are built in); foreign lines in a film are subtitled. Formulas can be written in LaTeX (MathJax, copied only into the books that use it).

The player engine lives in [`engine/`](engine), apart from the Skill, and every book keeps its own copy, so a book never breaks when the engine changes. To update the books, or to use your own fork:

```bash
python3 .claude/skills/papermorph/scripts/engine.py site                          # sync every book in site/
python3 .claude/skills/papermorph/scripts/engine.py site --from you/your-fork@main
```

Engine versions are tags (`engine-v2`, `engine-v2.1`, …); a new major number means a book may need a change, described in its [release notes](https://github.com/DozenTwelve/Papermorph/releases). Outside this repository, `engine.py` syncs from the latest compatible release, now `engine-v2.1`. Since `engine-v2` the maths helpers (number lines, tiles, planes, the number-set diagram) are in `lib/math.js`: a chapter that uses them loads `../lib/math.js` right after `engine.js`, and `lint.py` names the chapters that need it. `--from DozenTwelve/Papermorph@engine-v1` keeps the earlier engine.

evidence.heading: Video and LMS export
evidence.text:
With the site served locally, any chapter or episode renders to a 1080p MP4 with an `.srt`:

```bash
uv run --with playwright --with numpy .claude/skills/papermorph/scripts/export.py ch12 \
  --url http://localhost:8765/science/ --link https://papermorph.diamonddoge.org/science/ch12/
```

Frames are rendered from the lesson clock, so the video matches the page exactly; quizzes stay in the interactive version, and the video ends by pointing there.

For courses, a book can also be packaged for an LMS as SCORM 1.2 or 2004 (`scripts/scorm.py`), and a book can opt in to verified citation links and reviewed question banks ([authoring.md](.claude/skills/papermorph/references/authoring.md)). None of this is on by default.

evidence.heading: Try the examples locally
evidence.text:
```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/DozenTwelve/Papermorph.git
cd Papermorph
python3 .claude/skills/papermorph/scripts/serve.py 8765 site
```

Then open [localhost:8765](http://localhost:8765/). (The full history is large; `--depth 1` skips it.)

github_projects.name: eleven
github_projects.description: Agent-first reverse engineering for macOS, Windows and Linux: any ACP agent reads, renames and patches binaries, Android apps and GPU kernels next to you.
github_projects.description_zh: 针对 macOS、Windows 和 Linux 的以智能体为先的逆向工程：任何 ACP 智能体可读取、重命名并修补本地二进制文件、Android 应用和 GPU 内核。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Agent-first reverse engineering for macOS, Windows and Linux: any ACP agent reads, renames and patches binaries, Android apps and GPU kernels next to you.

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text:
Eleven

An agent-first reverse-engineering app for macOS, Windows and Linux.



**English** · [简体中文](README_zh.md) · [繁體中文](README_zh-TW.md) · [日本語](README_ja.md) · [한국어](README_ko.md) · [Türkçe](README_tr.md) · [Русский](README_ru.md) · [Tiếng Việt](README_vi.md) · [ไทย](README_th.md) · [Deutsch](README_de.md) · [Español](README_es.md) · [Français](README_fr.md) · [Українська](README_uk.md) · [Polski](README_pl.md) · [Português (Brasil)](README_pt-BR.md) · [العربية](README_ar.md) · [فارسی](README_fa.md) · [Bahasa Indonesia](README_id.md) · [Italiano](README_it.md)




  


Eleven is a reverse-engineering app built around agents. Drop in an app, a binary, an Android APK, a GPU kernel, a shader or a model and ask what it does. Any agent that speaks the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) can read the code, follow references, rename functions, leave notes and suggest patches, while you watch and approve in the same window.

Native code is read by [Ghidra](https://ghidra-sre.org) through [REA](https://github.com/morluto/rea), or by [Rizin](https://rizin.re) when you want files to open in seconds. Android apps are read by [jadx](https://github.com/skylot/jadx). The UI is React rendered natively on GPUI by [GPUIX](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@gpuix/react).

evidence.heading: Features
evidence.text:
- **Bring your own agent.** Aster, Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot, OpenCode and any other ACP agent. Run several on the same project, each in its own chat.
- **Agents drive the window.** Eleven serves its own MCP tools so an agent can open a function, switch views, rename, add notes, change types and propose patches.
- **Ask about any code.** Select lines in pseudocode, assembly or a source file and ask, explain or copy them. The answer opens under the lines, and a suggested rename arrives as a card you accept or decline.
- **You stay in control.** Every change by you or an agent is logged with its author and can be undone. Byte patches from agents arrive as suggestions you accept or decline.
- **Mach-O, ELF and PE.** Functions, pseudocode, assembly, control-flow graph, cross-references, strings, segments and hex. Change a line's type (code, procedure, data, string) and number format with Hopper's keys.
- **Android apps.** APKs open with Java from jadx, smali from apktool when it's installed, string resources, and the manifest, `res`, assets and native libraries in a Resources list. Split bundles (`.xapk`, `.apks`) open with every split in place.
- **Source files.** Eleven finds the source files a binary was built from, reads Swift types straight from the binary, and has your agent recreate a whole file, with each function linked back to its address.
- **Rewrite in any language.** Show a function's pseudocode rewritten by your agent in C, C++, Rust, Go, Swift, Python, TypeScript, Java, C# or Zig.
- **GPU kernels.** CUDA and HIP fat binaries open as highlighted PTX, with notes beside each block and rewrites in CUDA C++, HIP C++ or Metal.
- **Shaders, models and GPU profiles.** Metal shaders and ML model files (GGUF, safetensors, PyTorch, ONNX) open in the workben

evidence.heading: Support Eleven
evidence.text: Eleven is free and built by one person. If it saves you time, [sponsoring on GitHub](https://github.com/sponsors/Zfinix) keeps it going. It pays for signed releases and the debugger, and you can see what's coming next.

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
**macOS** 14 or later on Apple Silicon:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://eleven.chizi.app/install.sh | bash
```

This installs `Eleven.app` into `/Applications`. The app is signed and notarized by Apple.

**Windows** x64, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://eleven.chizi.app/install.ps1 | iex
```

**Linux** x64: download the AppImage or the `.tar.gz` from the [latest release](https://github.com/Zfinix/eleven/releases/latest).

On first run Eleven walks you through picking an engine and an agent, and installs what's missing for you:

- **Rizin** opens most apps in seconds.
- **Ghidra 12.x with Java 21** is slower and gives the clearest pseudocode. Eleven downloads both, or uses copies it finds in `~/.local/share`, `~/Applications` or `GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR`.
- **An agent.** Eleven installs ACP adapters when they are needed.

Android apps also need [jadx](https://github.com/skylot/jadx). [apktool](https://apktool.org) is optional and adds smali.

evidence.heading: Build from source
evidence.text:
You need [Bun](https://bun.sh), Node 20 or newer, Ghidra and a JDK as above, and a checkout of REA 6.x next to this repo (`../rea`), or `ELEVEN_REA` pointing at one.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Zfinix/eleven
git clone https://github.com/Zfinix/rea
cd eleven/app
bun install
bun run dev
```

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `bun run dev [file]` | Runs the app with hot reload, optionally opening a file |
| `bunx tsc --noEmit --noUnusedLocals` | Typechecks the app, tests and scripts |
| `./script/test` | Runs the test suite one file at a time |
| `./script/bundle-macos` | Builds `build/Eleven.app` |
| `./script/bundle-windows`, `./script/bundle-linux` | Builds the Windows and Linux apps on those systems |
| `./script/package` | Builds, signs and zips a release |

evidence.heading: Environment
evidence.text:
All of these are optional. Eleven finds the usual install spots on its own.

| Variable | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR` | Ghidra install to use |
| `JAVA_HOME` | JDK to run Ghidra with |
| `ELEVEN_REA` | REA to use instead of the bundled one |
| `ELEVEN_RIZIN` | Rizin to use |
| `ELEVEN_JADX` | jadx to use for Android apps |
| `ELEVEN_APKTOOL` | apktool to use for smali |
| `ELEVEN_LLDB_DAP` | `lldb-dap` for the debugger |
| `ELEVEN_SUPPORT` | Where Eleven keeps projects and settings |
| `ELEVEN_CACHE` | Where Eleven caches decompiled code |
| `ELEVEN_PROJECTS_DIR` | Where the save dialog starts (default `~/Documents/Eleven`) |
| `ELEVEN_EXPORT_DIR` | Where exports and patched copies go (default `~/Downloads/Eleven`) |
| `ELEVEN_SIGN_IDENTITY` | Code-signing identity for `./script/package` |

evidence.heading: Documentation
evidence.text:
- [MCP tools](docs/mcp-tools.md): every tool agents get in Eleven, what each one takes and returns, permissions and privacy.
- [Skills](docs/skills.md): the built-in playbooks and how to write your own.

github_projects.name: agentmemoryrepo
github_projects.description: Spec for Agent Memory Repo
github_projects.description_zh: 智能体记忆库规范

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Spec for Agent Memory Repo

evidence.heading: Agent Memory Repo
evidence.text:
Agents work better when they remember things across sessions. With Agent Memory Repo, your agent saves what it learns from you in real time, and that memory is live across sessions. Memories link to each other, so your agent navigates them like a wiki.

The spec is also published at [cognition.com/agent-memory-repo](https://cognition.com/agent-memory-repo).

evidence.heading: Give your next session a memory.
evidence.text:
Save a trial preference, then ask for it in a new session. Your memory lives in a separate repo, never in the public spec repository.

For this local trial, use the same machine with persistent storage. Cloud sessions or another machine need a private remote or other persistent storage to carry memory across sessions.

evidence.heading: 1. Install the skill
evidence.text:
**Devin CLI.** Run this in your terminal, then start a new Devin session. ([Installation guide](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/extensibility/plugins/overview))

```sh
devin plugins install AgentMemoryRepo/agentmemoryrepo
```

**Claude Code, Cursor & others.** Run this from your project and choose your agent in the installer. Requires Node.js and Git. Restart your agent if needed. ([Installation guide](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills#install-a-skill))

```sh
npx skills add AgentMemoryRepo/agentmemoryrepo --skill agent-memory-repo
```

evidence.heading: 2. Save a memory
evidence.text:
Send this to your agent. It will create the repo, save an entry, and commit it.

First session:

```text
Use the agent-memory-repo skill to set up a separate local memory repo for this trial. Save this trial preference: I prefer concise bullet-point summaries. Do not configure a remote. Tell me the full path to the memory repo so I can reuse it next session.
```

evidence.heading: 3. Start a new session
evidence.text:
Use the same project and machine, and replace the placeholder with the path your agent gave you. The new session should retrieve the saved preference from the repo.

Next session:

```text
Use the agent-memory-repo skill with the memory repo at <paste the full path from the previous session>. What trial preference did I save?
```

The memory repo stays local; no remote is configured by this trial. Invoke the skill when you want to use memory. Automatic startup and scheduled Dreaming are not included.

evidence.heading: The memory loop
evidence.text:
Every session follows the same steps.

1. **Clone** the latest memory.
2. **Grep** for what the task needs, or follow links.
3. **Update** entries as the agent learns, with no human in the loop.
4. **Push** after every edit.

evidence.heading: Use cases
evidence.text:
**Personal memory.** Remember a user's context across sessions, like who they work with or how their projects connect. Each session reads and updates the same memory repo.

**Agent swarms.** Share findings across agents working in parallel. Each agent pushes to the same memory repo, and git flags any edits that conflict.

**Team memory.** Share knowledge about customers, processes, and tools, especially for teams without a code repo. A lesson from one member's support investigation becomes available to everyone's agents.

**Multiplayer.** Memories compose because they are folders. When a new user joins a session, their memory repo can be cloned into the same machine.

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text:
Cinematic launch films and motion design from code, directed by your coding agent.


  
  
  



  


Kiln: a 25-second launch teaser that an agent branded, directed, scored and rendered from a two-sentence brief. The GIF is an excerpt; click it to download the full 1920x1080, 60 fps MP4 with sound (7 MB).

cinetic (cinema + kinetic) is an agent skill that makes your coding agent direct a short film instead of arranging animation components.

- **Idea first.** Before any code, the agent writes three concepts through different lenses, tests them, and picks one story device the film owns.
- **273 techniques, drawn at random.** A library of measured moves in 14 categories, each with a build recipe and timing at 60 fps. `pick.py` draws the film's plan, weighted for its format and energy, so two films don't share the same fade-up, push-in and end card.
- **Its own brand.** The look comes from three personality words, so a calm notes app and a fast CI tool don't end up looking alike.
- **Calm, with words in fragments.** Copy arrives a few words at a time, split around what the product does ("here is the newest" → the product → its name), with readable holds that drift instead of freezing and stretches of pure picture between. The fragment grammar comes from a frame-by-frame study of eight professional films; a crisp profile is there when a brief asks for energy.
- **One beat grid, measured sound.** `timeline.ts` drives the picture, the soundtrack and the QA scripts, so every hit lands on its frame. The effects come from an [earshot](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/earshot) sound kit: sounds designed in code and rendered with measured sync points, one soft sound per text fragment, one clean element on the lockup. Typing, clicks and ticks follow measured norms of top-tier launch fi

evidence.heading: The technique library
evidence.text:
An agent left to choose picks the familiar option every time. cinetic's agent draws instead. In Step 1, after it has chosen a concept, it runs:

```bash
python3 scripts/pick.py --format launch --energy high --seconds 25 --json out/qa/picks.json
```

and gets about one technique per 3.5 s of film at the calm default and per 2.5 s for an energetic one (7 or 10 for a 25 s launch, 5 for a 12 s vertical video, 4 for a loop or a sting), drawn in the order the format needs them and weighted toward proven workhorses and the film's energy. Each pick prints its build recipe and default timing. The agent builds the picks its concept can carry, retold in the film's own objects, and rerolls or drops the rest with a reason written into the treatment; it never adds a move the draw didn't give it. The seed is printed, so a plan can be reproduced.

| Category | Entries | | Category | Entries |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Opening hooks | 10 | | Logo and end card | 18 |
| Transitions | 22 | | Colour and light | 25 |
| Camera | 22 | | Texture and finish | 20 |
| Typography in motion | 25 | | Layout and composition | 16 |
| UI choreography | 19 | | Pacing and structure | 23 |
| Data and numbers | 17 | | Micro-interactions | 20 |
| Product demo | 22 | | Depth and 3D | 14 |

evidence.heading: Requirements
evidence.text:
- **macOS or Linux.** The scripts are bash (3.2 or newer, so macOS's built-in bash works); they were developed on Linux, and macOS is less tested. On Windows, WSL2 with the [Ubuntu steps](docs/setup.md#ubuntu-and-debian-apt) is the likely route; it has not been tested.
- **Node 22+** (Remotion 4)
- **ffmpeg 6+** with libx264, and ffprobe
- **Python 3.11+** with numpy, scipy, soundfile, pyloudnorm, opencv-python and librosa; fonttools, brotli and uharfbuzz for outlined SVG logos; pillow for banding-free gradient PNGs
- **[earshot](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/earshot) 0.3+ (optional, recommended)** in its own virtual environment, with `EARSHOT_PYTHON` pointing at its interpreter: it renders the film's sound kit and listens to the soundtrack. Without it a film uses the kit takes already rendered in its `audio/kit/`, or falls back to synthesized effects with a warning. Details: [Sound from earshot](docs/setup.md#sound-from-earshot).
- **Chromium or a Chrome headless shell.** Remotion downloads its own if allowed; set `REMOTION_BROWSER` or `CHROMIUM_PATH` to use a local one.
- **A Remotion licence if you need one.** cinetic is MIT, but Remotion, the default engine, has its own licence: free for individuals and companies of up to 3 people, a company licence from 4. HyperFrames is Apache-2.0.

Install the Python packages in a virtual environment:

```bash
python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/cinetic
source ~/.venvs/cinetic/bin/activate
pip install numpy scipy soundfile pyloudnorm opencv-python librosa fonttools brotli uharfbuzz pillow
```

The scripts call plain `python3`, so activate the environment before you start the agent, or put `~/.venvs/cinetic/bin` first on your `PATH` so the agent's shell finds it. A virtual environment also avoids the `externally-managed-environment` error that

**What the agent does.** If the brief names the product, the message and the length, it starts; otherwise it asks at most three questions. github_projects.description: Open source code review that runs in your coding agent before you push. Scanners plus a separate AI reviewer, on your own login, no key.
github_projects.description_zh: 开源代码审查，在推送前在你的编码智能体中运行。扫描器加独立 AI 审查员，使用你自己的登录，无需密钥。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Open source code review that runs in your coding agent before you push. Scanners plus a separate AI reviewer, on your own login, no key.

evidence.heading: OpenQodex
evidence.text:
[](https://www.npmjs.com/package/openqodex)
[](https://github.com/openqodex/openqodex/blob/main/LICENSE)
[](https://github.com/openqodex/openqodex/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[](https://github.com/openqodex/openqodex/discussions)

AI agents: read the [agent guide](https://github.com/openqodex/openqodex/blob/main/docs/for-agents.md). After the install, `~/.openqodex/bin/openqodex guide for-agents` prints the guide for the installed version.

OpenQodex reviews your code change before you push it. Your change is the commits you have not pushed plus everything uncommitted. OpenQodex runs on your machine, from your coding agent or your terminal.

First, OpenQodex runs the scanners that fit the files you changed. A scanner is a program that checks code without a model, such as gitleaks or semgrep. A finding is one problem at one place in the code, with a severity. OpenQodex keeps the scanner findings on the lines you changed. It drops findings in test fixtures and in rules you switched off. Every supported lockfile in the repository is checked against osv.dev at every review and scan of a change. Advisories outside the changed lines are shown, never counted, and kept out of the reviewer's brief. Each advisory names its fixed versions, or says no fixed version is published.

Then OpenQodex starts reviewers: separate Claude Code or Codex processes on your own login. By default, the agent that wrote the code does not review it. Finder sessions read each part of the change, with the code that calls it, and propose candidates with a quoted line as evidence. A script checks every quote against the code. Verifier sessions then judge each candidate and each scanner finding against the code, and must confirm or refute every one with a reason. Scripts check that every scanner finding was

evidence.heading: Where it runs
evidence.text:
| Coding agent | Starts a review | Can be the reviewer | Push gate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | yes | yes | yes |
| Codex CLI | yes | yes | yes, after you trust the hook in Codex |
| Cursor | yes | no | no, a rule asks Cursor to review |
| Cline | yes | no | no, a rule asks Cline to review |

In Cursor and Cline, the review needs Claude Code or Codex installed as the reviewer. A push gate is a hook that looks for a review before your agent runs `git push`.

evidence.heading: Requirements
evidence.text:
- Node 22 or newer, and git.
- macOS or Linux. CI runs the gate on Node 22, on macOS and on Ubuntu Linux. No test runs on Windows or WSL.
- For a full review: Claude Code or Codex, installed and logged in. OpenQodex needs no account or API key of its own.
- Some scanners need a language runtime that OpenQodex does not install. brakeman and rubocop need Ruby. golangci-lint needs Go. cargo-deny needs Cargo.

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
For people, in your terminal:

```
npx openqodex init
```

In a terminal, `init` finds Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and Cline on your machine. It lists the files it will write. It asks you once. It starts the scanner downloads that your repository needs. Then it reviews your current change when a reviewer can start.

After the install, say to your agent: "review my change with openqodex". In your own terminal, run `~/.openqodex/bin/openqodex review`. That path is the launcher, a small script that `init` writes. An `npx` install puts no `openqodex` on your `PATH`.

For agents, the same install with no question:

```
npx -y openqodex@0.14.0 init --yes --agent <host>
```

`<host>` is `claude-code`, `codex`, `cursor` or `cline`. In its default sandbox mode, Codex gives commands no network. From Codex, run this line in your own terminal. The [quickstart](https://github.com/openqodex/openqodex/blob/main/docs/quickstart.md) has a prompt to paste into your agent.

To install only the skill, run `npx skills add openqodex/openqodex -g`. That installs no push gate and downloads no scanner. A later `init` replaces that skill with the skill that `init` installs.

OpenQodex itself collects no usage data. The built-in scanners, as OpenQodex runs them, send no code. The reviewer sends your change to the model service of your Claude Code or Codex login. The [privacy page](https://github.com/openqodex/openqodex/blob/main/docs/privacy.md) lists each network use of this version.

evidence.heading: What it does today
evidence.text:
- `openqodex review` reviews your change in one command.
- It writes `report.html`, `report.md`, `report.json` and `report.sarif`. SARIF is a standard JSON format for scanner results.
- At the end, it prints a receipt. The receipt holds the verdict, one line per finding and the path of `report.html`. Here is an [example report](https://github.com/openqodex/openqodex/blob/main/tests/golden/expected/claude/run/report.md).
- The skill tells your agent to show you the receipt. It tells the agent to ask "Fix all, or tell me which?". It tells the agent to fix only the findings you name.
- `review --all` reviews every file of the repository, less the paths that `review.paths.exclude` leaves out.
- `review <branch>` reviews a branch. `review '#42'` reviews a pull request.
- A review is complete only when every stage ran. Otherwise, `review` prints "Review incomplete" with what is missing. Then it exits 2.
- The push gate inside your agent looks for a review of your current work. It does not know what a push sends. For a plain `git push`, it asks whether your current work has a passing review. For any other push command, it says it cannot tell. The git pre-push hook that `init` adds checks the exact commits a push sends, for each `git push` that runs git hooks. `git push --no-verify` skips that hook.
- Both warn by default. They block only when `.openqodex/config.yaml` sets `review.block_on_severity`. Severities run from `critical` through `major`, `minor` and `nitpick` to `info`. A finding at or above the set severity blocks the push.
- The GitHub Action runs the full review on a pull request when the workflow gives it an Anthropic API key. Without a key, it runs the scanners only. The pre-commit hook also runs the scanners only.
- `openqodex graph` answers questions about the

evidence.heading: What it does not do yet
evidence.text:
- No reviewer other than Claude Code or Codex. Cursor cannot be the reviewer. `cursor-agent` 2025.09.18 offered no way to limit it to reading.
- Without a reviewer, `review` prints "Full review unavailable" and exits 2. It saves the scanner findings, unchecked, to `unchecked-candidates.json`. It also names a fallback command, `review --agent`. In that fallback, your coding agent reviews its own change.
- Inside the Codex sandbox, a second Codex process does not start. So Codex cannot be the reviewer there. OpenQodex tested this with codex-cli 0.160.0 on macOS.
- No review on your own API key, except in the GitHub Action.
- No Homebrew formula, no install script and no Docker image in this version. Install through npm.
- No offline copy of the vulnerability databases. osv-scanner checks every lockfile at every review and scan of a change, through osv.dev. cargo-deny downloads the RustSec advisory database.
- No review finds every problem. The report names each stage that did not run.

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: An open-source take on ChatGPT's Intelligent UI: answers stream as interactive UI (maps, photos, charts, drawings and working tools). Built with OpenUI.

evidence.heading: Open Intelligent UI
evidence.text:
**An open-source implementation of the "Intelligent UI" experience introduced in ChatGPT, built on [OpenUI](https://openui.com).**

**[Try the live demo](https://www.openui.com/demo/intelligent-ui)**

In ChatGPT's Intelligent UI, a request such as "plan a day in San Francisco" returns an interactive answer (a map, photographs and an editable itinerary) rather than text. This repository reproduces that experience with open-source components, so that the same kind of interface can be built, modified and shipped inside any application.

[OpenUI](https://github.com/thesysdev/openui) is an open standard for Generative UI.

> This project is independent and is not affiliated with or endorsed by OpenAI. "Intelligent UI" refers to the ChatGPT feature that this demo recreates.

evidence.heading: Demo video
evidence.text:
ChatGPT's Intelligent UI (left) and this project (right) answering the same request. Select the image to play the video.

[](docs/openui-chatgpt-comparison.mp4)

evidence.heading: What's in the demo
evidence.text:
The model streams OpenUI Lang 1.0, and the app renders it with a library of primitives the model arranges itself: no layout is fixed in the components. The library (`src/lib/library.ts`, components in `src/lib/components/`) follows the Open Intelligent UI design. The components have light and dark tokens, but only `/gallery` (and the benchmark's `/preview`) switch to dark; the chat is light only:

- **Layout:** `Col`, `Row`, `Box` (background, radius, border, sizes, flex), `Grid`, `Card`, `Carousel` (a scrolling, snapping row), `Popover`, `Divider`, `Spacer`.
- **Text:** `Title`, `Text` (inline **bold**, *italic*, `code`, links), `Caption`, `Label`, `Badge`, `Link`, `List` and `ListItem` (bullets, numbers, a timeline), `Markdown`.
- **Inputs:** `Button`, `IconButton`, `Pressable`, `Input`, `TextArea`, `Select`, `SegmentedControl`, `Slider`, `Checkbox`, `RadioGroup`, `DatePicker`, `Timer` (a countdown), `Form`. Each input's first argument is its value, usually a `$variable` other statements read.
- **Media and data:** `SearchImage` (a photo the app finds for a query, like ChatGPT's server-resolved images), `Image` (a given URL), `Icon` (lucide names), `Table` (cells may be components), `Chart` (bar, line, area, pie, donut, scatter), `Map` with `MapMarker` ([MapLibre GL](https://maplibre.org), category filter, expansion, a street route), and `YouTube`.
- **More text and play:** `Text` takes a list mixing strings and inline components; `Quote`, `Code` (with copy) and `Math` (KaTeX); `Flashcard` (flips) and `Celebration` (confetti when a condition turns true).
- **Drawing:** `Svg` with `G`, `Circle`, `Ellipse`, `Rect`, `Line`, `Path`, `Polyline`, `Polygon` and `SvgText`, whose attributes take expressions so state can move them; `HtmlView` runs an HTML page (a game, a canvas

evidence.heading: Setup
evidence.text:
Requires Node 24.

```bash
cp .env.example .env
npm install
npm run generate:apiKey   # writes THESYS_API_KEY to .env
npm run dev
```

Open http://localhost:3000 and try: `I'm in San Francisco for a day, plan a sightseeing route for me`

| Variable | Required | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `THESYS_API_KEY` | Yes, unless using a direct API | OpenUI Cloud (Gateway) key, used only on the server. |
| `THESYS_MODEL` | No | A `{provider}/{model}` id. Defaults to `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. |
| `THESYS_BASE_URL` | No | The Gateway's Responses endpoint. Defaults to `https://api.thesys.dev/v1/embed`. |
| `LLM_BASE_URL` | No | Use any OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API directly instead of Cloud, e.g. `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1`; see [Use any OpenAI-compatible API](#use-any-openai-compatible-api). |
| `LLM_API_KEY` | With `LLM_BASE_URL` | That API's key. |
| `LLM_MODEL` | With `LLM_BASE_URL` | The model id it serves, e.g. `openai/gpt-6.1-sol` on OpenRouter. |
| `LLM_REASONING_EFFORT` | No | Reasoning effort for both paths. Defaults to `low` (about five times faster to the first line of UI on gpt-6.1-sol, same quality); `default` sends none. |
| `MODEL_PROVIDER` | No | Set to `ollama` to run a local model instead of Gateway; see [Run with a local model](#run-with-a-local-model-ollama). |
| `OLLAMA_MODEL` | No | The Ollama model to use. Defaults to `qwen3.8:27b`. |
| `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` | No | Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Defaults to `http://localhost:11434/v1`. |

evidence.heading: Use any OpenAI-compatible API
evidence.text:
Set `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_API_KEY` and `LLM_MODEL` to skip OpenUI Cloud and call a model directly, for example through OpenRouter:

```bash
LLM_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1
LLM_API_KEY=sk-or-...
LLM_MODEL=openai/gpt-6.1-sol
```

`/api/chat` then builds the full OpenUI 1.0 system prompt on the server, from the same library spec and prompt options (`generateSystemPrompt`), streams Chat Completions and relays the text as Responses events, so the browser is unchanged. The Ollama variables below are shortcuts for the same path. Output is rendered as written: Cloud's correction step is not there.

evidence.heading: Run with a local model (Ollama)
evidence.text:
The demo can also run on a local model through [Ollama](https://ollama.com), with no API key required.

It works with any OpenAI-compatible local server (Ollama, LM Studio) via `OLLAMA_BASE_URL`.

1. Install Ollama and pull a model. The default is `qwen3.8:27b` (about 18 GB, best with 32 GB of memory or more); `gpt-oss:20b` and `qwen3:8b` are smaller alternatives.

   ```bash
   ollama pull qwen3.8:27b
   ```

2. Give the model a larger context window. The OpenUI prompt for this app is about 8,000 tokens, and Ollama's default window is 4,096, which silently cuts the prompt and produces broken output. Either start Ollama with a larger default:

   ```bash
   OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 ollama serve
   ```

   or create a model variant with a larger window and use its name as `OLLAMA_MODEL`:

   ```bash
   printf 'FROM qwen3.8:27b\nPARAMETER num_ctx 32768\n' > Modelfile
   ollama create qwen3.8-32k -f Modelfile
   ```

3. In `.env`, set `MODEL_PROVIDER=ollama` (and `OLLAMA_MODEL` to use another model), then `npm run dev`.

What changes with a local model:

- **No output correction.** Gateway validates and corrects the generated OpenUI Lang; locally, the model's output is rendered as written, so larger models give better results.
- **Speed depends on your hardware.** The first request after Ollama loads the model has to read the whole prompt; later requests reuse it and are much faster. For reasoning models, `LLM_REASONING_EFFORT=low` cuts the wait considerably.

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
- **Generation.** `/api/chat` calls OpenUI Gateway's Responses API with `generateSystemPrompt({ cloud: true })`, so Gateway validates and corrects the generated OpenUI Lang against this app's component library. No search tool is sent: `SearchImage` finds its own photo (see Photos below), so the model never announces a search that shows nothing. Requests ask for low reasoning effort (`LLM_REASONING_EFFORT`).
- **Chat Completions.** OpenUI Gateway also supports the Chat Completions API, and OpenUI works with either. This example uses the Responses API because Gateway's hosted tools are available only there. An application already built on Chat Completions can keep that protocol and pair it with `openAIReadableStreamAdapter` or `openAIAdapter` in the browser.
- **State.** Inputs bind to `$variables` (`Slider($price, 0, 100)`), and any statement that reads them updates as the user interacts. Buttons and `Pressable` run `@Set`, `@Reset`, `@ToAssistant`, `@OpenUrl` and `@CopyToClipboard` steps.
- **Working tools.** The prompt options in `src/lib/prompt-options.ts` (rules and worked examples) teach the model to answer with a tool that works in the page: lists and inputs live in `$variables`, everything shown is computed from them with `@functions`, and buttons change them with `@Set`, instead of sending a form back to the assistant. `@Each` maps a list into rows, e.g. `@Each(@Range(0, $years + 1), "y", {year: y, balance: $p * @Pow(1 + $r / 100, y)})`.
- **Photos.** `SearchImage` (and `Image` when its URL fails) asks `/api/wiki` for the lead photo of the Wikipedia article titled like the query, then `/api/image-search` for Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons results whose titles match it.

github_projects.description: A TypeScript-shaped language built for coding agents. It compiles to small, fast native binaries.
github_projects.description_zh: 一个为编程智能体构建的 TypeScript 形语言。它编译为小型、快速的本地二进制文件。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: A TypeScript-shaped language built for coding agents. It compiles to small, fast native binaries.

evidence.heading: Tov
evidence.text:
**Tov is a TypeScript-shaped language that runs faster than Rust.** It compiles to a small native binary that, on most of our benchmarks, beats Rust and C, and runs several times faster than Bun or Node in a fraction of the memory.

```sh
tov run app.ts             # build and run
tov build app.ts -o app    # write a native binary
tov test src/              # run every *.test.ts (Jest's API: describe, it, expect)
```

evidence.heading: The goal
evidence.text:
1. **Run any TypeScript as it is.** Code written for TypeScript, Bun or Node should compile unchanged and behave exactly as it does there: the same semantics, Bun's and Node's APIs, npm packages.
2. **Be the fastest way to run it.** Faster than Bun and Node, and at least as fast as C and Rust, using less memory, on every benchmark.

Tov is early (version 0.0.1) and changes every day. Where it doesn't match TypeScript yet, the aim is that it tells you at compile time, with an error code and usually the fix, rather than quietly doing something different.

evidence.heading: Benchmarks
evidence.text:
The same `main.ts`, run by Node and Bun and compiled by Tov, next to C and Rust versions of the same program. Every version prints the same output. These are medians of 5 runs on an Apple M4 Max, 22 October 2026 ([all 25 benchmarks, and how they're run](bench/README.md)).

| benchmark | C | Rust | Node | Bun | **Tov** |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| binary_trees (allocation) | 746 ms | 849 ms | 488 ms | 408 ms | **268 ms** |
| dispatch (virtual calls) | 84 ms | 85 ms | 222 ms | 119 ms | **44 ms** |
| map_insert | 549 ms | 548 ms | 937 ms | 746 ms | **204 ms** |
| sort | 278 ms | 74 ms | 1,197 ms | 710 ms | **46 ms** |
| strings | 274 ms | 228 ms | 520 ms | 204 ms | **108 ms** |
| json (stringify + parse) | — | 274 ms | 485 ms | 280 ms | **246 ms** |
| fib (recursion) | 505 ms | **457 ms** | 1,522 ms | 959 ms | 467 ms |
| nbody (floating point) | 318 ms | 230 ms | 570 ms | 516 ms | **227 ms** |
| levenshtein | **486 ms** | 564 ms | 1,007 ms | 896 ms | 537 ms |
| mandelbrot | **523 ms** | 546 ms | 690 ms | 572 ms | 564 ms |
| async_calls (awaits) | — | **15 ms** | 653 ms | 547 ms | 19 ms |
| decimal_ledger | — | **139 ms** | 1,997 ms | 1,974 ms | 310 ms |

Across all 25, Tov beats Node and Bun on every one and is the fastest of the five on 16. It's furthest behind on exact decimals (Rust's `rust_decimal` is 2–4× faster) and on awaiting tiny async calls (Rust is 1.2× faster).

Memory is where the gap is widest. A small program peaks at 1.7 MB under Tov, against 20–30 MB under Bun. `binary_trees` peaks at 18.5 MB, against Bun's 185 MB.

**Web servers.** Running the Bun HTTP benchmark's own code on Linux, Tov serves 371k requests/s on one core (Bun 257k, Rust's axum 294k), and 1.61M on four in 1.6 MB of memory (Bun: 97 MB). See [bench/http](bench/http/README.md).

**`fetc

evidence.heading: Where it stands
evidence.text:
**Works today:** command-line programs and web servers; classes, generics, unions, async/await; `Bun.serve`, `fetch()`, `node:fs`/`path`/`process` and the rest of Node's built-ins; npm packages (run on JavaScriptCore, the engine Bun uses), including native addons; Jest-style tests; macOS (arm64) and Linux.

**Not yet:** `any` (beyond where the type is known anyway), classes kept in variables or arrays (they can be passed as arguments), Windows.

We measure TypeScript parity on real code. [TheAlgorithms/TypeScript](https://github.com/TheAlgorithms/TypeScript) is a library of 99 test files written for Jest and `tsc`; 72 of them build and pass unchanged under `tov test`, and most of the rest stop at a compile error naming the missing feature. A known case still behaves differently from JavaScript instead of failing to compile: reading past the end of an array outside a comparison or condition traps (JavaScript gives `undefined`). Each gap we close is tested in `tests/run/`. The full list of differences is in [docs/spec.md](docs/spec.md).

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
```sh
curl -fsSL https://tov.sh/install.sh | sh
```

This builds Tov from source. It needs git and a C compiler, and installs Rust if it's missing. Using a coding agent? Paste the prompt on [tov.sh](https://tov.sh): it installs Tov and has the agent read [tov.sh/llms.txt](https://tov.sh/llms.txt).

To build it yourself (Rust 1.95+): `git clone https://github.com/richiemcilroy/Tov && cd Tov && cargo install --path crates/tov`.

evidence.heading: Beyond TypeScript
evidence.text: Plain TypeScript is the main thing. Files ending in `.tov` can also use a few extras when you want more control: `int` and sized integers that trap on overflow, an exact `decimal` type, errors as part of a function's type (`try`), and `inout` parameters. See [docs/spec.md](docs/spec.md).

evidence.heading: Development
evidence.text:
```sh
cargo test                  # checker, runtime, HTTP and npm tests
python3 bench/run.py        # the benchmarks above
```

`crates/tov/` is the compiler (Rust, no dependencies). It generates C, which is linked with the runtime in `runtime/` (C). Benchmarks are in `bench/`, tests in `tests/`, and the landing page in `site/` is itself a Tov program.

evidence.heading: How to Use This AI System Design Guide
evidence.text:
- If we are new to AI System Design, we read it from top to bottom. Each section builds on top of the previous one.
- If we are preparing for an interview, we read [How to Solve Any AI System Design Problem](#how-to-solve-any-ai-system-design-problem) first, and then come back to the building blocks.
- If we want to go deep into any topic, we open the linked blog. Every linked blog explains one concept from the ground up.
- After every section, we try to explain it to a friend in our own words. If we can explain it, we have learned it.

evidence.heading: How is AI System Design different from regular System Design?
evidence.text:
In regular [system design](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/system-design), we deal with CPU, RAM, disk, databases, and network.

In AI System Design, we deal with all of these, and on top of that, we deal with:

- **GPUs:** LLMs run on GPUs, not CPUs. GPUs are expensive and limited.
- **Tokens:** LLMs do not work with characters. They work with tokens. Both input and output are billed per token.
- **Long requests:** A single LLM call can take 30 seconds or even minutes. Regular APIs return in milliseconds.
- **Streaming:** LLM responses are [streamed token by token](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/how-does-token-streaming-work). Not a single big response.
- **Non-deterministic output:** The same input can give different outputs. We cannot just unit-test like regular code.
- **Cost per request:** Every API call costs real money. A bug in a loop can burn thousands of dollars overnight.

So all the regular system design concepts (load balancers, caches, queues, databases) still apply. But we have to use them differently because the workload is different.

evidence.heading: How to choose
evidence.text:
We pick the scaling strategy based on our model size and traffic:

- Small model + low traffic: One GPU is enough.
- Small model + high traffic: Horizontal scaling with a load balancer.
- Big model + low traffic: Tensor parallelism within one machine (multiple GPUs).
- Big model + high traffic: Tensor parallelism for the model + horizontal scaling for the traffic.

evidence.heading: Rate Limiting in AI
evidence.text:
In regular APIs, we rate-limit by requests per second. Like 100 requests per minute per user.

In AI, this is not enough. Two requests can be very different in cost. One request can be 100 tokens, another can be 100,000 tokens.

So in AI, we rate-limit on multiple dimensions.

evidence.heading: Step 1: Requirements
evidence.text:
The main objective of this step is to understand the problem and the requirements clearly.

Before jumping into the solution, it is crucial to fully understand the problem statement, so we need to ask some clarification questions from the interviewer.

The following are some clarification questions for the Customer Support Chatbot:

**Candidate:** What kind of questions will users ask?
**Interviewer:** Mostly product usage, billing, and account-related questions.

**Candidate:** Do we have to support multiple languages?
**Interviewer:** For now, let's consider only one language, English.

**Candidate:** What is the expected scale?
**Interviewer:** 100k users, 50k chats per day, around 5 messages per chat.

**Candidate:** What is the latency expectation?
**Interviewer:** First token should appear in under 1 second.

**Candidate:** What is the monthly budget?
**Interviewer:** $5000 per month.

**Candidate:** Do we have access to the company's documentation?
**Interviewer:** Yes, we have a help center with around 500 articles.

**Candidate:** Should the bot only answer questions, or also take actions like canceling a subscription?
**Interviewer:** For now, only answer questions. No actions.

**Candidate:** What should the bot do when it does not know the answer?
**Interviewer:** Escalate to a human support agent.

**Candidate:** Do we have access to past conversations between users and human agents?
**Interviewer:** Yes, we have 1 year of past chat conversations.

So, now we have a clear picture. The next step is to define the AI Objective.

evidence.heading: Step 4: Architecture Design
evidence.text:
This step is the heart of the discussion.

For our Customer Support Chatbot, the architecture looks like below:

```
User -> Backend -> Embedding Model -> Vector DB (top 50 chunks)
                                              |
                                              v
                                      Reranker (top 5 chunks)
                                              |
                                              v
                          LLM (system prompt + chunks + question)
                                              |
                                              v
                                       Streamed Response
```

Components:

- **Chunker:** Recursive chunking with 500 tokens per chunk and 50 tokens overlap.
- **Embedding Model:** A small, fast embedding model.
- **Vector DB:** PostgreSQL with pgvector. We do not need a dedicated vector DB at this scale.
- **Hybrid Search:** Combine vector search with BM25 keyword search.
- **Reranker:** Cohere Rerank or BGE Reranker to pick the top 5 from top 50.
- **LLM:** A small chat model for most queries. Route harder queries to a bigger model using model routing.
- **Caching:** Prompt cache for the system prompt. Semantic cache for repeated questions.
- **Streaming:** SSE for the chat UI.
- **Storage:** PostgreSQL for users, conversations, and feedback. pgvector for embeddings.
- **Async:** No long-running tasks here. Everything is real-time.

It is time to discuss the Model Selection and Prompting.

Run `/plugin` → **Marketplaces** → **seecode** → **Enable auto-update** once. The plugin also adds `/seecode:export`, `/seecode:import`, `/seecode:doctor` and `/seecode:settings`.

**Any Agent Skills host** (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenCode…) via [skills.sh](https://skills.sh):

```

```

```

**Claude.ai / Claude Desktop:** download `seecode.zip` from the [latest release](https://github.com/Aryanutkarsh/seecode/releases/latest) and upload it under **Settings → Capabilities → Skills**.
