evidence.heading: How good are the voices?
evidence.text:
Measured on one character (Lamar, ten test lines): voice match is speaker similarity to 60 real clips that were
never used as references. Details and the method: [`skills/voice-likeness-eval`](skills/voice-likeness-eval).

| Setup | Voice match | Word error |
|---|---|---|
| ElevenLabs instant clone | 0.612 | 10.5% |
| Fish Audio Drama 3, default settings | 0.643 | 7.1% |
| Drama 3, tuned sampling, one take | 0.660 | 7.9% |
| **Drama 3, best of 8 takes, checked** | **0.704** | 8.6% |
| Fish Audio S2 Pro, its best reference clip | 0.707 | 5.6% |
| S2 Pro fine-tuned on the character (needs training) | 0.785 | 7.5% |

Without training, Drama 3 and S2 Pro tie on likeness; Drama 3 acts `[crying]` and `[laughing]` better and starts
talking faster. One early result here didn't survive a second run:
[how that was caught](docs/how-it-was-made.md#6-making-the-voice-sound-right-and-being-honest-about-it).

evidence.heading: Rules it follows
evidence.text:
- **Single-player games, or servers you run.** It never injects into online games with anti-cheat (GTA V: never
  launch GTA Online with a script hook installed) and never bypasses anti-cheat, DRM or ownership checks.
- **Voices you have the rights to.** It never commits or publishes voice clips, cloned voices, game audio or a
  game's dialogue; `npctalk check` blocks them.
- **No secrets in files.** Keys come from environment variables, and voice server URLs stay private (their
  `/health` wakes the GPU).
- **It asks before** driving your keyboard and mouse in a game, installing into game folders, keeping a GPU up,
  or publishing anything.
- **It measures before it claims** a voice setting is better.

Full reasoning: [`skills/make-npcs-talk/references/safety.md`](skills/make-npcs-talk/references/safety.md).

evidence.heading: Community
evidence.text:
NPCTalk is a [Universal Modder](https://github.com/rehan-remade/universal-modder) project. Universal Modder's skills and tools cover the rest of a mod (engine
recon, decompiling, fal-generated art, 3D and audio, in-game testing, showcase videos), and NPCTalk adds NPCs that
talk back. Install both and an agent can take a game from "can I mod this?" to characters you can talk to.

Show what you made, ask for help, and follow along in the **[Universal Modder Discord](https://discord.com/invite/sEZWaf7vV)**.

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text: Speech synthesis, speech recognition and voice activity detection for voice conversation, in C++ on ggml Models · Install · Quick start · Documentation · C API English · 日本語 speech.cpp is one command, `speech`, and one shared library, `libspeech`, behind one C API, on the CPU, Metal and Vulkan through [ggml](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml). The command speaks text, writes the text of recordings, finds where someone speaks in them, transcribes the microphone as someone speaks (`speech asr --live`), serves OpenAI's audio API and its Realtime transcription over HTTP, and runs a worker process for any program that keeps models loaded between requests, [ASIST](https://github.com/nyosegawa/asist) among them. **A time to first audio of a quarter of a second or less.** On an Apple M5, Qwen3-TTS 0.6B sends its first audio 0.029 s after the text and Irodori-TTS v4.1-Small-MF 0.16 s after it, and the rest follows while it plays. **One executable, nothing else to install.** No Python and no CUDA: `speech` fetches each model by name, one GGUF file with its codec, and runs it on Metal, Vulkan or the CPU. **OpenAI's API on your own computer.** `speech serve` answers OpenAI's audio API and its Realtime transcription, so an OpenAI client works by changing its base URL. **Checked against the official implementations.** Every stage of every model is compared with the model's official implementation, from the same inputs. The page of speech serve --open: pick a model of the catalog, fetch it and try it. Transcribe writes a file or a recording, a region at a time where someone speaks. Live writes the microphone as you speak; the grey text is the utterance still being said.

macOS on Apple silicon and Linux on x86-64:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nyosegawa/speech.cpp/main/install.sh | sh
```

Windows x64, in PowerShell:

```powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nyosegawa/speech.cpp/main/install.ps1 | iex
```

The installer checks the release's archive against its SHA-256, puts `speech` under your home folder, and adds it to
`PATH`. `speech update`, or running it again, updates it. On Linux it installs the Vulkan build when the Vulkan loader
is installed, and the CPU build otherwise; the Linux builds need glibc 2.34 or later. [docs/install.md](docs/install.md)
has the options, how to uninstall, and what each platform needs. On an Intel Mac or another system, [build from
source](docs/install.md#build-from-source).

evidence.heading: Quick start
evidence.text:
1. Speak a sentence. The model is fetched the first time (1.21 GB):

   ```sh
   speech tts qwen3-tts-0.6b --voice ryan -o hello.wav "Hello. It will be sunny in Tokyo tomorrow."
   ```

2. Write its text back (0.84 GB the first time):

   ```sh
   speech asr qwen3-asr-0.6b hello.wav
   ```

   ```
   Hello, it will be sunny in Tokyo tomorrow.
   ```

3. Open a page on which to pick models, speak and transcribe:

   ```sh
   speech serve --open
   ```

`speech models` lists every model and, for each language, the model to start with.

evidence.heading: Command line
evidence.text:
| Subcommand | What it does |
|---|---|
| `speech tts` | speaks text into a WAVE file or to stdout |
| `speech asr` | writes the text of WAVE files, or of the microphone as someone speaks |
| `speech vad` | writes where someone speaks in WAVE files |
| `speech voice` | makes a voice file for Irodori-TTS or Drama 3 from reference recordings |
| `speech info` | prints what a model file says of its model |
| `speech devices` | lists the devices a model can run on |
| `speech models`, `pull`, `rm` | list, fetch and remove models |
| `speech quantize` | writes a model file of F32 weights in F16, Q8_0 or a smaller type |
| `speech update` | installs the latest release, or says whether one is out |
| `speech serve` | serves models over HTTP with OpenAI's audio API, and a page to try them |
| `speech worker` | serves a model over JSON Lines on stdin and stdout, for programs |

```sh
speech voice irodori-tts-mf me.wav me.voice.gguf
speech tts irodori-tts-mf --add-voice me=me.voice.gguf --voice me -o - < story.txt | ffplay -nodisp -autoexit -
speech asr reazonspeech-v2 --timestamps meeting.wav
speech asr qwen3-asr-1.7b --language ja --prompt "Claude Code、渋谷" meeting.wav
speech asr reazonspeech-v2 --vad silero-vad --live
speech vad silero-vad --max-speech-duration-s 10 meeting.wav
```

Every request option is a flag, and `speech info MODEL` lists the ones a model takes. [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md) lists
every subcommand and option.

evidence.heading: Server and page
evidence.text:
`speech serve` holds a synthesis model, a recognition model and a detection model, and answers
`POST /v1/audio/speech` and `POST /v1/audio/transcriptions` as OpenAI's audio API does, for a web app, a script or curl:

```sh
speech serve qwen3-tts-0.6b qwen3-asr-0.6b
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/audio/speech -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"input": "Hello.", "voice": "ryan"}' -o hello.wav
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/audio/transcriptions -F file=@hello.wav
```

It listens on 127.0.0.1 and has no authentication. [docs/server.md](docs/server.md) has the endpoints, the formats, the
errors and the page.

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text: Open source. Our own quantised builds of GLM and Qwen. Built on ExLlamaV3, with speculative decoding, for 100 GB-class models in 128 GB. ModelPackPrefillSpeculative decode Qwen3.8-Flash-Next95 GB1621 at 8K47.5 to 73.2 GLM-5.3-Flash99.73 GB652 at 8K27.4 to 36.8 MiMo-V2.6-Flash (1.5)105.8 GB760 at 8K28.9 to 37.0 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (experimental, SSD tier)185 GB187 to 257 at 8K5 to 11 (plain) Tokens per second on one Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with 128 GB. Prefill at the context shown in each cell, speculative decode across chat, prose and code prompts. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash is larger than memory: most experts are read from the NVMe (about 3 GB/s), so its prefill is warm/cold and its decode is plain decoding on real sessions; a tool turn of about 2K tokens waits 21 to 35 s for the first token. Details: doc/DS41.md. Method, sources and full tables: doc/benchmarks.md. Long context: up to 500K tokens Model128K256K500K Qwen3.8-Flash-Next1505 / 54.81399 / 46.91224 / 48.1 GLM-5.3-Flash649 / 30.8619 / 34.3567 / 26.4 Prefill / speculative decode, tokens per second, Kyojin 1.5.10 on one Ryzen AI Max+ 395 with 128 GB. One real document read as a growing prompt (500K = 499,712 tokens); prefill as reported by the server. Both models recalled two facts hidden at 40 % and 85 % of a ~500K-token prompt (needle test, Kyojin 1.5.3, 15/10). 500K needs -c 524288 at launch. Qwen also needs --cache-bits 8: past 262K it uses the 8-bit cache.

evidence.heading: Made with our models
evidence.text:
One prompt each, written by the model running on Kyojin and published as it came out. [Open the gallery](https://yamz-labs.github.io/gallery/).


Voxel pagodaGLM-5.3-FlashVoxel pagodaQwen3.8-Flash-NextVoxel pagodaMiMo-V2.6-Flash


**Uncensored mode.** Each model has an optional mode that makes it refuse far less. The engine applies it at load and the weights stay untouched: ready-made packs for [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/yamz-labs/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-Yamz-Uncensored) and [MiMo-V2.6-Flash](https://huggingface.co/yamz-labs/MiMo-V2.6-Flash-MOPD-EXL3-Yamz-Uncensored), and a preset inside the [Qwen3.8-Flash-Next pack](https://huggingface.co/yamz-labs/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-EXL3-Yamz) that is off by default. How it works: [doc/refusal_hook.md](doc/refusal_hook.md).

These are first versions. Speed, context length and model support keep improving.

evidence.heading: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
evidence.text:
**Experimental.** A demonstration that a 763B model runs exactly on one 128 GB machine. It is slow and not meant for daily agent use: real decode is about 5 to 11 tokens per second, and a tool turn adding about 2K tokens takes about 20 to 35 seconds before the first token (the SSD floor is about 24 s).

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (763B parameters, about 16B active) runs on one 128 GB machine with an NVMe: the 172 GiB EXL3 pack is larger than memory, so the engine keeps a pool of experts in RAM and reads the others from the SSD, exactly. It uses the model's own DSpark draft stages and the original Engram tables (about 190 GB, downloaded from the DeepSeek repository). Pack: [yamz-labs/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-EXL3-Yamz](https://huggingface.co/yamz-labs/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-EXL3-Yamz). Setup, SSD tier, Engram and speeds: [doc/DS41.md](doc/DS41.md).

evidence.heading: NVIDIA RTX 3090
evidence.text:
Kyojin also runs on NVIDIA (sm_80 and up, tested on one RTX 3090 with 24 GB). It uses the same sources as the ROCm build; the CUDA path adds a quantized-KV decode attention kernel, a Flint sliding-window ring with whole-forward CUDA graphs, a grouped MoE prefill tier, an sm_86 GEMM layout and a decode GEMV policy. Build: [tools/cuda/README.md](tools/cuda/README.md). Switches: [doc/env_vars.md](doc/env_vars.md#nvidia-cuda-sm_80).

Measured on the 3090 with real text, greedy, one user, KV cache quantized (Flint 6/6 bits, Qwen27 4/4 bits), tokens per second:

| model | | 4K | 16K | 32K | 64K | 128K | 256K |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flint V1 (3.43 bpw, 17 GiB) | decode | 133.5 | 127.0 | 122.9 | 119.5 | 102.6 | 81.3 |
| | prefill | 6282 | 6956 | 5938 | 4449 | 2995 | 1807 |

| model (server, vision on) | | 5K | 39K | 79K | 150K | 250K |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen3.8-27B (EXL3 4.0 bpw, MTP + n-gram) | decode | 70.6 | 65.9 | 64.3 | 55.1 | 49.9 |
| | prefill | 1356 | 1143 | 977 | 787 | 611 |

Plain decode without speculation on Qwen27: 45.6 tok/s at 4K, 41.5 at 32K, 37.2 at 128K, 32.8 at 256K. Both models fit 256K tokens of context in 24 GB (peak 21 GiB for Flint, 20.5 GiB for Qwen27 with the vision tower).

Run at 256K:

```bash
# Flint V1: 256K with 6-bit K and V (fp16 KV fits about 131K)
python tools/flint/serve.py --model ./flint-pack -c 262144 --kv 6,6
# Qwen27: 256K, 4-bit K and V, vision and the MTP drafter on
python tools/qwen/serve.py --model ./qwen27-pack -c 262144 --k-bits 4 --v-bits 4
```

On NVIDIA both servers turn on the CUDA graph and these cache widths by default; `--kv` and `--k-bits`/`--v-bits` override them. The quantized caches are lossy: the Flint 6/6 cache measures about +9 % KL against fp16 and Qwen27 4/4 measures 1.4e-3 KL and finds

evidence.heading: Quickstart
evidence.text:
Install ROCm torch and build once ([doc/install.md](doc/install.md)), then:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Yamz-Labs/kyojin && cd kyojin
hf download yamz-labs/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-EXL3-Yamz --local-dir ./qwen-pack
python tools/qwen/serve.py --model ./qwen-pack --port 8000 -c 131072
```

kind_reason.text: Kyojin 是面向 AMD Strix Halo (ROCm, gfx1151) 的推理引擎，提供可复用的量化模型构建与部署能力，属于可复用技能/开发工具/框架。

summary.text: Kyojin 是 Yamz Labs 的开源推理引擎，为 AMD ROCm 平台（gfx1151）构建，基于 ExLlamaV3，支持在单台 128 GB mini PC 上运行 300B 级 MoE 模型。作者自称为 GLM、Qwen 等模型的量化构建版本，并引入推测解码（speculative decoding）以提升解码速度。README 中给出了具体

value.text: 让开发者在 AMD GPU 上获得接近消费级硬件的 LLM 推理能力，降低对 NVIDIA 生态的依赖；同时通过推测解码和长上下文优化，使 300B 级模型可在单台 128 GB 设备上运行，对边缘计算和本地化部署场景有实际价值。

audience.text: AMD GPU 用户、本地 LLM 部署者、需要高性能推理的开发者与研究者。

outcome.text: 在单台 128 GB AMD GPU 上启动一个支持推测解码的 LLM 推理服务，可处理 8K–500K 长上下文请求。

mechanism.text: 基于 ExLlamaV3 的量化推理内核，针对 AMD ROCm 平台做了适配；推测解码用于加速解码阶段；MoE 模型通过专家池管理（DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 在 NVMe 上按需读取专家，约 3 GB/s）；长上下文通过量化 KV cache（Flint 6/6 bits）或 8-bit cache 实现。

inspiration.text: 将大模型推理能力下沉到消费级硬件（128 GB mini PC），使非 NVIDIA 生态也能获得可用的本地 LLM 服务，可作为边缘 AI 推理平台的基础设施组件。

limitations.text: 作者称 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 为实验性，真实解码仅 5–11 tokens/s，不适合日常 agent 使用；长上下文 500K 需要大量显存，部分模型需 NVMe 支撑；CUDA 路径为后续适配，性能数据来自 RTX 3090 实测而非 AMD 平台。

how_to.text: 入口：克隆仓库后运行 `python tools/qwen/serve.py --model ./qwen-pack --port 8000 -c 131072`（README Quickstart，证据 R6）。
前提：安装 ROCm torch 并完成一次构建（doc/install.md），下载量化模型包（如 `hf download yamz-labs/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-EXL3-Yamz --local-dir ./qwen-pack`）。
操作：启动服务器后，通过 OpenAI API（端口 8000）调用模型；如需长上下文，使用 `-c 524288` 或 `--cache-bits 8`。NVIDIA 用户可使用 `tools/flint/serve.py` 或 `tools/qwen/serve.py` 配合 `--kv`、`--k-bits`、`--v-bits` 参数切换量化策略。

input.text: Kyojin 在 Ryzen AI Max+ 395 + 128 GB 上运行 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 的预填充速度约为 47.5–73.2 tokens/s（8K 上下文）。

output.text: OpenAI 兼容 API 服务运行在 8000 端口，可调用 Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 进行推理。

steps.text: 克隆仓库：`git clone https://github.com/Yamz-Labs/kyojin && cd kyojin`
下载量化模型包：`hf download yamz-labs/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-EXL3-Yamz --local-dir ./qwen-pack`
启动服务器：`python tools/qwen/serve.py --model ./qwen-pack --port 8000 -c 131072`

evidence.heading: Терминал «как Warp» + AI рядом

- **Интеграция с Claude Code как IDE**: `claude`, запущенный в OpsDeck, подключается к нему сам (MCP по WebSocket на 127.0.0.1) — видит выделение в заметках и получает ссылки на них.

github_projects.name: AgentGarten
github_projects.description: AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents
github_projects.description_zh: AgentGarten：演化智能体的代码世界

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text:
AgentGarten

  Code Worlds for Evolving Agents



  Code determines how the world changes, and the renderer learns how those changes should look.

evidence.heading: Overview
evidence.text:
Agents learn through interaction, and what they can learn is bounded by the
environment they practice in. That environment must be **faithful**, with
state, rules, and dynamics as consistent as those of the real world, and
**realistic**, with observations that follow the real world's visual
distribution.

**AgentGarten** builds real-time interactive environments that are both.
Simulators and game engines maintain persistent state and execute
program-defined rules, while a shared **neural renderer** generates the
agent's observations from the depth and surface normals each world exports.
Agents that practice in these environments improve from their own experience:
after each round they distill what happened into playbooks that later agents
inherit and build upon.

This is the official repository of AgentGarten. The neural renderer is
available now, with its training recipes and streaming inference; the code
worlds and the agent practice loop will be released here as well. The renderer
adapts [Cosmos3-Nano](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano) to geometry
conditions in three stages:

- **Bidirectional** rectified-flow training of whole clips from a first frame.
- **Autoregressive** block-causal training, with teacher forcing or diffusion
  forcing, sampled with a KV cache.
- **Adversarial Forcing**, which distills the autoregressive model into a
  few-step student. The replay of each rollout is exact, so losses on later
  blocks update how the student encodes its history, and a real-data
  discriminator with exact R1/R2 regularization improves visual quality.

evidence.text:

evidence.heading: Installation
evidence.text:
Python 3.11+ and PyTorch 2.9+ on a CUDA host.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/MirroS-Lab/AgentGarten.git
cd AgentGarten

cp .env.example .env    # weights, manifests, output root, interpreter
```

evidence.heading: Weights
evidence.text:
Training starts from [Cosmos3-Nano](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano)
and encodes video with the
[Wan 2.2 VAE](https://huggingface.co/Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B):

```bash
hf download nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano \
  --include 'transformer/*' 'text_tokenizer/*' 'assets/negative_prompt.json' \
  --local-dir weights/Cosmos3-Nano
hf download Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B Wan2.2_VAE.pth --local-dir weights/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B
```

Point `WM_COSMOS3_NANO` and `WM_WAN22_VAE` in `.env` at them.

evidence.heading: Inference
evidence.text:
`Cosmos3Stream` runs the renderer block by block with a bounded KV cache.
Each block is denoised in a few steps and then committed to the cache, so the
conditions of the next block can depend on what was just generated:

```python
import torch

from wm.inference.cosmos3 import inspect_artifact, load_artifact
from wm.inference.serving import prepare_serving
from wm.models.dmd import RCM_ENDPOINTS
from wm.models.flow import rf_interpolate, rf_x0
from wm.networks.cosmos3.streaming import Cosmos3Stream, StreamPolicy

artifact = load_artifact(inspect_artifact("weights/AgentGarten-renderer"))
prepare_serving(artifact.student)    # serving kernels and CUDA graphs
stream = Cosmos3Stream(artifact.student, StreamPolicy())

# anchor: the clean first-frame latent; every condition holds the text context
# and the depth and normal latents of one chunk.
stream.start(anchor, first_condition)
block = (1, anchor.shape[1], stream.policy.block_frames, *anchor.shape[3:])
for condition in blocks:    # one block is 4 latent frames
    clean = None
    for sigma in RCM_ENDPOINTS:
        sigma = torch.tensor([sigma], device=anchor.device)
        noise = torch.randn(block, device=anchor.device, dtype=anchor.dtype)
        noisy = noise if clean is None else rf_interpolate(clean, noise, sigma)
        clean = rf_x0(noisy, sigma, stream.denoise(noisy, sigma, condition))
    stream.commit(clean, condition)
```

`prepare_serving` serves the transformer with hand-written Triton kernels,
cuBLAS matrix products, and CUDA graphs, without `torch.compile`. Kernel JIT
and graph capture happen on first use, so warm the input shapes before
serving.

To render the validation clips of a checkpoint without training, add
`train.max_iterations=0 train.validate_at_start=true
trainer.callbacks.samples.every_n=1`

```

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Iris-3B: pixel-space generation & general vision learner. A 3B diffusion transformer that generates every pixel directly (no VAE); the same prior, fine-tuned, does monocular depth estimation and 4x image restoration. Paper, weights, training code and demo.

evidence.heading: Iris-3B
evidence.text:
**Pixel-space generation & general vision learner**

Generative priors are a promising foundation for downstream vision tasks. In
this project we explore pixel-space generative models as an alternative to
vision foundation models such as DINOv2.

Iris-3B is a 3B-parameter diffusion transformer that generates directly in
pixel space: no VAE, no latent space, every pixel is produced by the model, so
nothing is lost to a lossy, texture-biased latent. It is not only an image
generator: the same pixel-space prior, fine-tuned, estimates monocular depth and
restores and upscales images — one backbone, three tasks. This repository contains the
model, the training and fine-tuning code, and inference.

[Iris-3B Turbo](#iris-3b-turbo) is a 4-step distilled version of Iris-3B: a
1024×1024 image in about 0.7 s on one H100.

evidence.heading: Model
evidence.text:
| | |
|---|---|
| Parameters | 3B (excluding the frozen text encoder) |
| Trunk | 24 blocks at width 2560: 8 dual-stream (separate image/text weights, joint attention) + 16 single-stream; GQA 20 query / 5 key-value heads, gated attention, sandwich RMSNorm, shared-bias adaLN |
| Patch size | 16 |
| Pixel head | 4 pixel-transformer (PiT) blocks: each patch is decoded back to pixels with per-pixel modulation, attending across patches |
| Text encoder | Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (frozen), 12 hidden layers aggregated by a learned layer-attention adapter |
| Objective | rectified flow, v-prediction, logit-normal timesteps |

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
```bash
pip install -e .            # Python >= 3.11, PyTorch >= 2.7.1
pip install -e ".[dev]"     # + pytest, ruff
```

evidence.heading: Inference
evidence.text:
```bash
hf download speridlabs/iris-3b --local-dir iris-3b --exclude "depth/*" "upscaler/*" "turbo/*"    # ~12 GB
python scripts/sample.py --checkpoint iris-3b \
    --prompt "a red fox sleeping in fresh snow, golden hour"
```

`--checkpoint` is a directory holding `model.safetensors` + `config.yaml`, or a
training `.pth` (its EMA weights and embedded config are used). Defaults:
1024×1024, 100 DPM-Solver++ (order 2) steps, CFG 3. Use `--txt-file` for a
prompt list, `--steps`, `--seed`, `--negative-prompt` to adjust.

Turn a training checkpoint into a release directory (EMA weights only, FP32 by
default, config reduced to model/text-encoder/flow settings):

```bash
python scripts/export_checkpoint.py output/run/checkpoints/latest.pth exported/iris-3b
```

evidence.heading: Limitations
evidence.text:
- Dense or long rendered text is less reliable than with the base model.
- Less variety across seeds: different seeds for one prompt give more similar
  images.
- Faint grain or speckle can appear on flat, vector-style backgrounds.
- Sampling is fixed at 4 steps, with no CFG or negative prompt.

evidence.heading: The pitch
evidence.text:
Describe the video you want. A coding agent builds it as a real
[Remotion](https://www.remotion.dev) project. You watch the live preview change
while it works, and export an mp4 when it looks right.

This isn't another AI video editor. There's no timeline, no keyframes and no
track management. You write prompts, point at things and give notes.

**Not a generator. Not a template.** AI video tools usually make you pick one:
generate pixels you can't edit, or drag in templates everyone recognizes.
Remocn Studio takes a third route. The agent writes the motion design as code
and takes direction as you watch.

|                     | Pixel generators    | Template editors       | **Remocn Studio**               |
| ------------------- | ------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| What you get        | A video file        | Someone else's layout  | **A Remotion project**          |
| Changing one word   | Generate it again   | Hunt for the layer     | **Say it, or click it**         |
| What it looks like  | Close enough        | Everyone else's video  | **Your brand**                  |
| Where it lives      | Their cloud         | Their account          | **A folder on your disk**       |

evidence.heading: You direct. It shoots.
evidence.text:
Remocn Studio puts you in the director's chair. You watch the take, then give
notes:

> "Fix the text here."
> "The animation is too fast here."
> "Why did everything break here?"

There are three ways to say *here*:

- **Type it.** Plain words in the chat, taken exactly as you wrote them.
- **Point at it.** Click any element in the preview. Playback pauses and the
  properties pane opens, with type, spacing and easing curves as controls you
  can drag. Every change is saved into the source. You can double-click text
  to rewrite it in place, or drag an object to move or resize it. Add the
  element to the chat and it goes along with your message as `[Element #1]`.
- **Frame it.** Drag a **Snapshot** box over the frame and the crop goes into
  the chat as a picture, ready to talk about.

evidence.heading: How a video gets made
evidence.text:
You don't get a prompt box that hopes for the best. You get a production
pipeline with seven stages. At every stage the agent writes a document into
your project, so you can read, edit or overrule each decision.

| #   | Stage        | In the app you'll see            | It leaves behind                                                    |
| --- | ------------ | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | Analysis     | *Analysing the material*         | `analysis.md`: audience, promise, format, what's missing            |
| 2   | Brand        | *Collecting the brand*           | `brand.md`, plus your original logos, copied unchanged              |
| 3   | Script       | *Writing the script*             | `script.md`: every shot, its message, its timing                    |
| 4   | Motion       | *Defining the motion language*   | `motion.md`: which component plays which shot                       |
| 5   | Build        | *Building the video*             | The scenes themselves, plus keyframes it rendered to check its work |
| 6   | Choreography | *Choreographing the whole video* | `choreography.md`: rhythm, continuity, reading time                 |
| 7   | Review       | *Reviewing the result*           | `review.md`: every note, closed with evidence                       |

The agent doesn't guess what looks good. A curated set of motion design skills
ships with the app: easing, pacing, typography animation, and a record of what
has failed on screen before. Before calling a video done, the agent runs
`design_check`, which measures the rendered frames for readability, timing and
handoffs.

evidence.heading: On set
evidence.text: Inspect & edit Click an element and tune its type, tracking, easing and copy. The value goes back into the code. Snapshot Drag a box over the frame. It lands in the chat as a picture. Assets & stock Save clips, images and audio once, then say "use the intro clip". Components Save an animation that works as a component and reuse it in any project. The remocn motion set comes built in. Project brand Drop in a DESIGN.md or set the name and colors once. Every new video starts on brand. Export MP4, WebM, GIF or ProRes, up to 4K, rendered by the project's own Remotion. **Your machines fuse into one.**

ThinkTerm is an open-source **terminal with a built-in multiplexer, written in Rust**, built on [WezTerm](https://github.com/wezterm/wezterm). Its mux server runs your shells, tools, and coding agents; desktop, TUI, and browser clients connect to those sessions. Bring local and remote work into one workspace, and return to it from another device.

**Platforms:** macOS · Linux · Windows · Web · TUI — iOS and Android in development.

evidence.heading: A multiplexer at the core
evidence.text:
A terminal multiplexer manages multiple terminal sessions and lets clients attach to them. In ThinkTerm, **the mux server owns the sessions, tabs, and split panes**. The client displays them and sends your input.

- **Detach and return.** Disconnecting a client leaves its server-held sessions running. Reconnect later to continue the same shell, build, or agent task. Explicitly closing a pane is a separate action.
- **Access the same sessions from different clients.** Use the desktop, `thinkterm tui`, or the browser to connect to the server. Multiple clients can be attached at once; each offers its own interface to the shared sessions.
- **Work across machines.** Each host runs its own mux server. ThinkTerm Connect brings those remote workspaces into the desktop alongside local work, so you can switch machines from the sidebar. Processes continue to run on their original host.
- **Update without dropping sessions.** When the desktop updates ThinkTerm on a server, the running mux server hands its sessions to the new version, so shells, builds, and agents keep running.

Session persistence depends on the mux server and its host remaining available; it does not restore running processes after a server restart or host reboot.

evidence.heading: Why ThinkTerm
evidence.text:
Running several agents across different projects quickly turns a tab bar into a guessing game: which session is working, which needs input, and where did that build finish? ThinkTerm puts the project structure and work status beside the terminal, with local and remote work visible together.

Rust powers ThinkTerm's terminal core, mux server, desktop client, and TUI. The desktop renders through the GPU without Electron or an embedded web view. GPUI, Zed's UI framework, does not meet ThinkTerm's performance requirements for terminal rendering. Built on WezTerm, this native foundation supports workspace organization, persistent remote sessions, and tools for working alongside agents.

evidence.heading: Choose how you connect
evidence.text:
| Client | Current scope |
| --- | --- |
| **Desktop** | Native application for macOS, Linux, and Windows. |
| **TUI** | Workspace navigation and terminal control inside an existing terminal, through `thinkterm tui`. |
| **Browser** | A client served by your own mux server; requires WebGPU and a secure browser context. Browser access must be enabled explicitly. |
| **iOS and Android** | Native clients in development, with a shared Rust core, GPU rendering, and SSH transport. Mobile release readiness and device coverage are still being established. |

The clients connect to server-held sessions; their interfaces and feature coverage differ.

evidence.heading: Getting started
evidence.text:
For a desktop build on macOS or Linux, install Rust and your platform's build tools, then:

```sh
git clone --recursive https://github.com/RoversX/ThinkTerm.git
cd ThinkTerm
./get-deps
cargo build --release -p wezterm -p wezterm-gui -p wezterm-mux-server -p thinkterm-plugin-server -p thinkterm-tailnet-node
```

The binaries are written to `target/release`. See [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) for the source layout and development workflow. The [browser build script](ci/build-web.sh) builds the separate Web assets; mobile build entry points are [ios/build.sh](ios/build.sh) and [android/build.sh](android/build.sh).

Once the binaries are on your `PATH`:

```sh
thinkterm start              # Open the desktop application
thinkterm tui                # Open the terminal interface
thinkterm connect <name>     # Attach to a configured mux domain
thinkterm cli --help         # Inspect and control mux sessions
thinkterm plugin list        # List available plugins
thinkterm --help             # Show all commands
```

evidence.heading: Let your coding agent use ThinkTerm
evidence.text:
The repository includes a skill that teaches coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor to see and work with the other panes. Install it with:

```sh
npx skills add RoversX/ThinkTerm --skill thinkterm -g
```

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Agent skill to reverse engineer a SaaS product through the browser into a knowledge base for rebuilding it: screens, rules, data model, design tokens and production barriers, without touching production data.

evidence.heading: Turn a SaaS product into a build kit your team or your coding agent can ship.
evidence.text: **Study a web product through the browser, document how it works, and hand off everything needed to rebuild and launch it, without touching production data.** [](https://github.com/alextnetto/res/actions/workflows/test.yml) [](https://github.com/alextnetto/res/releases) [](#quick-start) [](LICENSE) [Quick start](#quick-start) · [How RES works](#how-res-works) · [What you get](#what-you-get) · [Examples](#examples) · [Safety model](#safety-model) · [FAQ](#faq) · [Documentation](#documentation) claude plugin marketplace add alextnetto/res > [!IMPORTANT] > RES drives a real browser on accounts you control. Use it only on products you are allowed to study, read the [safety model](#safety-model) before the first run, and prefer a trial account in a separate browser profile. --- Want to rebuild a product your team relies on, or launch a competitor in your market? Ask your agent to study it with RES. The agent explores the product in a test environment, records every change it makes, and writes what it learns to files: screens and states, business rules with evidence, the data model, API shapes, design tokens, and what could stop the clone from launching, such as integrations that need approval, licenses and certifications. At the end you get two files. `REPORT.html` is the report you read: one page that starts with the overview and the decisions you need to make, then walks through what the product does, every screen and rule, the data model and design, the build plan, and what to prepare before launch. The zip is for your coding agent: unzip it, give it the folder, and it starts from `BUILD.md`. RES is one agent skill with plain Markdown templates and a few dependency-free Node.js scripts. It adds about 130 tokens to every session and about 4,600

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
In a terminal:

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add alextnetto/res
```

```bash
claude plugin install res@res
```

Inside a Claude Code session, the same commands are `/plugin marketplace add alextnetto/res` and `/plugin install res@res`. Start a new session afterwards.

For other agents that read skills from disk, copy the skill folder where your agent reads skills:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/alextnetto/res.git && mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills && cp -R res/skills/reverse-engineering-saas ~/.claude/skills/
```

You need Node.js 22 or later and an agent that can drive a browser and run JavaScript in the page: Claude in Chrome, Playwright MCP or Chrome DevTools MCP.

evidence.heading: Prepare a safe environment
evidence.text:
Create a trial account of the product with an email you own, log in to it in a separate Chrome profile, and connect your agent's browser tool to that profile ([how](skills/reverse-engineering-saas/references/tools.md#separate-profile-for-l1)). This is the safest setup: the agent cannot reach your production account even by mistake.

Without a trial account, the agent writes only if you ask it to test or to create a test environment, and then only inside a separate workspace or a sandbox container. Otherwise it only observes.

evidence.heading: Use the scripts directly
evidence.text:
The scripts work without an agent, for example to inspect or repackage a knowledge base:

```bash
node skills/reverse-engineering-saas/scripts/init-kb.mjs --product "Acme CRM" --git
```

```bash
node skills/reverse-engineering-saas/scripts/check-kb.mjs re-acme-crm
```

```bash
node skills/reverse-engineering-saas/scripts/build-report.mjs re-acme-crm
```

```bash
node skills/reverse-engineering-saas/scripts/pack-kb.mjs re-acme-crm
```

Each script prints its options with `--help`.

evidence.heading: How RES works
evidence.text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Charter] --> B[Safe environmentand preflight]
    B --> C[Public docsand barrier scan]
    C --> D[Map screens]
    D --> E[Deep diveone feature at a time]
    E -->|next feature| E
    E --> F[Synthesis:PRD, parity, barriers]
    F --> G[Close:report and zip]
```

| Phase | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 Charter | Goal, scope, priorities and the clone's target market |
| 2 Environment | Pick the safest environment; check for automations, webhooks and integrations that could fire |
| 3 Recon | Public docs, API reference, pricing, integrations list and terms, read with web fetch; first barrier scan |
| 4 Map | Every screen and route; stack and design tokens |
| 5 Deep dive | One feature at a time: fixtures, states, rules, persistence, network, written to disk before the next feature |
| 6 Synthesis | Data model, design tokens, barriers, PRD, parity tests |
| 7 Close | Restore what changed, pass `check-kb`, send `REPORT.html` and the handoff zip |

The knowledge base on disk is the agent's only memory, so a study can span many sessions and survive context limits. Every statement carries its evidence: `[obs]` seen in the product, `[net]` captured on the network, `[doc]` from public documentation, `[inf]` an inference with an open question.

evidence.heading: Examples
evidence.text:
Two end-to-end studies, run by Claude Code with Claude in Chrome without a person at the keyboard:

| Product | Environment | Result | Read |
|---|---|---|---|
| ClickUp: board, task view, custom fields | L2, a new free workspace | 55 rules, 19 components, 14 production barriers | [Report](https://alextnetto.github.io/res/examples/clickup/REPORT.html) · [Knowledge base](examples/clickup/) |
| Pipedrive: pipeline, deals, next-activity rule, won and lost | L3, a sandbox pipeline in a production account, removed at the end | 46 rules, 8 components, 15 production barriers | [Report](https://alextnetto.github.io/res/examples/pipedrive/REPORT.html) · [Knowledge base](examples/pipedrive/) |

Each folder is the unzipped handoff. Notes on trademarks and terms: [examples/README.md](examples/README.md).

evidence.heading: Responsible use
evidence.text: Use RES only on accounts you own or are authorized to examine. Read the product's terms: many forbid reverse engineering or competing use, and that decision is yours. Rebuild from observed behavior; do not copy code, icons, illustrations, logos or long text. The barrier analysis is research, not legal advice.

> **设置 → 插件 → 添加插件**，在输入框里填 **`dsh-codex-effort-slider`**（包名，现在直接走 npm），
> 或填 `github:Microqian2th/dsh-codex-effort-slider`，点安装，**完全退出并重开** DSH Desktop。
> 装出来的就是上面那组真机截图的样子。

不想用 npm 也没问题 —— 下面两条路一样有效。

> 直接下载打包好的 zip：[**Releases → 最新版**](https://github.com/Microqian2th/dsh-codex-effort-slider/releases/latest)。

**只走 DSH Desktop 自己的插件面板**——命令行装不了 `desktop` profile：

```powershell
dsh plugin --profile desktop add link:"F:\Work Space\DeepSeek Harness\dsh-codex-effort-slider"
# error: profile "desktop" is managed exclusively by the Electron application
```

（这不是配置问题：`bin.js` 里对 `desktop` 直接 `program.error`，只有 Electron 应用本人被允许管理这个保留 profile。）

两条路：

1. **面板安装**（推荐）：**设置 → 插件 → 添加插件** → 填本地目录路径 → 安装 → 重启 DSH Desktop。
   面板会校验两件事，本插件都已满足：是有效的插件包、声明了组合包（`dsh.bundle.patch`）。
2. **手工安装**（当面板本身不可用时——例如 `profileContext` 没挂上，`dsh-base` 会把
   `plugin-manager` 整行 `disabled`，设置侧栏里就看不到「插件」）：
   备份 profile 的 `package.json` → 加一条 `link:` 依赖 → `dsh.profile.bundles` 追加本包名 →
   在 `profiles/<profile>/node_modules/` 下建一个指向本目录的 junction → 重启。

> 卸载用面板；手工装的用 `cmd /c rmdir <junction>`（**不要**用 `Remove-Item -Recurse`，
> 那可能顺着 junction 把插件目录里的文件删掉）。

想先看观感、不装也行：`node preview/make-preview.mjs` 生成 `preview/panel.html`，
用浏览器打开即可拖动、切浅深色、切 4/2/6 档模型（页面里连官方菜单外壳都复刻了，
CSS 与拖动数学都是从真产物抽出来的）。

evidence.heading: 打包
evidence.text:
```powershell
npm run pack      # = powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File pack-dist.ps1
```

解开就能装，接收方不需要 `pnpm install`。若要让人从 GitHub / npm 装，把**本目录的内容**推到仓库根

evidence.heading: 它怎么工作（两半）
evidence.text:
| 半边 | 干什么 |
|---|---|
| `lib/index.js`（宿主） | 空逻辑 + 一次客户端产物静态核对。存在的唯一理由是让本包成为 cordis 树上的一行，否则 `dsh.client` 的 bundle 不会被扫进启动图 |
| `lib/client.js`（客户端） | 一个不可见锚点（注册进 `conversation.input.right`，用来拿 `sessionId` 与 `ctx`）+ **DOM 桥** + 滑条（`react-dom` portal 注入官方那一行） |

evidence.heading: 已知限制
evidence.text:
- 需要重启 DSH Desktop 才生效（客户端 bundle 在启动时注入）。
- 控制项活在官方菜单里，所以**必须先点开模型菜单**才能改档位；输入框工具行上没有常驻读数。
- 依赖官方菜单的 DOM 语义属性。官方若改成非 `menuitem` 结构、去掉 `aria-controls`、
  或不再用 `data-composer-card`，本插件会**静默退回"什么都不做"**（官方菜单照常可用）。
- 那一行加高约 20px + 滑条 28px，菜单总高会变大；官方会自己重测位置，但极小屏幕上可能出现
  菜单贴边（官方自身的 `max-height` 与夹取逻辑仍在）。
- 主题令牌缺失时回退到中性灰 + `#4d93f8` 蓝，观感可用但不如在 DSH 内贴合。

English | [简体中文](README.zh-CN.md) | [中文功能与实测网站](https://luobosibing2.github.io/dsh-jev-plugin/)

**Native DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plugin with Jev or Luna Decisions as its judgment model.**

`deepseek-harness-jev` connects [DeepSeek Harness (DSH)](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) to [Jev by TypeSafe AI](https://typesafe.ai/) for agent skill and file selection, task supervision, shared-finding corrections, tool-output filtering, single-operation approval assistance, and historical stage navigation. The main model continues to plan, generate answers, and call native tools. Enabled features use the saved Jev or Luna Decisions connection at DSH extension points for skill catalogs, agent lifecycle, tool results, and approvals, then apply results according to each feature. DSH configures the main model separately. Integration uses public Cordis / DSH plugin APIs without modifying the host source.

This is an independent community project, not an official DeepSeek or Jev release. It is an early-stage plugin with a bounded [DSH compatibility range](#install-through-the-web-ui-recommended); its APIs and model judgments are not a correctness guarantee.

The [Chinese feature website](https://luobosibing2.github.io/dsh-jev-plugin/) explains each DSH integration point, the information sent to the judgment service, and the observed test cases and limits.

The Chinese [principles and all features explainer](https://luobosibing2.github.io/dsh-jev-plugin/explainers/dsh-jev-plugin.html) covers all 12 features and includes a complete skill-selection input/output example. Its [Markdown source](docs/explainers/dsh-jev-plugin.md) is maintained in this repository.

evidence.heading: What is included?
evidence.text:
The plugin provides the following features. **Every feature is independently disabled by default.** Installing the package does not enable them.

| Feature | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Skill selection | Recommends up to the configured number of skills whose relevance probability reaches the minimum; a successful judgment can recommend none. The main agent still loads the original skill. |
| File ranking | Ranks the original `glob` path results without another filesystem scan or file-content read. |
| Drift reminders | Checks progress between model steps and can deliver one nonblocking reminder. |
| Completion checks | Checks the current turn's requirements, latest Todo and final answer, with at most 3 automatic supplements by default. |
| Goal supervision | Checks native goal completion and pauses after a configurable run of rounds without progress. |
| Instruction guidance | Reads current user instructions and applicable agent rules, then supplies a nonblocking reminder when needed. |
| Interjection routing | Routes a running user's correction to the next step; queues other messages for a later turn. |
| Shared-finding corrections | Compares reports and messages already shared, then sends corrections to affected recipients. |
| Long-log admission | Can remove clearly unneeded progress or repeated notices after a command returns, with an original-output recovery reference. |
| Test-log admission | Protects failures, summaries, named and slow tests while judging whether ordinary passing details are needed. |
| Workspace approval | In `workspace-write`, can answer eligible native single-operation escalation requests; non-affirmative answers return to human approval. |
| Stage navigation | Classifies complete recorded model steps on request, then links consecutive stag

evidence.heading: Completion checks
evidence.text:
An enabled ordinary root turn is checked at its normal stopping point only if it used Todo during that turn. Pending items and a later empty list still qualify. A turn without Todo skips the check, and a Todo update during execution does not start a check. Native Goal turns retain their own supervision.

The judgment receives the current turn's original user request and later adjustments, the complete latest Todo, and the latest final answer. It excludes raw tool results, reasoning and earlier turns. A new turn saying only “continue” does not automatically import the previous task. While the feature is enabled, a short model instruction asks for actual actions, paths, commands and observed results in existing Todo content; it adds no Todo fields or requirement to create a list for a simple task.

One judgment request asks two Choice questions: `assessment` chooses `complete`, `omission`, `contradiction`, `needs-user` or `unknown`; `focus` selects an existing requirement, Todo item or final-answer reference. `complete` means the supplied report appears to meet the requirements. It does not independently verify code, artifacts or execution facts. Each check identifies only the most important issue.

`omission`, `contradiction` and valid `unknown` share the profile's **Maximum automatic supplement rounds** setting (`maxSupplementRounds`), default 3. The initial check is separate: a limit of N permits at most N automatic supplements and N+1 normal checks; the default permits 3 supplements and 4 normal checks. `complete` ends normally, `needs-user` stops for the user's decision, and an unresolved result at the limit ends with that last conclusion. Supplements stay in the same turn and retain existing authorization.

evidence.heading: Install through the Web UI (recommended)
evidence.text:
Supported DSH releases are **0.1.7-rc.1, 0.1.7-rc.2, 0.2.0-rc.1, 0.2.0-rc.2, 0.2.1-alpha.2, 0.2.1-alpha.3 and 0.2.1-rc.2**. The package declares `>=0.1.7-rc.1 <=0.2.0-rc.2 || 0.2.1-alpha.2 || 0.2.1-alpha.3 || 0.2.1-rc.2`; other releases, including 0.2.1-alpha.1, are outside this declaration. Install directly from the GitHub repository URL. No source checkout, manual packaging, or npm login is required.

1. Open **Plugins in the sidebar → Add plugin**.
2. Paste the GitHub URL below into **Package name or address**, then click **Install**.
3. Click **Enable now** after installation. Restart the current profile only if DSH says it will load on the next start.
4. Select **View @dsh-jev/plugin** in the installed plugin list to open its Jev page. Configure the endpoint, model, and API key, then enable the individual features you need.

```text
https://github.com/luobosibing2/deepseek-harness-jev
```



*Paste the repository URL into “Package name or address”, then click Install.*

**Enabling the package does not enable its 12 Jev features; they remain off by default.** Installation applies to the Host profile serving the current Web UI. The Host needs pnpm and access to GitHub. The repository includes the plugin entry and prebuilt files, so installation does not compile source on the user's machine or require an npm registry publication.

The GitHub entry provides the `main` features, not experimental branches. The older [v0.1.0 release](https://github.com/luobosibing2/deepseek-harness-jev/releases/tag/v0.1.0) does not include the newly integrated log filters. Build from source below only when changing or building the code yourself.

evidence.heading: Install from source (developers)
evidence.text: Use the following steps when modifying or building the plugin yourself. Existing DSH Web users can install using the GitHub URL above.

evidence.heading: Build requirements
evidence.text:
- Node.js **24.11 or later** is recommended; the publication build is checked on Node 24.14.1.
- pnpm **11.7.0** available on `PATH`.
- Development baseline: DeepSeek Harness CLI and development packages **0.2.1-rc.2**, with Cordis **4.0.5**. These exact build versions are separate from the supported installation range above. Use the explicit version below because npm's `latest` tag can point to a different release.
- A configured main-model provider in DSH, plus credentials for your selected Jev-compatible System One service or Luna API.

Legacy DSH support covers installing and running the built package. Source builds and TypeScript consumers of the generated Remote declarations use the rc.2 development baseline.

If needed, install the tools:

```sh
npm install --global pnpm@11.7.0 @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.1-rc.2
```

evidence.heading: Behavior and limitations
evidence.text:
- **Reminders are advisory.** Drift and instruction guidance do not block or cancel tools, and do not force the main model to comply. Evidence questions retain at least two choices even with one reference or no textual requirements; an uncertainty choice cannot supply a correction's supporting reference.
- **Completion checks in a fixed 16-slot diagnosis.** With scripted initial errors, real Jev judgments and DeepSeek supplements met the core requirements in 6/6 enabled error cases; 2/2 accurate enabled controls were judged complete without a supplement. See the [new results](docs/testing/2026-10-05-completion-recovery/public-results.zh-CN.md). Those trials used the earlier recorded-evidence semantics and do not establish real-task results for lightweight report checks. This diagnosis does not establish a natural-task error rate or average coding benefit. In an earlier long coding trial, the default evidence budget cropped the original requirement, leading to zero adopted judgments and zero automatic supplements before manual Retry/Cancel; see the [historical report](docs/testing/2026-10-02-completion-skill/README.md).
- **Approvals remain single-operation.** Workspace approval neither changes the session's sandbox mode nor overrides fixed host checks. Operation paths and direct-script evidence follow the current native working directory, including relative shell `workdir` overrides; the original workspace remains the sandbox boundary. `approve` can supply `allowed-once`; `unauthorized` or `unknown` returns to the original human approval flow. Technical failures retain manual Retry/Cancel.
- **Shared corrections have a limited scope.** They process already-shared reports and messages, not every agent's private exploration. Automatic delivery targets the live root agent

github_projects.name: Veda-on-ComfyUI
github_projects.description: Veda Sparse Attention for ComfyUI
github_projects.description_zh: ComfyUI 的 Veda 稀疏注意力

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Veda Sparse Attention for ComfyUI

evidence.heading: Veda Sparse Attention for ComfyUI (MiniMax-H3)
evidence.text: [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30325) · [Project Page](https://veda-sparse.github.io/) · [Predictor](https://huggingface.co/Veda-Sparse/Minimax-H3-T2VA-Veda-8NFE-600Step-Preview) · [Training Code](https://github.com/veda-sparse/Miowtion) · [中文说明](README.zh-CN.md)

evidence.heading: Introduction
evidence.text:
**Veda** is a learned sparse-attention method for video diffusion models.
Attention dominates the cost of a long clip, and a small distilled
predictor can say in advance which tiles of the attention map carry the
result. Veda computes roughly the top 10% of them and skips the rest.

This repository packages Veda as a custom node for ComfyUI's native
MiniMax-H3 (T2VA, FL2VA and R2VA): one node, MODEL in and MODEL out.

evidence.heading: Highlights
evidence.text:
- **Faster inference.** 2.9x end to end and 7.1x on attention alone
  against ComfyUI's default attention, measured on an RTX 5070. The gain
  grows with clip length.
- **Plug-and-play.** An attention override rather than a weight patch, so
  Turbo and style LoRAs, fine-tuned and quantized H3 checkpoints,
  first/last-frame and reference conditioning, and other block patches
  keep working.
- **Never silently off.** Every kernel passes a self-test on the GPU
  before it is used. When Veda cannot run, the prompt stops with the
  reason instead of quietly rendering without acceleration: a missing
  package or a node in the wrong place comes with the fix, anything else
  with a ready-to-paste report for a GitHub issue.
- **Nothing extra to install.** The sparse kernel ships with the node;
  installing from the Comfy Registry pulls in Triton (NVIDIA SM80 and
  newer, AMD RDNA3 / RDNA4 on ROCm) or MLX (Apple silicon).

evidence.heading: Installation
evidence.text:
Requires ComfyUI >= 0.38.0. In ComfyUI Manager, search "Veda". Or:

```bash
comfy node install veda-sparse-attention
```

Or clone this repository into `ComfyUI/custom_nodes/` and restart ComfyUI.

evidence.heading: Usage
evidence.text:
Open *Workflow -> Browse Templates -> Veda-on-ComfyUI* and pick "Veda
MiniMax H3 T2VA" or "Veda MiniMax H3 R2VA". The missing-model dialog
offers the predictor. Write a prompt and run.

To add Veda to an existing H3 workflow, put **Veda Sparse Attention
(MiniMax H3)** on the MODEL wire after the model and any LoRA loaders,
last before the guider or sampler. Select it and press **Ctrl+B** to
bypass it and render the same seed with full attention.

Do not combine it with ComfyUI's own "Model Sparse Attention" node on H3:
that one replaces the attention blocks outright, so Veda would never be
called. The node says so when it sees both.

Other attention nodes can stay. Veda runs on top of "Patch Sage Attention
KJ" (the calls it does not take go to sage), and KJNodes' "MiniMax H3 Low
VRAM Attention" keeps working. A node that swaps out the whole H3
attention, such as "MiniMax H3 Mem Eff Sage Attention Patch", must come
*before* Veda: Veda then runs the sparse layers and leaves that node the
full-attention ones, and says so on its node. Placed after Veda it would
hide every call from Veda; the node warns about that too.

evidence.heading: Predictor
evidence.text:
The node does not download anything itself. The predictor (275 MB)
reaches `models/veda` one of two ways:

* **From a template.** Open one of the Veda templates and ComfyUI offers
  the predictor in its missing-models dialog; one click fetches it.
* **By hand.** Download the predictor for your task into
  `ComfyUI/models/veda/` and restart ComfyUI:
  [T2VA / FL2VA](https://huggingface.co/Veda-Sparse/Minimax-H3-T2VA-Veda-8NFE-600Step-Preview)
  (`minimax_h3_t2va_veda_8nfe_600step_preview_fp8.safetensors`) or
  [R2VA](https://huggingface.co/Veda-Sparse/Minimax-H3-R2VA-Veda-Preview)
  (`minimax_h3_r2va_veda_preview_fp8.safetensors`), which is trained on
  the reference task and used by the R2VA template.

Any `.safetensors` in that folder appears in the `predictor` list, so a
predictor trained elsewhere is selected the same way. If the selected
file is not there, the node says so and prints the URL rather than
reaching out on its own.

evidence.heading: Node text
evidence.text:
```
Veda done · Triton INT8 (SM120)
Video: 1344x768 · 5.2 s
Attention computed: 10.9% of full attention (89.1% skipped)
```

Before sampling the node names the kernel it will use and the sparsity;
while sampling, the video size and the trained tile plan it matched; at
the end, how much of full attention was actually computed. If Veda
cannot run, the prompt stops with an error that says why; `nearest
trained size: ...` on the tile plan line means the video is outside the
trained set. `verbose` adds per-phase timing, call counts and predictor
details.

Warnings and errors come in English and Chinese, one after the other;
the node's name and tooltips follow ComfyUI's interface language.

kind_reason.text: 封装学习式稀疏注意力的 ComfyUI 节点。

summary.text: 为 MiniMax H3 用小型预测器选择重要注意力块，只计算约前10%，以 MODEL 输入输出节点接入现有工作流。

value.text: 降低长视频注意力计算量，并提供可观察的稀疏度与失败原因。

outcome.text: 作者报告 RTX 5070 上端到端加速2.9倍、注意力部分7.1倍。

mechanism.text: 覆盖注意力计算而不修改模型权重，GPU kernel 先自测；预测器匹配训练 tile 计划，结束展示实际计算比例。

inspiration.text: 可让加速路径先自测并显示实际工作量，失败时明确停止而不悄然关闭优化。

limitations.text: 需 ComfyUI 0.38+ 与匹配预测器；不要叠加自带 Sparse Attention 节点，速度数字仅针对报告设备。

how_to.text: 安装节点及对应预测器，置于模型与 LoRA 后、guider 或 sampler 前；可旁路以同种子比较全注意力。

github_projects.description: Component layer for AI agents: implementation-aware contracts for building project-native interface components.
github_projects.description_zh: AI 智能体组件层：用于构建项目原生接口组件的实现感知契约。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Component layer for AI agents: implementation-aware contracts for building project-native interface components.

evidence.heading: Bricks: Component Layer for AI Agents
evidence.text:
[](LICENSE)
[](https://github.com/kostja94/bricks/stargazers)
[](https://github.com/kostja94/bricks/commits/main)

Bricks gives coding agents implementation-aware contracts for building interface components that belong in an existing product, codebase, and design system.

It helps an agent understand a component's responsibility, context, variants, content, interaction states, technical boundary, and verification requirements before writing code.

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
```bash
npx skills add kostja94/bricks --skill component-builder
```

Give the agent a bounded component task and the context needed to integrate it:

```text
Use component-builder to build the footer for this bilingual SaaS site.

Read the existing routes, components, design tokens, framework, and responsive conventions first. Reuse project primitives, include the real product, resource, company, and legal destinations, and verify keyboard access on mobile and desktop.
```

See the complete [Footer request example](examples/footer-request.md).

evidence.heading: Why Bricks Exists
evidence.text:
Agents are already capable of writing component code. The harder problem is deciding what the component is responsible for and making it fit the product around it.

A generated Footer may invent routes. A FAQ may hide answers from assistive technology. A Task Input may omit loading, cancellation, invalid input, or result recovery. An Agent Workspace may look convincing in a demo while having no workable boundary between conversation, tools, artifacts, and user control.

Bricks addresses that reasoning layer. It guides the agent toward a project-native implementation instead of shipping an isolated demo or importing a second design system by habit.

evidence.heading: What Bricks Is
evidence.text:
| Bricks provides | Bricks does not provide |
|-----------------|-------------------------|
| One maintained contract per component concept | A separate Skill for every visual style |
| Semantic responsibility and ownership boundaries | A fixed React, Vue, or CSS component package |
| Context-aware variants and expected states | A universal design system |
| Integration and verification guidance | A gallery of interchangeable mockups |
| Stable component IDs for Agent tooling | Permission to replace project conventions |

One component can have many valid designs. Bricks keeps Footer guidance in one reference and lets the target product determine its layout, typography, density, content, and implementation.

evidence.heading: Component Coverage
evidence.text:
The catalog spans small primitives, content structures, conversion elements, and composed Agent interfaces:

| Group | Representative components |
|-------|---------------------------|
| Navigation and orientation | Navigation Menu, Footer, Breadcrumb, Sidebar, Table of Contents |
| Content and explanation | Article Content Layout, Author Bio, FAQ Section, How-to Section, Tabs, Accordion |
| Conversion and trust | CTA, Newsletter Signup, Comparison Table, Testimonials, Trust Signals |
| Layout and presentation | Card, Grid, List, Masonry, Carousel, Modal, Announcement Banner |
| Agent and tool interfaces | Task Input, Conversation, Chat Panel, Agent Workspace, CMS Editor Workspace |

Browse the machine-readable inventory in [`catalog/components.json`](catalog/components.json). Component IDs remain stable while their references can grow as new contexts and constraints are learned.

evidence.heading: From Request to Integrated Component
evidence.text:
The `component-builder` does not begin with a preferred library or visual treatment.

1. It inspects the page, nearby components, tokens, dependencies, data model, responsive conventions, and tests.
2. It identifies the canonical component concept, user task, surface, and ownership boundary.
3. It loads only the matching component reference and shared quality gates.
4. It selects a variant from real content and context.
5. It reuses the project's primitives and implements required states and interactions.
6. It verifies the component inside its actual page, not only in an isolated preview.

For components with complex domain behavior, such as editors, data grids, charts, calendars, or accessibility primitives, the agent should use a proven library when the project does not already provide one.

evidence.heading: Context Matters
evidence.text:
The same component identity changes meaning across surfaces and pages.

- A public marketing Footer organizes product, resource, company, and legal destinations.
- An authenticated application Footer may be absent or reduced to operational links.
- A documentation Sidebar needs hierarchy, active state, deep navigation, and narrow-screen behavior.
- A dashboard Sidebar must also account for permissions, workspaces, collapsed states, and task frequency.

Bricks records these contextual decisions without turning every combination into a new component name.

evidence.heading: Quick start
evidence.text: Choose one backend, then run the Python example below.

evidence.heading: Option A: PyTorch
evidence.text:
For NVIDIA GPUs. Supports text, images and video.

```bash
pip install "qev[torch] @ git+https://github.com/OmniJev/OneJev.git"
qev serve --model OmniJev/OneJev1.6-4B --port 8000
```

evidence.heading: Option B: llama.cpp
evidence.text:
For GGUF models. Supports text and images; use PyTorch for video. Install
[llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/install.md) first (`brew install llama.cpp` on macOS).

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/OmniJev/OneJev.git
qev serve --gguf mradermacher/OneJev1.6-0.8B-GGUF:Q8_0 --port 8000
```

evidence.heading: Option C: Docker
evidence.text:
The repo ships a Compose stack that detects your hardware and starts one backend.
The llama.cpp profiles download `mradermacher/OneJev1.6-0.8B-GGUF:Q8_0` on first start; set `QEV_GGUF` in `docker/.env`
for another size or quant.

```bash
cp docker/.env.example docker/.env   # set HF_TOKEN for gated/private repos
./docker/start.sh                    # auto-detect (Windows: .\docker\start.ps1)
./docker/start.sh logs               # follow logs
./docker/start.sh down               # stop every profile
```

Force a backend with `./docker/start.sh <torch|rocm|vulkan|gguf|gguf-rocm|cpu>`
(add `--build` to rebuild). Every profile serves the API and the playground on :8000.
On Windows only `torch` (NVIDIA) and `cpu` are available.

evidence.heading: Which picture model to use: the evidence
evidence.text:
**The test:** a shootout on 2026-10-16 with Studio 2.8.1, run on a Mac Studio M5 Ultra and one DGX Spark.
- **Pictures:** 8 prompts × 2 seeds × 4 models × 2 machines = **128 pictures at 1344x768, 0 failed jobs**.
- **Judging:** by eye, from the full-size pictures.
- **Full report:** every grid, the raw numbers and the method are in
  **[docs/picture-shootout.md](docs/picture-shootout.md)**.

**Speed and memory**, per picture with the model loaded (median):

| Model | Mac M5 Ultra | DGX Spark | Peak memory (Mac / Spark) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen 2.1 Turbo, 8 steps | **4.7 s** | 8.6 s | 33 / 31 GB |
| Qwen 2.1 Full, 40 steps at CFG 4 | 43.3 s | 80.1 s | 33 / 30 GB |
| FLUX3-K Fast, 16 steps | 9.8 s | 10.5 s | 38 / 37 GB |
| FLUX3-K Full, 50 steps | 59.9 s | 58.7 s | 40 / 37 GB |
| FLUX3-K prompt upsampler, once per prompt | 5.2 s | 12.5 s | |

- **Qwen:** runs about 2x faster a step on the M5 Ultra.
- **FLUX3-K:** runs at the same speed on both machines.

**Quality, the winner per prompt:**

| Prompt | Winner | The evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Poster with title and tagline | Qwen 2.1 Full | Most coherent scene. All 32 posters, every model, spelled both lines exactly |
| Photoreal portrait | Qwen 2.1 Full | Real skin and the whole face. FLUX3-K cropped off the mouth in 8 of 8 |
| Character turnaround | Qwen 2.1 Full, narrowly | Gear consistent across views. FLUX3-K wins for a labelled line-art sheet |
| Crowded night market | FLUX3-K Full | Lanterns, steam, mostly real words on signs. Qwen drew pseudo-script |
| "Red cube on a blue sphere, left of a green pyramid" | FLUX3-K Fast | Right in **8 of 8**; Qwen 2 of 8 |
| Food photography | FLUX3-K Fast | More professional styling. No model reliably drew the three pancakes asked for |
| Watercolor | FLUX3-K Full | Truest washes

evidence.heading: Upgrade an existing install (DGX Spark)
evidence.text:
```bash
cd Imagination-Studio-by-keys-Wasserman && git pull
bash oneshot-setup.sh --upgrade  # on Linux: oneshot-setup-spark.sh --upgrade
bash scripts/app.sh              # restart the app on the new version
```

`--upgrade` moves an existing install to the version of the clone: the environment's packages, ComfyUI at its pinned
commit, the engines (rebuilt or taken from the carrier only when their pinned commit changed), every optional part
already installed (Ref2VA, FLUX3-K, MOSS-Image, Music, Voice, sound, Bolt, training), the Motion Previs environment,
which it adds when it is missing, and motion graphics and Finish, which it adds to an install from before 3.2.0
(`--no-graphics`, `--no-finish` leave them out). Worker Sparks then take the head's code with **Sparks → Update and
start**. It **fetches no weights** (a model that is not on disk is named and left out; an image-only
install stays image-only), does not touch `~/ImaginationStudio` (clips, projects, LoRAs, settings), prints the version
before and after, and ends with `--verify`. Running it a second time changes nothing. Restart the app afterwards
(`bash scripts/app.sh`) so it serves the new pages. Run it when no clip is rendering.


The installer takes the prebuilt engine from the carrier image when Docker is there, and otherwise builds it from
source (`spark/build-engine.sh`: it fetches Zig 0.17.0 and the engine's source,
[drowzeys/TensorFold `h3-1.0.4`](https://github.com/drowzeys/TensorFold/tree/h3-1.0.4), and needs the CUDA toolkit's
`nvcc`, 12.9 or newer). Without it the Studio still works on ComfyUI's own blocks, slower.

Measured on one DGX Spark (2026-10-09, one run each; 124 frames, text to video, models already loaded):

| Size | Passes | TensorFold engine (int8) | A pass | ComfyUI's own blocks (bf16)

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
1. **You write two prompts**: what the picture shows, and what happens in the clip (action, spoken or sung words,
   sound).
2. **Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo makes the first frame** from the first prompt, in about 9 seconds (8 steps). Or it
   makes several scouts for you to choose from.
3. **MiniMax H3 animates that frame** from the second prompt, with sound, in one of two modes:
   - **Standard (Turbo 5).** The Turbo adapter denoises picture and sound together in 5 passes. The adapter is then
     dropped and the base model denoises the sound again from scratch, 20 steps, with the finished picture held
     fixed. Each of those steps recomputes only the audio rows (about 4% of the sequence) against the picture's
     stored attention keys and values, so 20 steps cost less than one full pass.
   - **High quality (`QUALITY=high`).** The base model denoises picture and sound together for 20 steps, no adapter.
     About three times slower; calmer motion, softer picture, and the sound the standard mode's audio step is
     borrowed from.
4. **The decoders finish it.** The video decoder turns latents into frames, optionally at twice the size (the 2x
   decoder, for 2K). The audio decoder's output is kept clear of clipping, and a take that comes out thin gets its
   bass lifted.

Both transformers, the samplers, the adapter merges, the audio step, the int8 kernels and the image and video
decoders run in TensorFold on MLX.

**Scout, pick, animate, finish in 2K.** Six scout images from one prompt in 27 seconds; pick one; MiniMax H3 animates
it with sound and a 2x decoder finishes it in 2K: an 8 second clip at 2048x1152 in five minutes, or at 2560x1440 in
under eleven. A 1344x768 draft of the same 8 seconds takes 108 seconds.

github_projects.name: cjkfold
github_projects.description: Fold look-alike CJK glyphs (Kangxi radicals, CJK radical supplements) so text extracted from PDFs matches again.
github_projects.description_zh: 将形似汉字的 CJK 部首字符（康熙部首和部首补充）归一，修复 PDF 提取文本的匹配问题。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Fold look-alike CJK glyphs (Kangxi radicals, CJK radical supplements) so text extracted from PDFs matches again.

evidence.heading: cjkfold
evidence.text:
[](https://github.com/cdcailf/cjkfold/actions/workflows/tests.yml)

Text pulled out of a PDF often contains characters that **look** like ordinary
Han characters but are not them. Comparison against them quietly fails.

```
⻆  U+2EC6  CJK RADICAL SIMPLIFIED HORN   renders as  角  U+89D2
⾊  U+2F8A  KANGXI RADICAL COLOR          renders as  色  U+8272
⺮  U+2EAE  CJK RADICAL BAMBOO            folds to    𥫗  U+25AD7
```

`cjkfold` folds them back onto the characters you meant:

```python
from cjkfold import fold

fold("标准颜⾊值与⻆色按钮")
# '标准颜色值与角色按钮'

"颜色" in "标准颜⾊值"          # False  ← the bug
"颜色" in fold("标准颜⾊值")     # True
```

Zero runtime dependencies. Pure functions. Python 3.9+.

---

**背景阅读 / Background:** [PDF 抽出来的中文，为什么搜不到](docs/why-cjk-text-breaks.md)
—— 完整的排查经过（中文），包括我自己踩的四个坑。
社区版：[掘金](https://juejin.cn/post/7695671592383807542)

**Built on this:** [corpusfold](https://github.com/cdcailf/corpusfold) — this
character layer wired into a full PDF → knowledge-base pipeline (抽取 / 分栏 /
表格 / 分块 / 混合检索).

evidence.heading: The problem
evidence.text:
Nothing raises. The text displays correctly, because the glyphs really are
identical. What breaks is everything downstream that compares characters:

- `"紫色" in text` returns `False` for a document that shows 紫色
- a keyword search misses
- a vector retriever ranks an unrelated *short* document above the one that
  contains the query verbatim, because a short document's embedding is tighter
  and scores a higher cosine — measured on a real corpus, the relevant document
  scored **0.29** against a decoy's **0.36**
- deduplication, caching and ground-truth checks all start disagreeing

evidence.heading: Why NFKC is not enough
evidence.text:
The reflex is `unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text)`. It handles the **Kangxi
Radicals** block completely — all 214 characters carry compatibility
decompositions — and then stops:

| Block | Characters | Repaired by NFKC | Repaired by cjkfold |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kangxi Radicals `U+2F00–U+2FDF` | 214 | **214** | 214 |
| CJK Radicals Supplement `U+2E80–U+2EFF` | 115 | **2** | **114** |

Unicode withholds compatibility mappings in the supplement block *on purpose*:
those glyphs are distinct encoded radicals, not compatibility variants of an
existing character. So NFKC leaves 113 of the 115 standing.

`cjkfold` closes that gap with the `EquivalentUnifiedIdeograph` property from
the Unicode Character Database (Unicode 15.1+), which maps 114 of them onto a
unified ideograph. The one remainder, `⺀ U+2E80 CJK RADICAL REPEAT`, has no
ideograph equivalent and is left alone.

evidence.heading: The characters that never show up
evidence.text:
There is a second family, and it is harder to catch. A zero-width space leaves no
glyph at all, so two strings that differ only by it look identical:

    数据
    数\u200b据

```python
"数\u200b据" == "数据"                                  # False
unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", "数\u200b据") == "数据"     # False as well
```

`fold()` does not repair these, deliberately: half the family is load-bearing. ZWJ
`U+200D` is what holds an emoji sequence together — 👨‍👩‍👧 is five code points rendered as
one glyph, and deleting the joiners does not tidy the text up, it turns one family
into three people.

`check` looks for the first family only, so a file full of zero-width spaces comes
back `clean`. `scan` looks at every family and says what to do with each finding:

```
$ cjkfold scan document.txt
document.txt  21 characters  5 findings

  lookalike  1
      1:4  U+2F8A  -> 色 U+8272                   fold   (KANGXI RADICAL COLOR)
           renders exactly like 色, but sits on a separate kangxi code point

  compat  1
      2:5  U+FF21  -> A U+0041                    nfkc   (FULLWIDTH LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A)
           NFKC would rewrite this; fold() leaves it alone on purpose, so the decision stays with the caller

  invisible  3
      3:2  U+200B  ZERO WIDTH SPACE               strip
           prints as nothing at all -- two strings that differ only by this character look identical
      4:2  U+200D  ZERO WIDTH JOINER              manual
           zero width joiner: it holds emoji sequences together -- a family of three is five code points, and deleting the joiners leaves three separate people
      4:4  U+200D  ZERO WIDTH JOINER              manual
           (same character as 4:2)

  fixable   lookalike: fold    compat: nfkc    invisible: strip, manual
  see also  cjkfold scan --cl

evidence.heading: Usage
evidence.text:
```python
from cjkfold import fold, has_lookalikes, iter_lookalikes

fold("紫⾊的⻆落")            # '紫色的角落'
fold("普通文本")              # unchanged; returns the same object

has_lookalikes("⻆")           # True
has_lookalikes("角")           # False

for item in iter_lookalikes("第一行\n第⼆行⻆"):
    print(item)
# 2:2  ⼆ U+2F06 -> 二 U+4E8C  (KANGXI RADICAL TWO)
# 2:4  ⻆ U+2EC6 -> 角 U+89D2  (CJK RADICAL SIMPLIFIED HORN)
```

`fold()` is idempotent, and it is deliberately **not** an NFKC pass: it will
not touch full-width punctuation (`，` `；` `（` `）`), compatibility characters
or ligatures, so it is safe to apply to text that is still going to be stored or
displayed. Combine with NFKC yourself if you want both:

```python
import unicodedata
clean = fold(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text))
```

evidence.heading: The other two rewrites
evidence.text:
`fold()` is no longer the only write, but it is still the only one the command line
will do for you. The other two are explicit API calls, and that is on purpose:
`fold -w` already rewrites files in place, and two more destructive operations
behind flags would be a loaded gun pointed at a corpus.

```python
from cjkfold import fold, normalize, strip_invisible

fold("标准颜⾊值")                          # '标准颜色值'  the look-alike layer
normalize("Ａ，b")                          # 'A，b'        NFKC, punctuation spared
normalize("Ａ，b", keep_punctuation=False)   # 'A,b'         ...or not spared

FAMILY = "\U0001F468\u200D\U0001F469\u200D\U0001F467"   # 5 code points, one glyph

strip_invisible("数\u200b据")               # '数据'        safe: ZWSP, BOM, soft hyphen, word joiner
strip_invisible(FAMILY)                    # unchanged     -- the joiners carry meaning
strip_invisible(FAMILY, policy="all")      # 3 code points -- three separate people
```

`normalize()` spares full-width punctuation by default, because NFKC turns `，`
into `,` — that rewrites the sentence rather than repairing it. `strip_invisible()`
defaults to `safe`, because the other half of the invisible family is load-bearing;
there is no `policy="smart"`, because no such thing exists.

The modules are `cjkfold.folding` and `cjkfold.rewrite`, so that every name means
exactly one thing: `cjkfold.normalize` is the function, `cjkfold.folding` is the
module. Until 0.4.0 both were called `normalize`, which made
`import cjkfold.normalize as m` hand you a function instead of the module — and
`import a.b as c` means `c = a.b`, so `m.fold` raised `AttributeError`. Renaming
the module is what fixed it.

evidence.heading: Command line
evidence.text:
```bash
cjkfold check document.txt      # report look-alikes, exit 1 if any (CI-friendly)
cjkfold check --quiet docs/*.txt
cjkfold scan document.txt       # report every class of finding, exit 0 (it is a report)
cjkfold scan corpus/            # walk a directory; non-text files are skipped and counted
cjkfold scan --strict corpus.txt    # ...or exit 1 when a foldable/compat character is found
cjkfold scan --json corpus.txt  # one JSON object per file
cjkfold fold document.txt       # print the folded text
cjkfold fold -w document.txt    # rewrite in place
cat document.txt | cjkfold check -
```

Exit codes: `0` clean, `1` look-alike characters found (`check`), or findings under
`scan --strict`, `2` the input is not a text file (or not UTF-8) and nothing was
scanned. `2` is separate from `1` on purpose — "I found something" and "I could not
look" are different answers. Pass a PDF and it will say so and hand you the
`pdftotext` command, instead of reporting phantom findings from binary data. `scan`
finds things and still exits `0`; the section above is why.

```
$ cjkfold check extracted.txt
extracted.txt: 3 look-alike character(s) (1 kangxi, 2 radical-supplement)
    1:4  ⾊ U+2F8A -> 色 U+8272  (KANGXI RADICAL COLOR)
    1:7  ⻆ U+2EC6 -> 角 U+89D2  (CJK RADICAL SIMPLIFIED HORN)
    2:5  ⺮ U+2EAE -> 𥫗 U+25AD7  (CJK RADICAL BAMBOO)

3 character(s) would change under `cjkfold fold`.
```

Drop `cjkfold check` into an ingest pipeline to catch extraction regressions
before they reach the index.

kind_reason.text: 修复 PDF 提取文本中的 CJK 同形字符的库与 CLI。

summary.text: 将 PDF 文本中看似汉字的部首码点归一到对应字符，修复关键词匹配、去重和检索中的隐性差异。

value.text: 识别肉眼难以发现的 Unicode 差异，避免文档显示正确但字符比较失败。

mechanism.text: 针对康熙部首与 CJK 部首补充做显式映射，提供幂等 fold、位置报告与 CLI 检查；其他归一操作单独暴露。

inspiration.text: 可把文本清洗分为可解释步骤，并在检索前保留码点级诊断报告。

limitations.text: fold 故意不处理不可见字符或做全量 NFKC，部分连接符承担 emoji 等语义，不能一概删除。

how_to.text: 先用 cjkfold check 或 scan 查看报告，再对需要的文本调用 fold。
