github_projects.description: 让 AI 读懂你在 B 站 @ 它的视频，自动回一条带可跳转时间戳的评论。DSH / AI Agent 技能。
github_projects.description_zh: 让 AI 读懂你在 B 站 @ 它的视频，自动回一条带可跳转时间戳的评论。DSH / AI Agent 技能。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: 让 AI 读懂你在 B 站 @ 它的视频，自动回一条带可跳转时间戳的评论。DSH / AI Agent 技能。

evidence.heading: bilibili-reply
evidence.text:
[English](README.en.md)

一个 **AI Agent 技能**：让 AI 读懂你在 B 站 @ 它的视频，然后回你一条**带可跳转时间戳**的评论。

```
你 @ 一个视频  →  AI 本地看懂视频（文字稿 + 关键画面）  →  生成回复  →  自动发到你的评论区
```

evidence.heading: 它解决什么
evidence.text:
普通 AI 没法处理「B 站 @ 通知 + 视频内容」这条链路：

- @ 通知里**只有评论文字，没有视频链接** —— 得先找到是哪个视频
- 视频内容**得先看懂** —— 需要转文字 + 看关键画面
- 回复**要发在对的地方** —— 发错位置对方收不到通知

这个技能把整条链路固定下来，并踩平了几个真实的坑。

---

evidence.heading: ⚠️ 前置条件（必读）
evidence.text:
**这个技能不是装进任何 AI 就能用。** 它需要「AI 能操控一个已登录 B 站的浏览器」——**没有这一条，技能完全无法工作**（读不到 B 站，也发不了评论）。

| # | 前置 | 说明 | 链接 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **DeepSeek Harness（DSH）** | 技能运行在它的 Agent 上 | <https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness> |
| 2 | **pnpm** | DSH 用它管理插件 | <https://pnpm.io/installation> |
| 3 | **浏览器自动化**（关键） | 让 AI 能操作浏览器 —— 见下 | <https://github.com/Tencent/BrowserSkill> |
| 4 | **`video-watch` 技能** | 负责视频理解 | 见它的 README |

evidence.heading: 第 3 项：装浏览器自动化
evidence.text:
推荐 **[BrowserSkill](https://github.com/Tencent/BrowserSkill)** —— 腾讯开源的浏览器自动化，⭐ 8.8k，MIT 许可。它提供 `bsk` CLI + 浏览器扩展，**让 AI 用你真实的、已登录的浏览器**，而不需要另开一个干净会话重新登录。

> **本项目实际使用的就是这一套。** 这是 monorepo，我们装的 DSH 插件是其中一个子包：
> - 仓库主页：<https://github.com/Tencent/BrowserSkill>
> - **DSH 插件子目录（含插件自己的 README）**：<https://github.com/Tencent/BrowserSkill/tree/main/packages/dsh-plugin-browserskill>
> - npm 包名：`@wxg-prc-cpg/browser-skill-dsh-plugin`

```text
① 按 BrowserSkill 的快速开始装 bsk CLI
   https://github.com/Tencent/BrowserSkill#quick-start

② 在 Chrome 或 Edge 里安装并连接 BrowserSkill 扩展

③ 确保 bsk 在「启动 dsh 时的 PATH」里
   —— 不在也行，稍后在插件配置里写 bskPath 绝对路径

④ 把 DSH 插件装进你的 profile（desktop / web 按你的实际用）
   dsh plugin --profile web add @wxg-prc-cpg/browser-skill-dsh-plugin
   dsh --profile web
```

**验证装好了**：在 DSH 对话里说

```text
/browser-skill 打开 bilibili.com 并总结页面
```

能返回页面内容 → 前置通了。

> **换别的浏览器自动化也可以。** 本技能需要的是「读页面 / 点击 / 填表单」这几样能力；`SKILL.md` 里的示例按 `browser_*` 工具写，换成你手上的工具即可，**流程逻辑不变**。

evidence.heading: 第 4 项：装 video-watch
evidence.text:
本技能**依赖 `video-watch` 技能**做视频理解（本地转写 + 抽帧，不传云端）。请先按它自己的 README 装好：ffmpeg、faster-whisper 等。

> 它是独立项目，不随本仓库分发。搜索 `video-watch` 技能，或找提供该技能的 DSH 插件包安装。

---

evidence.heading: 快速开始（完整流程）
evidence.text:
```text
① 装好上面 4 个前置
② git clone <本仓库地址> <DSH_HOME>/skills/bilibili-reply
③ cp config.example.md config.md   →  填写你的昵称和机器人账号
④ 在浏览器里登录你的 B 站账号（建议小号 —— 技能会用它发言）
⑤ 用主号在某个视频下发一条评论并 @ 那个小号
⑥ 对 AI 说：「我@你了，去看看」
⑦ 观察它：读通知 → 核对身份 → 分析视频 → 回评论
```

**第 ③ 步不能省** —— 技能靠昵称核对身份，没配就不知道该回谁。

---

evidence.heading: 功能
evidence.text:
| 能力 | 说明 |
|---|---|
| **身份核对** | @ 列表里混着别人的通知；技能会逐项核对昵称，对不上就不回 |
| **视频理解** | 调 `video-watch`：本地转文字 + 抽帧，不传云端 |
| **按类型回复** | 教学类给**分章时间戳**；玩乐类给情绪反应；沉重内容克制处理 |
| **可跳转时间戳** | 用纯文本 `00:00` 格式，B 站会自动转成点击跳转 |
| **自动模式（可选）** | 自带看门狗脚本：每 30 秒自动检查 @，命中就自己看视频、自己回，再推微信告诉你 |

github_projects.name: paradee
github_projects.description: An 8M-parameter English text-to-speech model distilled from Kokoro-82M. 9 MB, runs 18x real time on one CPU thread.
github_projects.description_zh: 一个从Kokoro-82M蒸馏出的800万参数英语文本转语音模型。9 MB，在单个CPU线程上运行18倍实时速度。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: An 8M-parameter English text-to-speech model distilled from Kokoro-82M. 9 MB, runs 18x real time on one CPU thread.

evidence.heading: Paradee
evidence.text:
Paradee is a small English text-to-speech model. It has 7.88M parameters and is distilled from
[Kokoro-82M](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M), and it speaks one voice, Kokoro's `af_heart`.

- **Small.** The int8 model is one 8.5 MB ONNX file, against 325 MB for Kokoro.
- **Fast.** It runs about 62x faster than real time on one CPU thread, with no GPU.
- **Close to its teacher.** It scores 4.39 on UTMOS (Kokoro: 4.52) and its word error rate is within a few tenths of a point of Kokoro's.

**New in 1.1:** a new decoder head that makes the model more than 3x faster and leaves less buzz in voiced sounds. See [What changed in 1.1](#what-changed-in-11).

Paradee also runs inside the browser. It is the light voice in the
[Chickadee](https://github.com/sahilmahendrakar/chickadee) Chrome extension, where it needs no WebGPU and no download.

**Paper:** [Paradee: Distilling Kokoro-82M into an 8M-Parameter Single-Voice Text-to-Speech Model](paper/Paradee-Mahendrakar-2026.pdf) ([arXiv:2610.06817](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06817))

**Model files and audio samples:** [huggingface.co/sahilmahendrakar/Paradee-8M-v1.1](https://huggingface.co/sahilmahendrakar/Paradee-8M-v1.1) (the earlier release is at [Paradee-8M-v1.0](https://huggingface.co/sahilmahendrakar/Paradee-8M-v1.0))

evidence.heading: Quick start
evidence.text:
```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/sahilmahendrakar/paradee
python -m paradee "Paradee is a small voice that runs anywhere." -o hello.wav
```

From Python:

```python
from paradee import Paradee, SAMPLE_RATE
import soundfile as sf

tts = Paradee()   # downloads the 8.5 MB model from the Hugging Face Hub the first time
audio = tts("Paradee is a small voice that runs anywhere.")
sf.write("hello.wav", audio, SAMPLE_RATE)
```

Text is turned into phonemes with [misaki](https://github.com/hexgrad/misaki), Kokoro's own
grapheme-to-phoneme library, which is what the training data used. The first run also downloads
misaki's English dictionary data. `Paradee(version="1.0")` loads the earlier release.

evidence.heading: What changed in 1.1
evidence.text:
Version 1.0 used Kokoro's own audio generator at a smaller width, followed by a filter that fixed
the phase of voiced sound. Version 1.1 replaces both with a new head. The rest of the model (the
text side and the first part of the decoder) is the same.

The new head works at 80 frames a second and never upsamples, which is where the speed comes from.
For voiced sound it builds clean sine waves at the pitch and its multiples, then predicts a smooth
gain and a small phase correction for them. For everything else it shapes real noise, including
noise that pulses in time with the pitch, which is what Kokoro's upper frequencies mostly are.
Because the sine waves are generated from the pitch, their timing is right by construction, and
the separate phase filter is no longer needed.

Both ONNX files, on the same 200 held-out sentences and one CPU thread of an Apple M4 Pro:

| Release | Params | int8 file | Speed | UTMOS | WER |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Paradee 1.0 | 8.07M | 9.0 MB | 18x | 4.41 | 5.9% |
| **Paradee 1.1** | **7.88M** | **8.5 MB** | **62x** | **4.39** | **5.9%** |

UTMOS does not measure the buzz. By ear, 1.1 is the cleaner of the two. One measure that does
track it is how much energy sits on the multiples of the pitch compared with halfway between them,
between 2 and 4 kHz. Kokoro measures 3.1 dB, version 1.0 measures 1.3 dB and version 1.1 measures 3.9 dB.

The paper describes version 1.0.

evidence.heading: How it compares
evidence.text:
All numbers are on the same 200 held-out sentences, from the paper, which describes version 1.0. Speed is on one CPU thread of
an Apple M4 Pro.

| Model (voice) | Params | File size | Speed | UTMOS | WER |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Kokoro-82M, teacher (af_heart) | 81.8M | 325 MB | 7.6x | 4.52 | 5.7% |
| **Paradee 1.0 (af_heart)** | **8.07M** | **8.45 MB** | **25.0x** | **4.41** | **5.7%** |
| Kokoro-7M-Distill (af_msa) | 7.48M | 30.1 MB | 35.5x | 4.18 | 7.4% |
| Piper, en_US-lessac-medium | 15.7M | 63.2 MB | 15.4x | 4.36 | 8.8% |
| KittenTTS nano 0.8 (Bella) | 14.0M | 56.8 MB | 10.7x | 4.01 | 5.5% |

UTMOS is a neural network trained on human ratings. It predicts how natural a clip sounds, on a
scale from 1 to 5. WER is the share of words that Whisper (base) transcribes wrongly.

The paper's speed is for PyTorch. The numbers for the released ONNX files are in the table under
[What changed in 1.1](#what-changed-in-11).

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
Kokoro has two halves. A text side reads phonemes and predicts how long each one lasts, the pitch
and loudness over time, and a feature vector for each phoneme. A decoder turns those into audio.
Paradee is mostly Kokoro's own code at smaller widths, trained half by half against the frozen teacher.

1. **Corpus.** Kokoro reads 12,000 WikiText-103 sentences (23.9 hours of audio), and every
   intermediate value is saved.
2. **Text side (4.23M parameters).** It learns to predict the teacher's durations, pitch, loudness
   and phoneme features directly.
3. **Decoder (3.65M parameters).** It learns to turn the teacher's saved values into the teacher's
   audio, first with spectrogram losses and then with adversarial training. In 1.1 its last part is
   the new head described above, trained the same way with two extra losses that match how tonal
   and how pulsing the teacher's upper frequencies are.
4. **Assembly.** The two halves are joined with no further training, and the weights are stored
   in int8.

Version 1.0 also needed a filter with no parameters that corrected the phase of voiced sound
between 2 and 8 kHz (phase is the timing of each frequency's wave), to remove a slight buzz. In
1.1 the new head does not have that problem and the filter is gone.

The code for every step is in [`training/`](training/). It runs on one laptop.

evidence.heading: Using the ONNX file directly
evidence.text:
The model is one ONNX graph that goes from token ids to audio:

- **Inputs:** `input_ids`, int64 `[1, T]`. These are phoneme ids from Kokoro's vocabulary (in
  `config.json` on the Hub), with a `0` pad token at each end, at most 512 in total. The second
  input is `speed`, float32 `[1]`, where 1.0 is normal speed.
- **Output:** `waveform`, float32 `[1, samples]` at 24 kHz.

[`web/misaki.js`](web/misaki.js) is for the browser. Browser phonemizers such as
[kokoro-js](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro/tree/main/kokoro.js) use eSpeak NG, which writes
some sounds differently from misaki. Paradee only learned misaki's spelling. Without this
conversion Whisper mishears about 31% of words, and with it about 2%.

evidence.heading: License
evidence.text:
Apache 2.0, the same as Kokoro. The sentences in `training/data/` come from WikiText-103 and are
under CC BY-SA 3.0.

github_projects.name: aa-agentperf-local
github_projects.description: Benchmark local LLM serving by replaying real agent trajectories
github_projects.description_zh: 通过重放真实智能体轨迹来基准测试本地 LLM 服务。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Benchmark local LLM serving by replaying real agent trajectories

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text:
agentperf-local


  Benchmark how fast your machine serves an AI agent.
  An open-source tool from Artificial Analysis.



  
  


`agentperf-local` measures how fast your machine serves an AI agent. It replays
recorded agent conversations against an OpenAI-compatible model server and
reports throughput and latency. Each request carries the full conversation so
far, as a real agent's would. It measures speed without measuring output quality.

It can benchmark a server you already run, or it can download a pinned model,
start the server, and benchmark it for you.

evidence.heading: Quick start
evidence.text:
You need [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). It fetches Python 3.12 if you do
not have it. Docker and Rust are optional. macOS, Linux, and Windows are
supported. On Windows, managed runs need an NVIDIA GPU and llama.cpp; vLLM and
SGLang run only on Linux.

You also need either a model server that you already run with an
OpenAI-compatible API, such as llama.cpp, LM Studio, vLLM, SGLang, or Ollama,
or a serving framework that the tool can start. The bundled recipes use
llama.cpp (`llama-server` on your `PATH`), vLLM or SGLang on NVIDIA GPUs, or
Splash on Apple Silicon, at the exact version each recipe pins. The tool does
not install frameworks.
`agentperf-local deployment-options --profile-id <id>` shows which frameworks
can serve a recipe on this machine.

```console
uv tool install agentperf-local
agentperf-local
```

To try it without installing, run `uvx agentperf-local`. `pipx install
agentperf-local` also works.

To work from a source checkout instead:

```console
git clone https://github.com/ArtificialAnalysis/aa-agentperf-local.git
cd aa-agentperf-local
uv sync
uv run agentperf-local
```

The examples below use `uv run agentperf-local` from a checkout. With an
installed tool, drop the `uv run`.

The TUI walks you through choosing a model, setting up, and running. Arrow keys
move, Enter continues, Escape goes back, `?` opens help, and `q` quits. To
prefill settings with flags, use `agentperf-local tui`. See
[TEXTUAL_TUI.md](https://github.com/ArtificialAnalysis/aa-agentperf-local/blob/main/docs/TEXTUAL_TUI.md).

To run without the TUI, pick a catalog profile and a framework you have
installed:

```console
uv run agentperf-local managed-run \
  --profile-id qwen38-27b-q4-k-m \
  --framework llama-cpp \
  --output-dir results/qwen38-27b
```

`managed-run` downloads t

evidence.heading: The default run
evidence.text:
The default replay is `agentperf-default-v1`: eight recorded agent tasks with
168 model turns. It uses the `exact` output policy, which makes every turn
generate its recorded number of tokens. This is the comparable run.

`--replay aa-mini-v1` selects a six-turn synthetic replay. It is a quick
install check. Its results are not comparable.

evidence.heading: Context requirement
evidence.text:
A full run needs a 65,536-token context at batch size 1. Every catalog profile
launches at that context. An attached server that serves more, such as
131,072 tokens, also counts as full.

The default replay's largest turn needs about 58,000 tokens, so it only runs
at the full 65,536. If your device cannot fit that, you can still check your
setup with `aa-mini-v1`, which needs 8,192:

```console
uv run agentperf-local managed-run \
  --profile-id gemma4-12b-it-q4-0 \
  --framework llama-cpp \
  --replay aa-mini-v1 \
  --context-tokens 8192 \
  --output-dir results/gemma4-12b-mini
```

In the TUI, start with `uv run agentperf-local tui --replay aa-mini-v1` and
choose a smaller context on the Setup screen. A run below 65,536 tokens is
marked `reduced: true` and is not comparable with full-context results.

For an attached server, the tool reads the context at the start of the run:
`meta.n_ctx` from llama.cpp, `max_model_len` from vLLM and SGLang, or
`maximum_context_tokens` from the Splash status endpoint. A server that
reports none of them is recorded as not comparable.

evidence.heading: Attached servers
evidence.text:
Point `run` at a server you already run:

```console
uv run agentperf-local run \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 \
  --model served-model \
  --output-dir results/my-server
```

Use your server's base URL and the model name it reports:

| Server | Typical base URL |
| --- | --- |
| llama.cpp | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1` |
| LM Studio | `http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1` |
| vLLM | `http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1` |
| SGLang | `http://127.0.0.1:30000/v1` |

The `exact` policy sends `ignore_eos`, which is not part of the OpenAI API.
Before the replay, `run` and `managed-run` check that the server honors it. If
it does not, they stop and name the flag to change. The TUI switches to the
`recorded` policy instead and says so.

**Ollama cannot honor `ignore_eos`.** The tool detects Ollama before the run
and warns you. The run then uses the `recorded` policy, which lets the model
stop on its own and reports end-to-end latency as a normalized estimate. That
result is not directly comparable with `exact` runs.

To send an API key, put it in an environment variable and pass the variable's
name with `--api-key-env`. No flag takes a literal key.

evidence.heading: Real tool calling
evidence.text:
By default the replay skips tool time between turns. `run --tool-mode fixed_delay`
sleeps after each turn for the tool time recorded there. `run --tool-mode live`
runs the recorded shell commands in Docker containers, so tool time is real.
This mode is opt-in and needs Docker and prebuilt images. The build scripts
are in the source checkout. They are bash scripts, so on Windows run them from
Git Bash or WSL:

```console
scripts/install-swebench-validation.sh   # arm64 hosts only, once
scripts/build-default-containers.sh

uv run agentperf-local run \
  --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 \
  --model served-model \
  --output-dir results/live-tools \
  --tool-mode live
```

Security caveats:

- The recorded commands are untrusted input. Docker reduces the risk but is not
  a security boundary.
- Access to the Docker daemon is equivalent to root on most hosts.
- Containers have no network by default, but a replay manifest can ask for one.
  Pass `--live-network none` to force no network.
- The task workspace is mounted read-write. It lives under the output directory
  unless you pass `--live-workspace-root`.
- The scripts pull or build third-party images and clone the SWE-bench harness
  from GitHub.

evidence.heading: Rust client (experimental)
evidence.text:
Python is the default client. An optional Rust client records timings outside
Python. It needs a [Rust toolchain](https://rustup.rs):

```console
uv sync --extra rust
uv run agentperf-local tui --client rust
```

With an installed tool, use `uv tool install 'agentperf-local[rust]'`
instead. A plain `uv sync` removes the extension again. Both clients produce the same
metrics.

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: The agent harness you can fork. A working agent loop with compaction, sessions, approvals, a terminal REPL, a local dashboard and ACP, where every tool, skill, hook and policy is a file you can change. Build your own internal or coding agent on any model.

evidence.heading: raw-cli
evidence.text:
[](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@tlelabs/raw) [](https://github.com/lploc94/raw-cli/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [](LICENSE)

`raw` is the agent harness you can fork. The parts every agent needs already work: the tool loop, context compaction, saved sessions, approvals, a terminal REPL, a local browser dashboard and the Agent Client Protocol for editors. Everything an agent does is a file you can change, so you build an internal agent, a coding agent or an ops agent by editing parts instead of starting from an empty loop.



- **Fork a tool.** Built-in tools are plain plugins. Copy one with Fork to local, or write your own as one `index.mjs`.
- **Teach a procedure.** Skills are Markdown files the agent lists and loads when it needs them.
- **Set the rules.** Ordered policy rules allow, ask or deny a tool or a pattern, and hooks run your scripts on session, prompt and tool events.
- **Connect your systems.** Selected MCP tools and runtime variables sit next to the built-ins.
- **Share the result.** Package an agent with its tools and skills as a `.rawpkg` that your team installs.

Each agent selects ordered tools, skills and hooks, and can supply a system prompt, so a request carries only what that agent was given. That also keeps models with limited context useful. Raw ships fourteen tools as editable plugins: `read_file`, `write_file`, `edit_file`, `apply_patch`, `bash`, `powershell`, `view_image`, `list_skills`, `load_skill`, `list_vars`, `read_var`, `todo`, `ask_user`, and `process`. Apply patch, PowerShell, Todo, Ask, and Process are selected explicitly; they are not added to the starter tool selection, except that on Windows without Git Bash the starter selects PowerShell in place of Bash. Tools, skills and hooks can also live in the user's config directory or beside

evidence.heading: Install and run
evidence.text:
Requires Node.js 22.13+ on macOS, Linux or Windows 10/11, and Bash for the `bash` tool. Documentation: [raw.tlelabs.com](https://raw.tlelabs.com). To shape Raw into your own agent, read [Design an effective agent](https://raw.tlelabs.com/docs/guides/design-an-agent/) and the [FAQ](https://raw.tlelabs.com/docs/start/faq/).

```sh
npm install -g @tlelabs/raw
raw config init
```

Run it once without installing with `npx @tlelabs/raw --help`. To install the latest commit from GitHub instead, use `npm install -g github:lploc94/raw-cli`; installing from a Git ref runs the `prepare` build, so it downloads build tooling and takes longer. Each [GitHub release](https://github.com/lploc94/raw-cli/releases) also attaches the packed tarball. To work from a checkout, run `npm ci` (which also builds) and `npm install -g .`.

evidence.heading: Windows
evidence.text:
Raw runs natively on Windows; WSL is not needed. Install [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) for the `bash` tool: Raw finds its Git Bash (`RAW_BASH_PATH` wins) and never picks WSL's `bash.exe` on its own. Without Git Bash, `raw config init` selects the `powershell` tool instead, and either tool can be selected later. The `powershell` tool runs PowerShell 7 (`pwsh`) when installed, which is recommended, else the Windows PowerShell 5.1 every Windows has; `RAW_POWERSHELL_PATH` picks another. Config lives in `%USERPROFILE%\.config\raw` and sessions in `%USERPROFILE%\.local\state\raw`. Stopping a command or background job ends its whole process tree at once. Policy rules and hooks written for `builtin/bash` do not cover `builtin/powershell`; add rules for each shell an agent selects.

`config init` creates `~/.config/raw/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/raw/config.json`) once with setup-capable agent `raw`; edit the local model ID or add your hosted model. `raw "query"` uses the configured `default_agent`, which may name a different agent in an existing config. `--config PATH` selects another strict JSON config file.

```sh
raw --agent raw "Explain the tests in this repository"
raw --agent deepseek "Fix the failing tests"
raw                         # saved REPL with ❯ prompt on an interactive terminal
raw --continue "Follow up on that change"
raw sessions
raw sessions show SESSION_ID
raw --acp --stdio           # IDE/parent agent transport
raw dashboard              # local browser chat and setup
raw dashboard --port 0 --no-open
```

`raw dashboard` serves the bundled browser app locally. Create or continue sessions,
inspect reasoning/tool activity and context usage, handle matching approvals, and
manage agents, models, skills, tools, vars, MCP and package

evidence.heading: Models and agents
Tools, images and MCP
Shared tool UI and editing
evidence.text:
Tool views use one block renderer in chat and the sidebar. `builtin/ask_user` gathers durable structured answers; `builtin/process` runs bounded background jobs across turns. The dashboard Commands section combines foreground Bash and background jobs, with paged output and policy-controlled Stop actions that remain available during a model turn.

The opt-in `apply_patch` applies a strict multi-file patch. Patch preflight stages all files before mutation; later I/O failures report partial completion and stop subsequent changes. One shared Files changed panel records successful writes, edits and patches with their line counts and latest diff, including completed files in an interrupted call. It does not track Git state or shell edits. See [tools](docs/tools.md), [processes](docs/processes.md), and the [verification evidence](docs/evidence/tool-ui-and-builtins.md).

Mermaid fences and tool diagram blocks share a lazy renderer in chat and the sidebar, with source/copy controls and readable failure fallback. See [diagrams](docs/diagrams.md) and the [local diagram example](examples/tools/diagram/).

evidence.heading: Conversation, compact and cache
evidence.text: The REPL saves turns across process restarts. Use `raw --continue` for the latest session in this workspace, `raw --resume ID` for a specific saved cwd, and `raw sessions show ID --before CURSOR` to page older visible history. Host commands are `/compact`, `/clear`, `/stats`, and `/exit`; `/clear` starts a new saved session. When the model declares `context_window_tokens`, automatic compaction defaults to 80% of the input budget (context minus output reserve and margin); `compact.trigger_tokens` sets another threshold and `false` keeps compaction manual. With a threshold, Raw estimates the complete next request, emits visible compact progress, and sends bounded summary requests to the selected model when the threshold is reached. It excludes image base64 from summary prompts and retains a stable main cache key until a deliberate compact boundary. Cache reuse

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Eleven free Claude skills that run a LinkedIn account: posts off 21 hook formulas, comments, replies, profile score, weekly plan, and a humanizer that strips the AI fingerprint.

evidence.heading: The LinkedIn agent skill
evidence.text:
Eleven Claude skills that run a LinkedIn account. Free, MIT, no signup, no API
key, nothing to connect.

One of them writes your posts off 21 hook formulas. One comments on other
people's posts. One handles the replies under yours. One scores your profile
out of 100 and rewrites what lost points. One plans the week: what to post,
when, and who to engage with.

And one is the humanizer, which is the reason the rest are usable. It strips
the em dashes, the slop vocabulary and the invisible watermark characters out
of a draft, then scores what is left against a five-check detection panel
before you ever see it.

**Nothing gets posted until you say yes.** These skills write. You post.

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
Paste this into Claude:

```
https://github.com/avi691/linkedin-agent-skill

Install this skill, then confirm /li-post works.
```

Or do it yourself, in Claude Code:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/avi691/linkedin-agent-skill.git
cp -r linkedin-agent-skill/skills/li-* ~/.claude/skills/
```

Or as a plugin:

```
/plugin marketplace add avi691/linkedin-agent-skill
/plugin install linkedin-agent
```

Project-local instead of global: copy the same folders into your repo's
`.claude/skills/`. No Claude Code at all? Paste any single `SKILL.md` at the
top of a chat and it runs as a mode - you lose the two Python tools, which is
most of the point of `/li-human`, but the rest works.

Then spend ten minutes on `templates/voice.md`. Copy it to
`~/.claude/linkedin/voice.md` and fill it in, or paste three of your own posts
into Claude and say "write my voice.md from these". Every skill reads that
file. Skip it and everything comes out sounding like everyone else.

evidence.heading: The eleven
evidence.text:
| command | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `/li-post` | One idea into a post. Three hook options from [21 formulas](skills/li-post/hooks.json), one full draft, humanized before you see it. |
| `/li-comment` | Comments on other people's posts. Nine types, picked by what the post actually is. Never "Great post!". |
| `/li-reply` | The thread under your own post. Sorts every comment into lead / substance / peer / support / noise, then writes in that order. |
| `/li-profile` | Scores your profile against a [12-part rubric](skills/li-profile/rubric.json) out of 100, then rewrites in fix-first order. |
| `/li-plan` | The week. What to post, when to post it, and the 10 people to engage with. Writes `~/.claude/linkedin/plan.md`. |
| `/li-human` | The humanizer. Two scripts that actually run. See below. |
| `/li-carousel` | Document posts. Slide-by-slide copy, the cover that earns the swipe, and the PDF to upload. |
| `/li-repurpose` | One video, newsletter or transcript into a week of posts that each stand alone. |
| `/li-dm` | The 200-character invite note, the first message, and the two follow-ups. Two. |
| `/li-inbox` | Triages the inbox into lead / recruiter / peer / ask / spam, and tells you which tell gave the sequence away. |
| `/li-audit` | Post-mortem on what you have already published. Ranks by engagement rate and reach multiple, not impressions. |

evidence.heading: The humanizer
evidence.text:
`/li-human` ships two Python scripts with no dependencies. They run on your
machine, on your text, and nothing is uploaded.

```bash
python3 humanize.py draft.txt --report      # clean it, show every change
python3 detect.py draft.txt                  # score it, five checks
python3 detect.py before.txt after.txt       # prove the delta
```

**What comes out automatically:**

- **Invisible characters.** Zero-width spaces and joiners, word joiners, soft
  hyphens, byte-order marks, Unicode tag characters, non-breaking and narrow
  spaces. Your keyboard does not make these. They survive copy-paste and they
  are invisible in every editor you own.
- **Typography.** Em dash to comma, en dash to hyphen, curly quotes to
  straight, ellipsis to three dots.
- **The lexicon.** 113 stock words and phrases with plain-English
  replacements - delve, leverage, robust, seamless, crucial, testament to, "in
  today's fast-paced world", "let that sink in" - with capitalisation preserved
  and URLs untouched. It lives in
  [`slop.json`](skills/li-human/slop.json) and it is meant to be edited.

**What gets flagged instead of fixed:** "It's not just X, it's Y", rule-of-three
triads, one-word rhetorical questions, hashtag walls, reflex engagement bait,
uniform sentence length. Changing the shape of a sentence needs judgement, so
those are handed back for a rewrite rather than mangled by a regex.

**The five checks**, scored 0-100, higher is more human:

| check | what it measures |
| --- | --- |
| BURSTINESS | sentence-length variation. Models write even. |
| SPECIFICITY | numbers, names and concrete markers per 100 words |
| SLOP DENSITY | lexicon hits per 100 words |
| FINGERPRINT | invisible characters, em dashes, curly quotes per 1,000 |
| VOICE | contractions, person, structural tells

evidence.heading: The fine print, which is the honest part
evidence.text:
**These skills do not post to LinkedIn, and they should not.** There is no
official API for posting to a personal profile without an approved partner
app, and automating the site with a browser or a third-party tool violates
[LinkedIn's User Agreement](https://www.linkedin.com/legal/user-agreement) and
gets accounts restricted. So every skill here ends the same way: a copy-ready
block, and you paste it. That is not a limitation bolted on afterwards, it is
the design. It is also why the approval gate is real rather than a setting.

**The five checks are local heuristics, not detector APIs.** They are modelled
on the signals public detectors key on, and they run entirely on your machine.
They are not GPTZero, Originality, Copyleaks, Winston or Turnitin, they do not
call those services, and they cannot promise those verdicts. Fixing what they
measure tends to move those numbers, because they are measuring the same
underlying things. That is the whole claim. Nobody can honestly sell you
"undetectable", and anybody who does is selling you something.

**The invisible-character pass is real and it is narrow.** It removes the
zero-width and format characters that end up in generated text and survive a
copy-paste. That is a genuine, checkable fingerprint. It is not a claim about
defeating a cryptographic watermarking scheme, and this repo does not make
one.

**Nothing here fabricates.** No invented metrics, clients or outcomes go under
your name. If a draft needs a number you have not given, it comes back with
`{{your number}}` in it and a flag, every time.

evidence.heading: Files
evidence.text:
```
skills/li-post/hooks.json        21 hook formulas: template, example, what it is for, how it gets ruined
skills/li-human/slop.json        the lexicon: 113 terms, 17 invisible classes, 11 structural tells
skills/li-human/humanize.py      the three cleaning passes
skills/li-human/detect.py        the five-check panel
skills/li-profile/rubric.json    the 100-point profile score
templates/voice.md               your voice profile. Fill this in first.
```

evidence.heading: What Synapass does
evidence.text:
Synapass is an **inference gateway** and **control plane**. It sits between your
applications and your model providers, presents a single OpenAI-compatible
endpoint, and decides — per request, under policy — which provider serves it,
what happens when that provider fails, and what it cost.

It is also where providers, models, policies, tenants, keys, tools and caches are
managed. Changing which model answers production traffic is a dashboard edit
rather than a deployment.

Any client that speaks OpenAI works by changing its base URL. The extra response
fields are namespaced under `synapass`, so OpenAI SDKs ignore them.

evidence.heading: Why it exists
evidence.text:
Inference stacks rarely get chosen. They accrete. By the time a few applications
are live you have:

- **A provider integration per service**, each with its own error handling, so a
  `429` means something slightly different everywhere.
- **No failover.** One upstream hiccup becomes an outage, because nothing knows a
  second provider exists.
- **Routing logic in application code** — a `if model == "gpt-4o"` here, a
  provider SDK there, copied into every service.
- **No cost control.** A runaway loop produces a bill nobody notices until it
  arrives.
- **No central answer** to "what did we spend, and which model produced the bad
  answers?"

Each is small. Together they are an operating burden that competes with the
product. Synapass moves all of it into one layer you can operate.

evidence.heading: Key features
evidence.text:
| | |
| --- | --- |
| **OpenAI-compatible API** | `POST /v1/chat/completions`, streaming and buffered, plus `/v1/models`. An SDK swap, not a rewrite. |
| **Multi-provider routing** | Five strategies — `priority`, `weighted`, `lowest_cost`, `lowest_latency`, `highest_quality` — over a registry that knows each model's real context window, capabilities and price. |
| **Fallback chains** | Ordered failover with bounded retry and deterministic jitter. A started stream is never appended to; it is reported instead. |
| **Policy engine** | Match on model, tenant, key, task, size, region, sensitivity and endpoint. Resolved by specificity, so a specific rule always beats a broad one. |
| **Cost control** | Per-request ceilings checked against projected cost *before* the call, token and request rate limits, daily and monthly budgets. |
| **Provider & model management** | Add, test, probe, kill and revive providers. Discover remote models while preserving your local pricing, aliases and disables. |
| **Tool calling** | Client-executed by default. Optional bounded gateway-side execution with operator-owned limits and a durable step trace per run. |
| **Local caching** | Exact, prefix and semantic tiers, tenant-isolated by construction, invalidatable by scope with an audit trail. Off by default. |
| **Observability** | Task classification, policy verdict, cache decision and routing reason on every request. Prometheus, OTLP traces, JSON logs, Grafana dashboards and alert rules. |
| **Dashboard** | A full control plane for providers, models, policies, tenants, keys, tools, cache and tunnels, behind a first-run operator account. |
| **Deployment** | Docker Compose, native systemd, and temporary Cloudflare tunnels. One configuration model across all three. |

evidence.text:

evidence.heading: Architecture
evidence.text:
The request path, end to end:

```
   client
     │  OpenAI SDK · curl · any OpenAI-compatible client
     ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  POST /v1/chat/completions                   │
│                                              │
│  1  authenticate      API key → tenant        │
│  2  resolve policy    most specific match     │
│  3  enforce budgets   rate limits, ceilings   │
│  4  check cache       exact → prefix → semantic
│  5  classify task     rules-first             │
│  6  shape prompt      normalize, trim         │
│  7  route             filter → order → pick   │
│  8  execute           retry · fail over      │
│  9  tools loop        bounded, when allowed   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │                          │
     ▼                          ▼
  provider                response + synapass
  adapter call            metadata block
        │
        └──────────────────────────────────────┐
                                               ▼
                              telemetry · asynchronously
                              usage · traces · metrics · logs
```

The deployment topology:

```
   client ──▶ gateway :8080 ──┬──▶ PostgreSQL   system of record
        ▲     │              ├──▶ Redis         limits, cache, credentials
        │     ▼              ├──▶ NATS          usage, eval jobs, audit
   dashboard  └──▶ workers ──┴──▶ ClickHouse ──▶ OTel ──▶ Prometheus · Loki · Grafana
```

Every request records why it was routed the way it was. Read it back with
`GET /admin/v1/requests/{id}/explain`.

evidence.heading: Example request
evidence.text:
Mint a tenant key, then call the public endpoint:

```bash
export GATEWAY=http://127.0.0.1:8080
export SYNAPASS_ADMIN_KEY=<from .env>

TENANT=$(curl -s $GATEWAY/admin/v1/tenants \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SYNAPASS_ADMIN_KEY" | jq -r '.tenants[0].id')

export SYNAPASS_KEY=$(curl -s $GATEWAY/admin/v1/keys \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SYNAPASS_ADMIN_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"tenant_id\":\"$TENANT\",\"name\":\"first-key\",\"scopes\":[\"inference\"]}" \
  | jq -r .plaintext)
```

```bash
curl -s $GATEWAY/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SYNAPASS_KEY" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-4o-mini",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize refunds in one line."}],
    "max_tokens": 256,
    "temperature": 0.3
  }' | jq
```

```json
{
  "choices": [{ "index": 0, "message": { "role": "assistant", "content": "…" }, "finish_reason": "stop" }],
  "usage": { "prompt_tokens": 26, "completion_tokens": 81, "total_tokens": 107 },
  "synapass": {
    "request_id": "5e0804c7-…",
    "provider": "openai-prod",
    "requested_model": "gpt-4o-mini",
    "routed_model": "gpt-4o-mini",
    "fallback_used": false,
    "latency_ms": 2851,
    "estimated_cost_usd": 0.0000026
  }
}
```

`provider` is who **answered**, not who was chosen first. An answer cut short by a
limit says so rather than looking short:

```json
"completion": { "truncated": true, "reason": "max_tokens", "budget_ms": 300000 }
```

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Fish Audio Drama 3 text to speech, natively in ComfyUI: voice cloning, dialogue and inline cues on cards from 8 GB, plus a native Qwen3-ASR. Built with Fish Audio.

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text: Run **[Fish Audio Drama 3](https://huggingface.co/fishaudio/drama-3)**, a 35B text-to-speech model for voice cloning, dialogue and inline cues such as `[sighs]` or `[whispers]`, **natively in ComfyUI on cards from 8 GB**. 90% of the model is routed experts and each audio frame uses only 8 of the 256 in a layer, so the experts stay in system RAM and the GPU keeps a cache of the ones in use. The pack also brings a native **Qwen3-ASR** that writes a voice clip's transcript for you, and nodes to save a cloned voice and load it again. Built with Fish Audio. > [!NOTE] > **3× faster since 2026-10-17.** The pack's own CUDA kernels read the experts the cache misses straight from RAM while > the CPU computes others, and every layer replays as a CUDA graph: one RTX 3090 now speaks a 9 s line in 6.7 s instead > of 16.7 s, about twice as fast as real time, two GPUs take 2.8 s, and an 8 GB card keeps pace with real time. > Nothing new to install. [Numbers](#performance). Drama 3 FP8 · experts in RAM · temperature 1.0, top_p 0.9, top_k 30 · RTX 3090 and RTX 4090 · no real person cloned: the clones copy voices the model made up, the rest are voices it invents per seed. Click to listen. Clone a voice from seconds of audioA clip and its transcript are all it takes; save the voice and reuse it without the codec. Up to 16 speakers in one textStart each line with <|speaker:N|> and give each speaker a voice. Cues where they should land[laughs], [whispers], [sighs] and plain-language directions inside the text (how to write them). Long texts in one goRead in chunks the way Fish Audio's server does, each chunk hearing the ones before it. Faster than real time, experts in RAMAbout 6 GB of the mod

evidence.heading: Tags and directions
evidence.text:
Directions are free natural language, not a fixed list: any wording works, and the examples below are Fish Audio's.
The full syntax is Appendix C of their [Drama 3 technical report](https://github.com/fishaudio/fish-speech/blob/main/docs/assets/Fish_Audio_Drama_3_Technical_Report.pdf).

| Control | How to write it | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Speaker | `<\|speaker:N\|>` at the start of a line, N from 0 to 15; the voice in Generate's slot `voiceN` speaks for speaker N, unless its transcript starts with a tag of its own. The lines reach the model joined by `<\|audio_separator\|>`, the dialogue layout of Fish's report (Figure 11) | `<\|speaker:0\|> Ready?` `<\|speaker:1\|> Always.` |
| Point tag | `[tag]` where the sound should land | `Well [sighs] fine, you win. [laughs]` `[pause]` `[gasps]` `[clears throat]` |
| Scoped tag | `<tag>...</tag>` around the words it shapes | `Promise me <whisper>you won't tell her</whisper>.` `<slow>...</slow>` `<emphasis>...</emphasis>` |
| Style prefix | `[style]` at the start of a line | `[with bright eager excitement] We won!` |
| Director's note | `Direction:` with the note, then `Line:` with the text on the next line | `Direction: icy calm, as if you already accepted it.` `Line: So this is goodbye.` |
| Language hint | `[language: xx]` after a line; it is not spoken | `Welcome back to the show. [language: en]` |

Text in round parentheses is spoken. Long text is cut into chunks of about 300 bytes without splitting a tag; keep a
director's note in one chunk with its line, or turn off `split_long_text`. Notes against an earlier take ("softer than
before") need that take in the prompt, which these nodes don't send.

evidence.heading: Requirements
evidence.text:
| | Minimum | Tested |
|---|---|---|
| GPU | NVIDIA, 8 GB of VRAM with experts in RAM | RTX 4090 and RTX 3090 (24 GB); 12 GB and 8 GB simulated on the 3090 |
| System RAM | the model file plus ~8 GB: ~32 GB for W4A8, ~48 GB for FP8 | 188 GB |
| CPU | any; with int8 experts in RAM it computes part of the experts, so more cores help on small cards | Intel Core i9-14900K |
| Disk | 26 GB (W4A8 and the codec) | NVMe |
| ComfyUI | v0.40 | v0.41.0 and master after v0.41.2 |

evidence.heading: Choosing a file
evidence.text:
**Start with FP8**: it holds Fish Audio's own expert weights, byte for byte, next to the checkpoint's bf16 layers.
**On a card under 24 GB take int8**: it is the same size and measured as close to the original, and only int8 experts
are computed by the CPU when the VRAM cache misses them, which makes it twice as fast as FP8 with a 4 GB cache. Take a
smaller file when your RAM is short of the FP8 file's ~48 GB; on a 24 GB card they are also the fastest.

| File | Size | Experts | RAM with experts in RAM | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `drama3_fp8experts_bf16` | 38.6 GB | FP8, as Fish Audio ships them | ~48 GB | the original weights |
| `drama3_int8experts_bf16` | 38.7 GB | int8 ConvRot | ~48 GB | the fastest on cards under 24 GB; no silent take in 12 cloned test takes |
| `drama3_w6a8experts_bf16` | 32.7 GB | W6A8 | ~40 GB | no silent take in 16 cloned test takes |
| `drama3_w4a8experts_bf16` | 24.6 GB | W4A8 | ~32 GB | falls silent more often with real voice clips |

Qwen3-ASR comes in two sizes, `qwen3_asr_1.7b_bf16` (4.1 GB) and `qwen3_asr_0.6b_bf16` (1.6 GB). In our tests both
wrote nearly the same transcripts of clean speech, and the 0.6B took half the time. `qwen3_forced_aligner_0.6b_bf16`
(1.8 GB, also on [Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI](https://huggingface.co/PedroMarinhoDev/Qwen3-ASR-ComfyUI)) gives Drama 3 Editor the time of every word; on a 40 s
take its times match Qwen's own aligner within 0.16 s, 121 of 131 words exactly.

evidence.heading: Performance
evidence.text:

evidence.heading: Troubleshooting
evidence.text:
A take falls silent after a second, or speaks only part of the text

Set `top_k` to 0: workflows saved before this fix keep the old 30, which makes takes fall silent at pauses. Then check
the voice: the transcript must cover every word of the clip, and the clip should be clean speech cut between
sentences. Some clips make the model fall silent in Fish Audio's own code too (known issue); try another stretch of the
recording. A take that goes silent is stopped and its silent tail cut, with a warning in the console; a new seed
usually helps.




Speakers swap voices in a dialogue

Give every speaker a voice. A long dialogue is generated in chunks, and an earlier chunk's take in the prompt hands the
voice it ends in to the next chunk: with two cloned voices, 6 of 16 lines after the first chunk came out in the other
voice. When every speaker has a voice, Generate leaves earlier takes out of dialogue chunks and the references keep
the voices apart (1 of 18). A speaker without a voice still needs the

evidence.heading: Folivox
evidence.text:
**The audiobook workhorse. A powerful tool in a simple interface, free.**

Drop in a book, pick a voice, press Render. Get a chaptered audiobook read in any voice you like,
on your own computer.

FB2 · EPUB · DOCX · PDF · TXT  →  `.m4b` / `.mp3` with chapters, cover and metadata

evidence.heading: 1. Install
evidence.text:
Pick one way. Each needs no administrator rights and is safe to run again.

**One command** (recommended). Open a terminal (macOS: **Terminal** in Applications → Utilities; Windows:
**PowerShell** from the Start menu; Linux: any terminal), paste the line for your system and press Enter.

macOS and Linux:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vatavale/folivox/main/scripts/install.sh | bash
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vatavale/folivox/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex
```


With git (if you want the source code)

macOS and Linux:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vatavale/folivox.git
cd folivox
bash scripts/install.sh
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/vatavale/folivox.git
cd folivox
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\install.ps1
```




With Docker (home server or NAS)

Optional, not needed on a normal computer. Create a stack from [docker-compose.yml](docker-compose.yml) (or
[docker-compose.nvidia.yml](docker-compose.nvidia.yml) for an NVIDIA GPU), set `FOLIVOX_UI_TOKEN` to a password, deploy
and open `http://<server>:8765/`. Works from Portainer, Dockhand or `docker compose up -d`. Details:
[docs/docker.md](docs/docker.md).

evidence.heading: 4. Uninstall
evidence.text:
```bash
folivox uninstall               # delete the downloaded models (asks first; --dry-run only shows what would go)
folivox uninstall --everything  # also delete your voices and settings
uv tool uninstall folivox       # last step: remove the program itself
```

It removes only what Folivox created. Your books, audiobooks, ffmpeg and uv are never touched.

Details, options, manual install and troubleshooting: [docs/install.md](docs/install.md).

evidence.heading: Choose how your book is read
evidence.text:
| | Free, on your computer | With an online engine (your API key) |
|---|---|---|
| **Who reads** | CosyVoice 3 or Fish Audio Drama 3 (80+ languages), local and offline | ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Gemini, Cartesia or Fish Audio |
| **Voice** | Clones any sample: bundled, recorded, uploaded, cut from a video or generated; several voices in one book | The provider's voices, or a voice designed or localised for the book |
| **Cost** | Free (Drama 3 needs a Mac with enough memory) | Estimated before you start, confirmed by you, with an optional spending cap |
| **Your text** | Never leaves your computer | Sent to that provider |

Paste a key for any of the five providers in the studio (it is stored in your OS keychain) and they appear
next to the local engine. With the model set to `auto`, Folivox asks the provider which models your key can
use and takes the newest one, so new releases are picked up without updating Folivox.

evidence.heading: Recommended: the almost-free workflow
evidence.text:
The best results we get come from combining one cheap online sample with the free local engine:

1. **Generate a voice sample with Gemini 3.8.** In the studio: voice gallery → **Generate a voice sample** →
   Gemini, describe the narrator (or press **Suggest from my book**), generate a few short takes. With a paid
   Gemini key this costs well under one cent (about $0.0023 per 10 s of audio on the paid tier); Google also has
   a free tier.
2. **Keep the best take** (Whisper ranks them) as a voice in your library.
3. **Render the whole book locally** with CosyVoice (or Drama 3) cloning that voice: free, unlimited, offline.

You pay once for about ten seconds of a top-quality voice, and the open model reads the remaining hours
with it. CLI equivalent:

```bash
export GEMINI_API_KEY=…
folivox voices design narrator -g gemini --mode design --lang en --describe "calm, warm audiobook narrator" --keep takes/
folivox render book.epub --voice narrator
```

evidence.heading: Features
evidence.text:
- **Many formats in.** FB2 (also `.fb2.zip`), EPUB, DOCX, PDF (text layer, no OCR) and TXT. Chapters, nested sections, poems and epigraphs are kept; PDF headers, footers and page numbers are removed and hyphenation is undone.
- **Fish Audio Drama 3.** Directed in plain words (`[calm, warm narration]`), 80+ languages, several speakers in one scene. Runs locally on a Mac with enough memory; an online variant with your key is optional. [Details](docs/fish-engines.md).
- **9 languages with full rules, 80+ with Drama 3.** Russian, English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Chinese, Japanese, Korean get their own text rules. Any other language Fish Audio Drama 3 reads, also locally (84 in all, e.g. Polish, Portuguese, Arabic, Hindi, Thai), works too. Detected from the book's text; `--lang` overrides it. Books with passages in other languages are read fragment by fragment in the right language.
- **Text prepared for speech.** Numbers, dates, times, money, units, roman numerals and abbreviations read in full, with case and gender agreement where the language has it (Russian cases, Spanish `veintiuna`, French `une`, German `eine`, Korean native counters, Chinese `两`); sentences split and packed into fragments; dialogue pauses. [Per-language table](docs/how-it-works.md#what-the-normaliser-reads-out-per-language).
- **Stress, `ё` and your own pronunciations.** For Russian, `ё` is restored automatically with ruaccent, and full stress marks are available (`--stress all`, experimental). Names and invented words: a plain-text dictionary next to the book (`Kvothe = Quothe`), also editable in the studio. [Details](docs/pronunciation.md).
- **Quality control.** Every fragment is listened back with Whisper. If it does not match the text it is read again, and the best take is kept (`--take

evidence.heading: Usage in short
evidence.text:
```bash
folivox inspect book.epub                     # chapter tree, size, estimated duration
folivox book.fb2 -v me.wav -o book.m4b        # render the whole book with your voice
folivox book.fb2 -c 1-2 --preview 600         # a quick test: chapters 1–2, first 600 characters each
folivox book.pdf --mp3 -o out/                # one mp3 per chapter
folivox render book.epub --tts openai --tts-voice coral --max-cost 5   # an online engine with a cap
folivox voices                                # your voice library
folivox doctor --bundle                       # check the setup / write a redacted support bundle
folivox bench                                 # speed test: characters per second on each device (CPU, CUDA, MPS)
```

`folivox bench` synthesises one short fragment on every device it finds, each in its own process, and prints
characters per second, RTF and peak GPU memory, so you can see what actually helps on your machine and compare
machines (`--devices cpu,cuda` picks devices; CUDA is tried even if `auto` would skip a small GPU).

`folivox --help`, `folivox render --help` and `folivox help <topic>` (`voices`, `providers`, `config`,
`languages`, `resuming`, `quality`, `speed`) explain every option. Full list: [docs/cli.md](docs/cli.md).

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: dsh-sieve: context engineering & token optimization plugin for DeepSeek Harness (DSH) — tool output filtering, context pruning, progressive skill disclosure. 36% smaller payload in offline replay. DSH 上下文管理与 token 优化节省插件。

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text:
English | 简体中文

sieve / dsh-sieve

**LLM agent context engineering and token efficiency plugins for DeepSeek Harness (DSH)**

sieve filters tool output, prunes older context and progressively discloses skills to reduce redundant input tokens in AI coding agents, improve context window utilization and provide observable usage data for LLM inference cost optimization. Originals are archived before rewriting and can be retrieved on demand.

**Over 30% less request payload in offline replay, measured in characters**: a **36.28%** aggregate reduction across 100 public agent trajectories. See [offline replay results](#offline-replay-results).

**Historical live model results: 21.2% lower main model input token usage** across 80 paired runs on deepseek-flash, with cache hit rate moving from 93.4% to 92.9%. This experiment used the now-removed session-model judge path; the current Jev / Laya configuration has not been remeasured. See [live model results](#live-model-results-deepseek-flash) and the [cache FAQ](#faq).

Built around context engineering and token efficiency, sieve manages the context delivered to the model within the agent loop, reducing repeated input across multi-step tool use.

[](LICENSE)
[](tsconfig.base.json)
[](package.json)
[](packages/dsh-sieve/package.json)
[](packages/dsh-sieve/package.json)



[](#design-constraints)
[](#design-constraints)



---

> [!IMPORTANT]
> sieve works only with a judge model configured: **Jev** (hosted, needs an API key) or **Laya** (local, macOS on Apple Silicon). sieve never uses the session's model in its place. With neither configured, the plugin loads but changes no context. See [judge models](#judge-models-jev--laya).

evidence.heading: Why sieve
Core capabilities and use cases
evidence.text:
For AI coding agents running on DeepSeek Harness, especially tasks with verbose test logs, frequent tool calls, long sessions or large skill catalogs.

| Optimization area | How sieve handles it |
|---|---|
| **Input token reduction** | Filters redundant tool content before it enters the session, reducing input resent on later steps |
| **Tool output filtering** | Handles build logs, test reports and command output by category, protecting failure details and test summaries |
| **Context compaction / pruning** | Replaces irrelevant older tool results in batches, retaining archive pointers for on-demand retrieval |
| **Progressive skill disclosure** | Shows skills by task relevance, reducing context window usage from unrelated descriptions |
| **Prompt cache awareness** | Processes new results before they are recorded and batches historical pruning to control prefix rebuild frequency |

evidence.heading: Quick start
evidence.text:
1. Install the plugin (the web profile also gets the panel):

   ```bash
   dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-sieve@0.3.0 dsh-sieve-web@0.3.0
   ```

2. Configure a judge model, one of:
   - **Jev**: paste a TypeSafe or OpenRouter API key on the **Sieve** page of the DSH Web sidebar, or set the `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` environment variable;
   - **Laya**: start the Laya server on this machine and set `judge.type` to `laya` in the profile, see [Using Laya](#using-laya).
3. Restart `dsh web` and reload the page, then enter `/sieve status` in a session and check that the "判断模型" (judge model) line does not say "未配置" (not configured).

For other ways to install (GitHub Release, building from source) see [Installation](#installation).

evidence.heading: Architecture
evidence.text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Loop["DSH Agent Loop"]
        T[Tool execution] -->|post-execute| A
        P[agent/pre-step] --> F
        S[Skill catalog injection] --> D
    end

    subgraph Sieve["dsh-sieve"]
        A["tool.admissiontool.admission.test-log"]
        F[context.forget]
        D[skills.disclosure]
        K(("Judgment kernelJudge Engine"))
        A <--> K
        F <--> K
        D <--> K
    end

    K <-->|"System One / local HTTP"| J[("Judge modelJev · Laya")]
    A & F -->|originals| SP[(spill archive)]
    K -->|decision records| L[(ctx.storage ledger)]
    L --> W["/sieve command · Web panel"]

    A & F & D -->|reduced context| M[Main model request]
```

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **Judgment kernel** | One decision engine: builds the questions, calls the judge model, validates the structured answers and decides by confidence threshold whether to rewrite; a timeout or failure always keeps the original |
| **`tool.admission`** | Admission control for tool results before they enter the session; handles long output in tiers and rewrites only `content`, never the tool call |
| **`tool.admission.test-log`** | A dedicated admission path for test runs that protects failures, summaries and anything it does not recognize |
| **`context.forget`** | Forgets older tool results in batches through DSH's native `compaction/prune` and result replacement; a batch is committed only when it saves enough, see the [cache FAQ](#faq) |
| **`skills.disclosure`** | Filters the first skill catalog by task relevance and announces skills that become relevant in later turns; hidden skills can still be loaded directly |
| **Ledger** | One `ctx.storage` document per session with each judgment's result, usage and estimated saving |
| **`dsh-sieve-web`** | DSH We

evidence.heading: How does sieve improve LLM inference costs and token efficiency?
evidence.text:
sieve reduces redundant content repeatedly sent from tool output, older results and skill catalogs, lowering main model input token usage. Context compression here means content selection, pruning and retrieval from an archive; it does not modify model weights or the tokenizer.

Lower input usage does not translate directly into the same reduction in API costs. Net cost evaluation must include cached and uncached main model input, output tokens, Jev judge fees and any additional retrieval of originals; Laya also uses local compute resources. Existing experiments report request characters and main model token usage separately and do not establish an end-to-end net cost reduction for the current version.

evidence.heading: Do judge model calls use the main model's context?
evidence.text: No. A judge request carries only the content being judged and the task goal (redacted), goes to Jev or Laya, and its probabilities are used inside sieve only. Nothing of it is written to the session, and the main model never sees it.

github_projects.name: dsh-block-ptc
github_projects.description: Model-controlled context blocks for DeepSeek Harness PTC mode
github_projects.description_zh: 用于 DeepSeek Harness PTC 模式的模型控制上下文块。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Model-controlled context blocks for DeepSeek Harness PTC mode

evidence.heading: dsh-block-ptc
evidence.text:
**English | [中文](README.zh.md)**

[](https://github.com/mengwEX/dsh-block-ptc/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-block-ptc)
[](LICENSE)

Blackboard blocks for **PTC mode** in [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness).

Version `0.4.0` uses `block_compact({ ids, content })`. The old `block_summary`
tool and `summary`/single `id` arguments are not supported. Restart DSH and
start a new **Block PTC** session after updating.

The block protocol uses the built-in `run_code` transport.
DSH's PTC presentation allows only `run_code` to be called directly, so the
model declares blocks in the tool description:

```
run_code({ description: "[block: <ids>] <goal>", code })
```

A *block* is a blackboard region. Every program the model runs is tagged with
block ids. When the content is no longer needed, or its results have already
been reported and the model is moving to other work, it can submit retained
content **it writes itself** to replace the block's messages. Information still
needed for execution, replies or discussion remains available. The original messages stay in the append-only session log, so the
human transcript keeps everything and replay stays deterministic.

- DeepSeek Harness **0.2.1-rc.2 or newer**; no upper version bound
- Community plugin maintained by [mengwEX](https://github.com/mengwEX)
- **Zero runtime dependencies** — the only external import is `node:crypto`
- License: **MIT**

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
The model's whole surface is the built-in PTC transport plus one
program-callable:

```
run_code({ description: "[block: <ids>] <goal>", code })   the only tool it may call directly
await tools.block_compact({ ids, content })                  callable from inside a program
```

1. The header in `run_code.description` names the blocks a program advances.
   Its ids apply to the complete assistant message, including preceding
   thinking/text, and its tool results. Calls in the same assistant message
   contribute the union of their ids.
2. `tools.block_compact({ ids, content })` replaces the complete interval from
   the earliest to the latest occurrence of any target id with the retained content.
3. The summary inherits the union of the interval's ids minus the target ids.
   It can participate in a later summary. A summary with no remaining ids stays.
4. If a tool pair in the interval is unfinished, the request is queued until
   its result lands. A protected system/developer message refuses the
   entire interval; no prefix is silently replaced.

```text
A A B A C B  -- compact([A]) --> S[B] C B
S[B] C B    -- compact([B]) --> T[C]
T[C]        -- compact([C]) --> U[]
A A B A C B -- compact([A, B]) --> S[C]
```

What the human sees afterwards: the transcript still shows every original
turn (the log is append-only); the model's next request shows the summary
instead. In the Web UI the summary renders as a compaction checkpoint node.

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
Requirements: DeepSeek Harness `>=0.2.1-rc.2` and its bundled runtime, with
Cordis `>=4.0.5`. Neither peer range has an upper version bound. The plugin
is a profile **bundle**: installing it adds one row to `dsh.profile.bundles`
and one new agent preset, `block-ptc`. It does not modify the shipped `ptc`
preset.

The version ranges allow newer hosts to load the plugin; they are not a record
of completed compatibility checks. Live host verification for this release used
DSH `0.2.1-rc.2`. DSH's plugin loader includes prereleases when evaluating its
peer ranges. The plugin checks the required tool/prompt methods before mounting
and the session methods before summarizing, and reports missing capabilities.
Method presence does not verify event semantics, preset configuration or model
behaviour; these still need validation when the host changes.

evidence.heading: Manual install (equivalent, if you prefer files)
After installing
evidence.text:
1. The preset appears in the session preset picker as **Block PTC**.
2. **Restart the application once.** The loader keeps a plugin module per
   resolved URL, and installing a bundle changes the composition; a running
   host keeps the old module generation until it restarts.
3. Start a session with the **Block PTC** preset.

evidence.heading: Uninstall
evidence.text:
```
plugin_manager  remove_bundle  dsh-block-ptc
```

then restart. `plugin_manager set_bundle dsh-block-ptc enabled=false` disables
it without removing the package.

evidence.heading: Known limits
evidence.text:
- One summary replaces one complete contiguous first-to-last interval. A
  protected system/developer message rejects that interval; it is not
  skipped and no prefix is treated as a completed summary.
- The block header is model-authored. A call without it is refused before
  execution, so untagged work never enters a block.
- Omitted information is unavailable in later model requests. Preserve all
  details still needed for subsequent work in `content`.
- Checkpoints inherit remaining ids and may be summarized again. A checkpoint
  with empty ids is retained as the completed result.
- Blocks are per session. Sub-agents run their own context and their own blocks.
- Peer dependencies declare minimum versions without an upper bound. Newer
  hosts are allowed, but compatible event semantics and preset configuration
  still need verification.

evidence.heading: Agent Py
evidence.text:
[](https://github.com/kkjiangk/agent-py/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

A personal engineering project for investigating alerts with tool-backed evidence, retrieving runbooks, and reviewing remediation proposals. Built with **Python, FastAPI, Vue 3, LangGraph, Kafka, Redis, SQLite, and Milvus**.

The backend coordinates persistent work, enforces user ownership, and streams progress to the browser. It uses actual configured MCP tools and model providers for diagnosis. The current UI is Chinese; repository documentation is English.

evidence.heading: Features
evidence.text:
- **Authentication and ownership:** Argon2 password hashes, hashed bearer tokens, logout revocation, and user-scoped repositories and vector queries.
- **Streaming chat:** persistent conversations, LangChain agents, knowledge/MCP tools, configurable prompts, progressively loaded skills, and session memory.
- **Hybrid retrieval:** Markdown/PDF ingestion, durable indexing, Milvus vector recall, BM25L lexical recall, reciprocal rank fusion, and reranking with traceable citations.
- **Incident diagnosis:** a LangGraph Plan-Execute-Replan workflow, active Prometheus/Alertmanager alerts, evidence-linked reports, and persisted SSE events that survive browser disconnection.
- **Reliable event delivery:** manually committed Kafka offsets, retries before advancing to another record, Redis lease ownership checks, and sanitized dead letters.
- **Remediation approval:** an approval and dispatch job committed in one SQLite transaction, atomic dispatch leases, restart recovery, and a stable `commandId` for downstream deduplication.
- **Release and verification:** API/worker ECS revision checks and rollback tooling, real Kafka/Redis integration tests, Playwright browser tests, and public-only frontend configuration.

evidence.heading: Architecture
evidence.text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR

    API --> DB[(SQLite repositories and durable jobs)]
    API --> Chat[LangChain chat agent]
    API --> Kafka[Kafka alert events]
    Kafka --> Worker[Event worker]
    Worker --> Redis[(Redis leases and checkpoints)]
    Worker --> DB
    DB --> Graph[LangGraph diagnosis]
    Graph --> RAG[Hybrid retrieval]
    Chat --> RAG

    Graph --> MCP

```

See [Architecture](docs/architecture.md) and [Engineering decisions](docs/engineering-quality.md) for failure semantics, caching, and storage boundaries.

evidence.heading: Local development

evidence.heading: Retrieval benchmark
evidence.text:
A fixed-seed BM25 microbenchmark compared rebuilding an index for each query with reusing it:

| Chunks | Rebuild P95 | Reused index P95 | Rankings and scores |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1,000 | 6.83 ms | 0.91 ms | Identical |
| 10,000 | 104.23 ms | 44.32 ms | Identical |
| 100,000 | 1160.79 ms | 283.43 ms | Identical |

At 100,000 chunks, measured P95 fell by approximately **75.6%**. This measures only lexical index construction and ranking; it excludes database scans, Milvus, embeddings, reranking, network traffic, and concurrent API load. See [Benchmark methodology and raw results](docs/benchmarks/README.md).
