evidence.heading: dsh-workbuddy-trae-qoder-connect
evidence.text:
**WorkBuddy（国区版 + 国际版）、Qoder CN、Trae CN 的免费额度都能在这里用起来。这一个插件把三家接进 DeepSeek Harness：一个模型下拉、一份对话历史，打开面板顺手把能领的积分领掉。国际版另有限时免费模型（`deepseek-v4.1-flash` 当前 `x0.00`）。**

[](LICENSE)

> **English** — WorkBuddy (China and international), Qoder CN and Trae CN all hand out free quota. This one DSH plugin pools all three into a single model picker with one shared conversation history, and claims the day's check-in for you when the panel opens. The international edition has no check-in campaign but does carry limited-time free models (`deepseek-v4.1-flash` at `x0.00`). Switch channels mid-conversation without losing context, with live credit multipliers, per-model reasoning effort and image input.
---

evidence.heading: 它解决什么
evidence.text:
三家的额度散在三个客户端里。想都在 DSH 里用起来，就得装三个插件、开三个面板、维护三套凭据——而且每换一个渠道，对话历史就断一次。同类插件都是单渠道的，这个"散"一直没人收。

| | 三个单渠道插件 | **本插件** |
|---|---|---|
| 免费额度 | 三处分别看 | 一个面板看全部 |
| 模型下拉 | 三块，互不相通 | **一个列表**，按渠道分组，旁标积分倍率 |
| 中途换渠道 | 换插件 / 重开会话 | **直接换**，历史不丢 |
| 每日签到 | 点三次 | **打开面板一次全领** |
| 安装包 | 三个 | **一个** |

三家协议完全不同（OpenAI 方言、私有 agent 协议、带自定义编码的流式响应），插件在中间做翻译，对 DSH 和你来说它们长得一样。

evidence.heading: 你会得到什么
evidence.text:
**一个下拉装下三家。** 模型按渠道分组，每个模型旁标着积分倍率，哪个贵一眼可见。Trae CN 的目录最全，独占 `glm-5.3-flash`、`kimi-k2.8-preview`、`qwen3.8-flash` 等；WorkBuddy 国际版带来 `gpt-6-astra`、`grok-4.7`、`deepseek-v4.1-flash`（当前 `x0.00`，白用）这些国区没有的。

**对话中途换渠道，历史不断。** 从 Trae 的模型换到 WorkBuddy 的接着聊，上下文原样带过去。

**签到不用记。** 打开面板自动领当天能领的积分，重复打开也只领一次、不重复扣分。可以在设置里关掉。（国际版没有签到活动，会显示「不适用」；企业号同理。）

**额度看得见。** 每个渠道剩多少积分、按套餐怎么拆、什么时候重置，面板直接显示。

**思考档位是按模型给的。** 每个模型能选哪些档，来自上游目录的声明。点「更新模型」，档位连同目录一起刷新，哪些模型变了会直接告诉你；没手动选档时，新会话自动用该模型声明的默认档。上游没给的档位不硬造——实测「关思考」在两家上游直接返回 400，就不提供这个选项。少数老模型上游不声明档位，设置里留了一键实测补上（消耗少量额度，结果缓存）。

**能干活，不只是聊天。** Agent 工具调用（读文件、跑命令、改代码，Trae 渠道端到端实测过）、按模型开放读图、主力模型普遍 1M 上下文（上游对同一模型声明多档窗口时，插件默认取最大的那档，可在面板里关掉退回默认档）。

**管理和凭据省心。** 渠道就地增删改名，模型勾选即时生效、不用重启；新增渠道时选「国区 / 国际版」，插件按区域去读对应客户端的上游与凭据文件；国际版还能单独选这个槽位是**跟随桌面客户端的登录态**还是**只认自己的凭据**（默认后者）。凭据只写进 0600 权限的本地文件，界面从不回显，仓库里没有任何账号数据。

evidence.heading: 渠道一览
evidence.text:
| 渠道 | 接入内容 | 免费额度 | 登录方式 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WorkBuddy** | 个人版多账号（槽位不限）+ 企业版 | 每日签到领积分 | 脚本生成授权链接，浏览器登录 |
| **WorkBuddy AI 国际版** | 国际版客户端全部模型（GPT-6 / Gemini-3.x / GLM-5.3 / Kimi-K3 / Grok-4.7…） | **限时免费模型**，如 `deepseek-v4.1-flash`（倍率 `x0.00`） | 装客户端后扫码登录，或勾选跟随桌面客户端的登录态 |
| **Qoder CN** | 账号下全部模型 | 每日签到活动 | 官方 PAT，或直接用桌面 App 的登录态 |
| **Trae CN** | IDE 里的全部模型 | 每日签到领积分 | 本机客户端凭据导出 |

国际版（`www.workbuddy.ai`）和国区版是**两个独立客户端**，模型阵容差别很大——国际版有 `gpt-6-astra` / `grok-4.7` / `deepseek-v4.1-flash` 这些国区没有的，国区有 `deepseek-v3-2-volc` 等。装了哪个就自动读哪个；两个都装就两个渠道并排。每个国际版槽位还能单独选**跟随桌面客户端的登录态**（适合只有一份账号）还是**只认自己的凭据**（多账号时的默认，扫码登录互不干扰）。

**国际版没有签到活动**，它的免费额度体现在**限时免费模型**上：`deepseek-v4.1-flash` 当前倍率 `x0.00`，按倍率算不扣积分（倍率是上游实时给的，以模型列表里显示的为准）。国际版凭据是加密存的，插件用客户端自己的 Electron 解封，**不碰钥匙串、不落明文**。

**Trae 现在只有一个产品：Trae CN IDE。** 旧的独立客户端 TRAE SOLO CN 已被厂商并进 IDE（SOLO 变成 IDE 里的一个模式），所以只接 IDE 那一份目录——它也是模型最全的那份：

```bash
node scripts/export-trae-plain.mjs --app cn     # Trae CN IDE（默认，也是唯一在用的）
node scripts/export-trae-plain.mjs --list       # 看本机数据目录的登录态
```

并入前导出的旧 SOLO 快照（`$DSH_HOME/trae/`）仍然照常可用、不用重导；`--app solo` 只为还没迁移的机器保留。

evidence.heading: 安装
evidence.text:
前置：DSH 桌面版、Node ^22.19 或 ≥24。在 DSH 插件页粘贴仓库地址，重启一次 DSH，再配凭据：

```
https://github.com/chengshenyangtai/dsh-workbuddy-trae-qoder-connect
```

evidence.heading: 配凭据：把一句话发给 AI
evidence.text:
把下面这段复制给你的 AI 助手，剩下的它全包——生成 WorkBuddy 授权链接发到对话里、你浏览器点开授权、它轮询到成功落盘、导出 Trae 凭据、接上 Qoder 登录态，最后汇报各渠道状态与模型数：

```text
跑 scripts/ 下的脚本配好 dsh-workbuddy-trae-qoder-connect 三个渠道的凭据，
WorkBuddy 登录要轮询到成功为止。完成后汇报各渠道状态与模型数，提醒我重启 DSH。
```

想自己跑也行：`scripts/export-trae-plain.mjs`（Trae）、`scripts/workbuddy-login.mjs workbuddy1`（WorkBuddy，第二个账号换 `workbuddy2`，会持续轮询到授权成功）、Qoder 用桌面 App 登录态或把 `pt-…` PAT 存到 `$DSH_HOME/qoder/pat`。新建的账号槽位（如 `workbuddy3`）重启 DSH 后装载。

evidence.heading: 面板
evidence.text: 渠道中心 → 设置页：自动签到开关；停用渠道（模型隐藏、不参与签到，凭据保留，随时开回来）；模型勾选「已选 X / 共 N」（改完即生效）；档位实测入口（上游不声明的少数模型用）；侧栏入口开关。「更新模型」按钮按渠道独立刷新。

evidence.heading: Skill này làm gì?
evidence.text:
Pipeline đã kiểm chứng qua dự án thật "The Last Lantern" (8 cảnh, 2D Disney/Pixar):

| # | Giai đoạn | Kết quả |
|---|-----------|---------|
| 0 | Thu thập đầu vào | Thời lượng → số cảnh, ngôn ngữ, tỷ lệ 16:9/9:16 |
| 1 | Character sheets | Khóa nhân vật (nhiều góc + biểu cảm) |
| 2 | Story bible | Chốt kịch bản: logline, character lock, từng cảnh |
| 3 | Keyframes | K1..K(N+1), luật match-cut |
| 4 | Mega prompt | 1 prompt copy-paste cho mỗi cảnh |
| 5 | Generate video | Từng clip first-frame → last-frame |
| 6 | Làm VO | Kịch bản thuyết minh kiểu kể chuyện |
| 7 | Dựng phim | ffmpeg: normalize, nối, mix VO |

Kèm theo: **luật realism** (hành động vật lý phải đúng thực tế), **STRICT ASPECT RATIO LOCK** (ref đầu vào phải cùng tỷ lệ với output), và **10+ bài học xương máu**.

evidence.text:

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text:
Murmur


  



  Chat with your own AI agents, one at a time or all together.
  In the browser, on your Mac or PC, and on your phone.



  
    
      
      
    
  



  Get Murmur ·
  Your Hermes ·
  Features ·
  How it works ·
  Develop


Murmur is the app for [Hermes Agent](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent), the open-source agent that runs on your own hardware, remembers what matters, uses tools and gets things done. Murmur is the friendly face on top. There are no terminals, config files or jargon. Make a few agents, give each one a personality, and talk to them from anywhere.

evidence.heading: One Murmur, everywhere
evidence.text: Open it in any browser on your network, install the app for **macOS**, **Windows** or **Linux**, or add it to your phone's home screen. It's the same Murmur everywhere, with the same agents and chats, and every chat picks up where you left off on another device.

evidence.heading: Bring your Hermes, or start fresh
evidence.text: Murmur comes with Hermes built in, so you can start fresh with nothing else to install. Already have Hermes? It can live anywhere: on your Umbrel, a Mac in the closet, a Raspberry Pi or a server in the cloud. Murmur finds the ones on your network, or you can paste an address. Your agents, their memories and every past chat come along, including chats from the Hermes dashboard, Hermes Desktop, the terminal and Telegram. Nothing is imported or copied: it all stays in your Hermes.

evidence.heading: Make an agent in seconds
evidence.text: Start from a template (Researcher, Writer, Planner, Coder, Coach or Chef) or from scratch. Pick a name and a colour, say what it's for, and it's ready to talk.

evidence.heading: No model yet? Connect one in a minute
evidence.text: Sign in with your ChatGPT plan, or run a model right on your Umbrel: Murmur picks one that fits its memory and sets it up in one tap, using its graphics when it has them. Or use Ollama or another model server, or an API key from OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic and others. You can switch any time.

evidence.heading: Chats that show their work
evidence.text: Answers stream in as they're written. For bigger jobs, the agent writes a plan and ticks it off as it goes, and sends helpers off to work side by side, each with a line on what it's doing. When it's done, it all folds away. Searches, pages and commands show up in plain words, and you can open any step. Stop it, steer it mid-answer, or have the answer read aloud. Tap a heart on a reply, and your agents react to you, too.

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
- **Hermes does the work.** Agents are Hermes profiles and chats are Hermes sessions. Murmur reads and writes the same data, so it stays in sync with the Hermes dashboard, Hermes Desktop and Telegram.
- **Hermes comes along.** On umbrelOS and with Docker Compose, Murmur runs its own Hermes right beside it, private to Murmur. Or it uses a Hermes you already have.
- **Murmur is the experience.** A mobile-first React app and a tiny Node server with no dependencies. The browser never sees Hermes's access key.
- **The desktop app** is the same Murmur in a native window, with its server built in.

**[Get an API key](https://go.apimart.ai/k-f2714a)** · **[Live pricing](https://go.apimart.ai/k-7e8a7e)** · **[Model page](https://go.apimart.ai/k-b9e8bc)** · [⚡ 60-second quickstart](#quickstart)

**Why teams call Nano Banana Pro (official) (`gemini-3-pro-image-preview-official`) through APIMart**

- **One key, entire catalog.** The same `https://api.apimart.ai/v1` base URL and `Authorization` header reach Nano Banana Pro (official) (`gemini-3-pro-image-preview-official`) and 300+ other image, video and language models — switch the `model` field, not your client.
- **$1 minimum, pay as you go.** No subscription and no prepaid plan to size up front: top up from $1 and spend it on calls.
- **The charge comes back in the response.** Every completed task reports the amount billed (`cost` / `credits_cost`); a task marked `failed` is refunded.
- **Async by design.** Submit, take the `task_id`, poll `GET /v1/tasks/{id}` — batching and retries are ordinary queue work, not a bespoke integration.



The token-billed official route for Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image) on APIMart.

evidence.heading: Model id and routes
evidence.text:
| Route | `model` value | Billing | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Per-image | `gemini-3-pro-image-preview-official` | per delivered image, by resolution | see the [model page](https://go.apimart.ai/k-b9e8bc) for the exact tiers |

Endpoint: `POST https://api.apimart.ai/v1/images/generations` (OpenAI-compatible), then poll `GET /v1/tasks/{task_id}`.

| Output | List price | Effective price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| default | $0.0375 | $0.02 |
| 4K | $0.05 | $0.03 |

The token-billed official route bills per million tokens instead: `text_input` $1.60, `cached_text_input` free, `image_input` $1.60, `cached_image_input` free, `text_output` $9.60, `image_output` $96.00.


Prices are a snapshot; the [pricing page](https://go.apimart.ai/k-7e8a7e) and [`data/model.json`](data/model.json) are refreshed by CI, and a completed task reports the exact amount in its `cost` field.

evidence.text:
| Field | Type | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `model` | string | required | the model id shown in the route table above |
| `prompt` | string | required | what to generate, or what to change when editing |
| `size` | string | `auto` / `1:1` | aspect ratio, or `auto` where the route supports it |
| `resolution` | string | `1K` | output resolution tier — cost scales with it |

The table lists the fields accepted by the APIMart OpenAI-compatible image endpoint. Check the [model page](https://go.apimart.ai/k-b9e8bc) for anything this model adds on top.

evidence.heading: Quickstart
evidence.text:
```bash
curl --request POST --url https://api.apimart.ai/v1/images/generations \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $APIMART_API_KEY" --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"gemini-3-pro-image-preview-official","prompt":"A bamboo forest at sunrise, slow push-in","size":"1:1","resolution":"1K"}'
```

```python
import os, time, requests

BASE = "https://api.apimart.ai/v1"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['APIMART_API_KEY']}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}

created = requests.post(f"{BASE}/images/generations", headers=HEADERS, timeout=60, json={
    "model": "gemini-3-pro-image-preview-official", "prompt": "A bamboo forest at sunrise, slow push-in",
}).json()
task_id = created["data"]["id"]

while True:
    task = requests.get(f"{BASE}/tasks/{task_id}", headers=HEADERS, timeout=60).json()["data"]
    if task["status"] in ("completed", "failed"):
        break
    time.sleep(5)
print(task.get("cost"), task["result"]["images"][0]["url"])
```

Runnable versions: [`examples/`](examples). The task lifecycle is `pending → processing → completed | failed`.

github_projects.description: Distributed image and video generation in ComfyUI for two NVIDIA DGX Sparks.
github_projects.description_zh: 在 ComfyUI 中进行分布式图像和视频生成，适用于两台 NVIDIA DGX Sparks。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Distributed image and video generation in ComfyUI for two NVIDIA DGX Sparks.

evidence.heading: Use both Sparks in ComfyUI
evidence.text:
[](https://github.com/Deen-Media/dgx-monarch/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[](https://github.com/Deen-Media/dgx-monarch/actions/workflows/comfy-canary.yml)
[](LICENSE)

Generate images and video across two DGX Sparks from one ComfyUI window. Split a render between the GPUs, run separate prompts at once, or shard supported model weights to fit larger checkpoints.

DGX Monarch provides model loaders, samplers, memory controls, and 71 example workflows. Text encoding, VAE decode, saving, and the rest of your graph stay in ComfyUI.

[Get started](docs/QUICKSTART.md) · [Installation](docs/INSTALL.md) · [Model support](docs/MODELS.md) · [Benchmarks](docs/BENCHMARKS.md)

evidence.heading: Why use it?
evidence.text:
- **Wait less for a render.** Distribute one supported image or video job across the pair. The results below compare the same graph on one GPU and two.
- **Work on two prompts at once.** Fleet runs a separate render on each GPU, useful for trying prompts or processing independent jobs.
- **Fit larger models.** FSDP divides supported model weights between the GPUs. It is a capacity option and can be slower; text encoders, VAEs, and other driver work still need local memory.
- **Avoid unnecessary model copies.** Slab residency and low-RSS LoRA handling reduce duplicate weights in shared memory. Built-in checks compare these paths with stock residency before reuse.
- **Start with a model workflow.** Choose a template, select your files, and queue it. Automatic selection chooses a supported GPU layout for the model; the model guide explains the manual options.
- **See what the pair is doing.** The ComfyUI sidebar and `dgxm top` show memory use, render progress, connection state, and errors.

evidence.heading: Studio
evidence.text:
Studio is an optional browser workspace for the pair. Pick a bundled
workflow, write the prompt, queue renders on the driver and follow them on
one page, with Gallery, Queue, Grids, Fleet and Library views beside it.
Studio listens only on this computer. It signs your browser in with a link
that holds its access token; treat that link like a password. Install the
`studio` extra ([INSTALL](docs/INSTALL.md#optional-studio-companion)), tell
Studio once where ComfyUI listens, in `cluster.toml`
([CLUSTER](docs/CLUSTER.md#studio-optional)):

```toml
[studio]
driver = "http://127.0.0.1:8188"
```

Use the address your ComfyUI listens on; Studio keeps its records for the
first driver address it uses. Then start it on the computer that runs
ComfyUI:

```bash
dgxm studio
```

`dgxm studio` reads your `cluster.toml`, starts Studio and opens it in your
browser, or prints the link when there is no display. `dgxm studio up` keeps
it running as a user service, and `dgxm studio tunnel <host>` prints the SSH
line that reaches it from a laptop.

[](docs/STUDIO.md)

Shown with the CPU test fixture, so no model ran. Studio is a draft; the
[Studio guide](docs/STUDIO.md) covers setup, remote access and what is not
finished yet.

evidence.heading: Featured workflows
evidence.text:
Krea2 RAW and Turbo
Image generation, with LoRA support and several ways to split work across the pair.



MiniMax H3
Video with audio, plus image-guide and reference-video workflows.





Ideogram4
Image generation with support for its two-model workflow.



Qwen Image 2.1
Image generation and editing with up to ten references, including alpha-masked images.




The pack also includes [Kroma BF16, INT8 and 2x upscale workflows](docs/MODELS.md#model-kroma),
Flux, FLUX.3 Klein, MOSS-Image and its Kromoss fine-tune, Chroma, LTX, Hunyuan, Wan, and other families. Kroma uses the Krea2 runtime;
its resident BF16, local INT8 and BF16 2x refinement graphs matched their
[listed stock references](docs/VALIDATION.md#evidence-kroma). Manual
`uly2+fsdp` also matched these three workflows at batch 1; batch-2 `dp2+fsdp`
remains **CHECK** for stock fidelity. [Model support](docs/MODELS.md) lists the
tested configurations and limits for each. Support for one workflow does not
mean every precision, LoRA, or parallel mode has been tested.

evidence.heading: Measured results
evidence.text:
Recorded renders on two DGX Sparks connected over ConnectX-7 200G:

| Workflow | One GPU | Two GPUs | Speedup |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Krea2 RAW BF16, 1536×1536, 8 steps, CFG++ sampler, Ulysses | 74.1 s | 48.1 s | 1.54× |
| Ideogram4 FP8, dual-model, 1024×1024, 20 steps, Ulysses | 36.0 s | 26.0 s | 1.38× |
| MiniMax H3 INT8 ConvRot, 1280×720, 241 frames, 20 steps, Ulysses | 42m 03s | 23m 07s | 1.82× |

Krea2 and Ideogram4 timings are warm renders of matching graphs. Their separate one-step output checks matched one GPU; those checks do not prove equality at every step of a full render. Automatic selection now takes cfg2 for the Krea2 graph: on 2026-10-14 cfg2 was bit-identical to one GPU and ran the sampler 1.23× faster than Ulysses (36.3 s against 44.8 s; one GPU 72.9 s). Those are sampler times from [Campaign K](docs/BENCHMARKS.md#campaign-k-cfg2-against-uly2-2026-10-14-head-capped), with the first Spark capped at 2100 MHz, so compare them with each other, not with the table. H3 uses exact attention: the one-GPU timing is stock ComfyUI, while one Monarch worker took 42m 20s and matched the pair's output. Results depend on the settings and hardware; [benchmark details](docs/BENCHMARKS.md#selected-results) describe each comparison.

**Qwen Image 2.1:** 12 model formats matched native ComfyUI output in one-step tests. Separate full 25-step generation and editing tests also matched, including ten-reference editing. A comparable speed measurement has not been recorded. [Qwen test results](docs/VALIDATION.md#evidence-qwen-image-2-1).

[Full benchmarks](docs/BENCHMARKS.md) include slower configurations. [Validation](docs/VALIDATION.md) explains output comparisons and remaining gaps. [Campaign results](docs/CAMPAIGN_RESULTS.md) provide the detailed measurements.

evidence.heading: Watch the pair
evidence.text:
Run `dgxm top` to see memory use, render progress, GPU activity, and connection status in your terminal. The ComfyUI sidebar shows the same cluster while you work on a graph.

[](docs/TUI.md)

Dashboard shown with sample data. See the [TUI guide](docs/TUI.md) for setup, keyboard controls, and recording.

evidence.heading: Set up with a coding agent
evidence.text:
Use an agent with a shell on the driver Spark, approved SSH access to the other
Spark, and access to the selected ComfyUI and model directories. It needs
network access for source and dependency downloads. A browser-only agent cannot
complete the hardware steps without a connection to those machines. You may
need to approve maintenance or complete sudo, SSH trust, repository access, or
model-license steps yourself. Grant read or write access only where needed,
using the narrowest existing parent directories for files it will create.
Keep its sandbox enabled. Never paste private keys or tokens into chat.

Copy this prompt into your agent:

```text

Discover the existing setup and prerequisites first. Ask together for missing inputs and the specific read or write directory access you need. Then present one concise installation and recovery plan, explicitly listing package, service and any security changes for approval. Reuse that approval for the listed work; ask again only if the scope changes. Preserve existing environments, models, credentials and unrelated work. Never print credentials. Reuse my existing installation where suitable; ask where new permanent files should live. Ask whether I want the dgxm TUI and an easy launch script, and where to save the script. Do not install into temporary or chat-output folders. This is a normal installation, not a clean-machine acceptance test.

Use a supported model and workflow I already have or choose. Chroma is optional; recommend it only if

github_projects.name: gimp-openfill
github_projects.description: Generative Fill, object removal and Generative Expand for GIMP 3. A free, local alternative to Photoshop's AI tools, using Stable Diffusion through ComfyUI.
github_projects.description_zh: GIMP 3 的生成填充、对象移除和生成扩展。一款免费的本地替代 Photoshop AI 工具，通过 ComfyUI 使用 Stable Diffusion。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Generative Fill, object removal and Generative Expand for GIMP 3. A free, local alternative to Photoshop's AI tools, using Stable Diffusion through ComfyUI.

evidence.heading: OpenFill
evidence.text:
[](COPYING)     

*Generative fill, expand and object removal for GIMP 3, running on your graphics card. You own the whole pipeline, nothing leaves your computer.*


**Remove objects, fill a selection from a prompt, and expand the canvas, all inside GIMP.**




> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Beta.** This is an early release of OpenFill. It works end to end on Windows with GIMP 3.2.6 and an 8 GB laptop GPU, which is what I build and test on. It also runs end to end on Linux (GIMP 3.2.6 Flatpak on Fedora, RTX 2070 Max-Q), where the demo above was recorded, and on macOS (GIMP 3.2.6, Apple M3); the macOS steps are under Install. Most of the rough edges are in what the models draw, not in the plug-in; [Status](#status) lists them.

evidence.heading: Why I made this
evidence.text:
I moved to GIMP 3 as my Photoshop replacement after paying Adobe an outrageously expensive cancellation fee. GIMP turned out to be a great alternative, but Adobe's AI image editing tools had become part of my workflow and I wasn't ready to give them up, so I made OpenFill. It's meant to feel familiar and easy to use, especially if you're coming from Photoshop. The selection is the mask, the result is a layer you can paint on or delete, and the AI backend (ComfyUI) starts hidden, stays warm while you work, and shuts down when GIMP closes. No terminal, no browser tab, no second app to babysit.

Here's what you get:

|                        |                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Fill with a prompt** | Select, type "a red door with brass handles", Enter. The fill lands on a new layer with a mask that fades at the edges. |
| **Remove object**      | Select, switch to Remove object, Enter. No prompt. It erases the selection and continues the background.                |
| **Generative Expand**  | Drag the canvas edges outward or pick a ratio, and it paints the new border. The prompt is optional.                    |
| **Text to Image**      | A new layer or a new image from a prompt, sized to the selection if there is one.                                       |

Everything is under `Filters > OpenFill`. Results always go on new layers, in one undo step, so your existing layers are never painted over.

evidence.heading: Nothing leaves your computer
evidence.text:
Generation runs in ComfyUI on your machine, listening on `127.0.0.1` only. A small supervisor starts it hidden, watches GIMP, and stops it after an idle timeout or when GIMP closes. `Filters > OpenFill > Stop AI Backend` frees the graphics card right away.

The network comes into it twice: when the Models tab searches Hugging Face and Civitai (no account, no token, and you can turn it off), and when you press Download (a model, or ComfyUI itself when none is installed). Every file is checked against its size and SHA-256 before it's used. The gated FLUX files need a free Hugging Face token; it stays in your GIMP profile and only ever goes to Hugging Face. No accounts, no telemetry, nothing that phones home: the only outbound requests are the ones above. Details in [docs/security.md](docs/security.md).

evidence.heading: The dialogs
evidence.text:
| | |
|:---:|:---:|
|  |  |
| **Generative Fill.** Prompt, Recent prompts, what to avoid, the model and the number of variations are all on the first screen. Change amount and seed sit under Advanced. | **Remove object.** Same dialog, other tab. Nothing to type: it uses an installed removal model (LaMa or MAT) when there is one. |
|  |  |
| **Generative Expand.** Drag any edge of the thumbnail outward, or pick a ratio (1:1, 4:5, 3:2, 16:9 and the rest) and where the image sits on a 3x3 grid. It shows the new size as you drag. | **Progress.** Floats over your image without stealing focus: the step, time left, a live preview of the picture forming, and Cancel. |
|  |  |
| **Models.** The download manager. What you have installed first, then Recommended for this PC, then the rest, from Hugging Face and Civitai. | **Variations.** Ask for up to eight and click through them. The ones you don't keep stay hidden in a layer group in case you change your mind. |

evidence.heading: Models, and what fits your PC
evidence.text:
OpenFill doesn't ship a model. On first run it opens the download manager, where you get and manage models without leaving GIMP. Its Recommended for this PC list only shows models that fit your graphics memory and free disk space, so you never find out after a 7 GB download that a model is too big.

| Job | Default model | Graphics memory | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Remove object | LaMa (MAT also available) | 2 GB | about 3 s |
| Fast fill | DreamShaper 8 Inpainting | 4 GB | about 9 s |
| Quality fill | RealVisXL V5 with the Fooocus inpaint patch | 8 GB | about 21 s |
| Generative Expand | SD 1.5 Inpainting, then DreamShaper 8 | 4 GB | |

Times are for a 512 px selection on an RTX 4070 Laptop (8 GB); the first request of a session adds about 35 s while the backend starts. FLUX.1 Fill (8 GB as a GGUF, 16 GB full size) and Qwen-Image-Edit (12 GB) are opt-in and much slower. Without an NVIDIA card, SD 1.5 runs on the CPU in minutes rather than seconds; AMD GPUs are untested; on an Apple M3 a warm fill takes 50 to 90 s.

The defaults come from a judged benchmark of 33 cases per model. Every download is checked against a published SHA-256, and the live Hugging Face and Civitai search never offers pickled `.ckpt` or `.bin` files, since those can run code when loaded. Details in [docs/models.md](docs/models.md) and [docs/performance.md](docs/performance.md).

Already have models? OpenFill also finds your own SD 1.5 inpainting and SDXL checkpoints in ComfyUI's `checkpoints` folder, and FLUX.1 Fill files in `unet` or `diffusion_models`, and lists them in the model menu as "your file", with no download. It reads only `.safetensors` and `.gguf` files, and only their headers, to tell the model family apart.

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
1. **Install [GIMP 3.2](https://www.gimp.org/downloads/).**
2. **Add the plug-in.** Download `openfill-<version>.zip` from the [Releases page](https://github.com/beckettharriman/gimp-openfill/releases), unzip it, and drag the `gimp-openfill` folder into GIMP's plug-ins folder (`Edit > Preferences > Folders > Plug-ins`; on Windows that's `%APPDATA%\GIMP\3.2\plug-ins`).
3. **Restart GIMP and run `Filters > OpenFill > Generative Fill...`.** If ComfyUI isn't found, **Download ComfyUI** sets it up for you (Windows with an NVIDIA card, about 2 GB), or **I already have ComfyUI** lets you pick an existing install.
4. **Get the starting models** when the model manager opens: LaMa (object removal, 0.2 GB) and DreamShaper 8 Inpainting (fill and expand, 2 GB). The first request starts the backend in about a minute; after that it's seconds.


What Download ComfyUI does

It checks your graphics card, free disk space and port 8188 first, then fetches the official Windows portable build (about 2 GB, about 7 GB unpacked) into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenFill\ComfyUI`, checks it against a published SHA-256, unpacks it with Windows' own `tar.exe`, adds the inpaint nodes at a pinned commit and OpenCV, and remembers the folder. Git is not needed.

Without an NVIDIA card the notice says so and offers the download only as "very slow" (the processor does the work). For an AMD card it points to ComfyUI's AMD instructions, after which you choose "I already have ComfyUI". The same notice appears, instead of an error, whenever you start Fill, Remove or Expand and ComfyUI can't be found.




If something goes wrong

Every error message ends with what to do next, and the same advice shows in the progress window. For a bug report, turn on Verbose log in Settings, do it again, and attach the log file. Never a

evidence.heading: Status
evidence.text:
Works end to end on Windows, on Linux (GIMP 3.2.6, including the Flatpak) and on macOS (GIMP 3.2.6, Apple M3): fill, remove, expand, text to image, the model manager, variations, and the backend starting and stopping itself. On Windows, 25 failure scenarios (no backend, corrupt settings, port in use, ComfyUI or GIMP killed mid-job, no network, cancel at every stage) pass in a real GIMP, and the unit tests run on any Python 3.10 or newer.

Where the models still fall short:

- **SD 1.5 often ignores the prompt** on flat areas and small selections. Pick an SDXL model in the dialog.
- **Remove object struggles with very large holes.** LaMa smears and MAT invents shapes; both are fine on small objects.
- **Generative Expand gets weaker beyond 25% per side.** Expand in rounds; OpenFill also splits large expansions itself.
- Fine textures like fabric come back softer in large fills.

Not tested yet: FLUX and Qwen end to end, Intel Macs, and the AUTOMATIC1111 backend. Next up: ControlNet and reference images, and LoRA selection. Changes are in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md); [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) covers the tests.

github_projects.description: Eleven free Claude skills that run an X account, with a virality engine behind every idea: posts off 21 hook formulas, threads, replies, profile score, weekly plan, analytics audit and a humanizer. Free, MIT.
github_projects.description_zh: Eleven 免费的 Claude 技能，可运行 X 账户，每个创意背后都有传播引擎：发布 21 个吸引公式、帖子、回复、个人资料评分、每周计划、分析审计和人性化。免费，MIT。

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Eleven free Claude skills that run an X account, with a virality engine behind every idea: posts off 21 hook formulas, threads, replies, profile score, weekly plan, analytics audit and a humanizer. Free, MIT.

evidence.heading: The X agent skill
evidence.text:
Eleven Claude skills that run an X account. Free, MIT, no signup, no API key,
nothing to connect.

They write your posts, comment on other people's threads, handle your replies,
fix your profile and plan your week. And one of them is the virality skill: it
finds the posts that are actually outperforming in your niche, breaks each one
down into hook, structure and format, and recreates the winners in your voice,
for your audience.

Under the skills are nine tools that actually run. One counts a post the way X
counts it (links are 23, emoji are 2). One scores your first line before you
post it. One cuts a draft into a thread that fits. One reads X's own published
ranking code and tells you what it rewards this week. One reads your analytics
export and tells you what worked, with the sample size on every claim.

**Nothing is posted until you approve it.** These skills write. You post.

evidence.heading: Install
evidence.text:
Paste this into Claude:

```
https://github.com/Jakeschincariol/x-agent-skill

Install this skill, then confirm /x-post works.
```

Or do it yourself, in Claude Code:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Jakeschincariol/x-agent-skill.git
cp -r x-agent-skill/skills/x-* ~/.claude/skills/
```

Or as a plugin:

```
/plugin marketplace add Jakeschincariol/x-agent-skill
/plugin install x-agent
```

Project-local instead of global: copy the same folders into your repo's
`.claude/skills/`. No Claude Code at all? Paste any single `SKILL.md` at the
top of a chat and it runs as a mode. You lose the Python tools, which is most
of the point of `/x-post`, `/x-viral` and `/x-human`, but the rest works.

Then spend ten minutes on [`templates/voice.md`](templates/voice.md). Copy it
to `~/.claude/x/voice.md` and fill it in, or paste five of your own posts into
Claude and say "write my voice.md from these". Every skill reads that file.
Skip it and everything comes out sounding like everyone else on the timeline.

evidence.heading: The eleven
evidence.text:
| command | | what it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/x-post` | Post Writer | One idea into a post. Three hooks from [21 formulas](skills/x-post/hooks.json), scored, one draft, counted the way X counts, humanized. |
| `/x-comment` | Comment Drafter | Replies on other people's posts and threads. Nine types, picked by what the post is. Reply or quote, decided first. |
| `/x-profile` | Profile Optimizer | Scores your profile against a [12-part rubric](skills/x-profile/rubric.json) out of 100, then rewrites bio, pinned post and header in fix-first order. |
| `/x-reply` | Reply Handler | The replies under your own posts, sorted into lead / substance / peer / question / support / noise, then answered in that order. |
| `/x-plan` | Content Planner | The week: what to post, which format, when, and the 10 accounts to engage with. |
| `/x-viral` | Virality Engine | Finds what is outperforming in your niche, ranks it by multiple over each account's own median, breaks down hook, structure and format, recreates the top three for you. |
| `/x-thread` | Thread Builder | Thread, long post or single post, decided first. Then post 1, one idea per post, cut to fit, and a last post people act on. |
| `/x-human` | Humanizer | Strips em dashes, slop and invisible characters, then scores the draft on a five-check panel. |
| `/x-repurpose` | Repurposer | One video, podcast, newsletter or LinkedIn post into a week of X posts and a thread. |
| `/x-dm` | DM Handler | The first message, two follow-ups, and triage for your inbox and message requests. |
| `/x-audit` | Account Audit | Reads your analytics export. Ranks by engagement, replies and shares per impression, not by impressions. |

evidence.heading: The nine tools
evidence.text:
Every one runs on a clean Python 3 with no dependencies. Seven never touch the
network. `pull.py` calls X's documented oEmbed API and `weights.py` reads a
public GitHub file; neither needs an account or a key.

```bash
python3 skills/x-post/count.py post.txt                   # X's weighted count + six lints
python3 skills/x-post/hookscore.py hooks.txt              # score and rank first lines, name the formula
python3 skills/x-thread/thread.py draft.txt --number      # cut a draft into a thread that fits
python3 skills/x-human/humanize.py draft.txt --report     # strip the fingerprint
python3 skills/x-human/detect.py before.txt after.txt     # five-check panel, before and after
python3 skills/x-viral/pull.py urls.txt > swipe.tsv       # post URLs you picked -> text, format, date
python3 skills/x-viral/swipe.py swipe.tsv                 # outliers, broken down, as a swipe file
python3 skills/x-audit/audit.py analytics.csv             # what worked, with n on every claim
python3 skills/x-plan/weights.py                          # what X's ranker rewards, live from X's code
```

evidence.heading: Counting the way X counts
evidence.text:
X does not count characters. It counts weighted characters: every link is 23
however long it is, every emoji is 2 (a family emoji built from seven code
points is still 2), Chinese, Japanese and Korean are 2, and "…" is 2, which is
more than the three dots it replaces. `count.py` implements those rules, then
draws the post the way the timeline shows it:

```
  WHAT FITS
  +------------------------------------------------------+
  | Most people use AI to post more. I used it to post   |
  | less.                                                |
  |                                                      |
  | In March I cut from 3 posts a day to 1. Followers    |
  | went from 2,100 to 6,800 by August.                  |
  |                                                      |
  | The system: one idea a day, drafted with Claude, cut |
  | in half by me, and I'm there for the first hour of   |
  | replies.                                             |
  |                                                      |
  | Showing up beats post                                |
  +------------------------------------ cut here, 4 over +

  FAIL  LENGTH      284 / 280, 4 over. X will not let you post it.
  PASS  FIRST LINE  56 characters, reads in one glance
  PASS  LINKS       none
  PASS  HASHTAGS    0
  PASS  MENTIONS    0
  PASS  ENDING      no reflex bait
```

With `--premium` the limit is 25,000 and the box shows where the timeline cuts
a long post to "Show more", at about 280. It also flags an @mention past that
point, because X does not notify it.

evidence.heading: The hook
evidence.text:
On X the first line is not the start of the post. It is most of the post.
`hookscore.py` scores it on five properties (length, specificity, stakes,
whether the payoff is up front, who it is aimed at), flags the dealbreakers,
and names which of the 21 formulas it uses:

```
HOOK RANKING
==============================================================================
-> 100.0 STRONG  Nobody tells you your first 1,000 followers come from rep...
        #6 Nobody Tells You  ·  weakest: LENGTH (100)
    78.4 STRONG  I posted every day for 90 days. Here's what actually move...
        #2 Number Reveal  ·  weakest: FRONTLOAD (70)
    52.2 OK      The hottest new marketing hire is a skill file.
        #7 The Hottest New  ·  weakest: SPECIFICITY (15)
    36.2 WEAK    Hey guys, here are some thoughts on growing on X
        #21 The One-Liner  ·  weakest: STAKES (20)
        dealbreaker: Greeting. Nobody opened X to be greeted.
     4.8 WEAK    A thread 🧵
        #16 Thread Promise  ·  weakest: FRONTLOAD (0)
        dealbreaker: Opens on the word "thread". That is packaging. Put the
                     payoff in line 1 and let X's own UI say it is a thread.
```

Every formula in [`hooks.json`](skills/x-post/hooks.json) carries a template,
a filled example, what it is for, how it usually gets ruined, and a regex, so
the same 21 names describe a hook you are writing and a hook you found in
someone else's feed. That is what lets `/x-viral` say "the top third of your
niche is The Hottest New and Field Report" instead of "posts that did well".

evidence.heading: The fine print, which is the honest part
evidence.text:
**These skills do not post, reply, like, follow or DM.** X's API does allow
posting with your own developer app and OAuth, unlike LinkedIn's. As of
September 2026 it is pay-per-use: $0.015 a post, $0.20 for a post with a link,
credits bought upfront ([pricing](https://docs.x.com/x-api/getting-started/pricing)).
It is still not built here, on purpose. X's
[automation rules](https://help.x.com/en/rules-and-policies/x-automation)
prohibit automated likes, bulk follows and unsolicited automated replies, and
AI reply bots need X's written approval, and replies and comments are most of
what this pack writes. So every skill ends the same way: a copy-ready block,
and you paste it.

**`/x-viral` reads, it does not scrape.** X's Terms prohibit crawling or
scraping "in any form, for any purpose" without written consent. You pick the
posts; `pull.py` only fetches URLs you give it, through the documented oEmbed
API, one per second, capped at 100 a run. It never logs in, never uses your
session and never fetches counts. You read those off the screen.

**`hookscore.py` is a lint, not a predictor.** The same five-property panel,
tested on 74 real short-form hooks in the Instagram version of this pack,
separated real hooks from deliberately bad ones well (AUC 0.83) and a
creator's own hits from their own misses barely at all (AUC 0.56, a coin flip
is 0.50). It has not been re-calibrated on X. It catches labels, greetings and
hooks with nothing concrete in them. It will not tell you which of two decent
hooks will travel. `/x-audit` on your own posts will.

**The link question is left to your data.** X says it stopped down-ranking
posts with links more than a year ago (Musk and Nikita Bier, July 2026). An
independent analysis in January 2026 still measured fewer views on them. The
pack do

github_projects.description: Long-term memory for AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, opencode) as a tree of plain files

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Long-term memory for AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, opencode) as a tree of plain files

evidence.heading: IHMT — Infinite Hierarchical Memory Tree
evidence.text:
[](https://mcpservers.org/servers/gonzaroman/ihmt-memory)
[](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/gonzaroman/IHMT-MEMORY)



**Long-term memory for your AI coding agents.** Tell your agent something once — a decision, how
your setup works, a correction — and it remembers it in every future session, in any project, with
any of your agents.

evidence.heading: What IHMT does
evidence.text:
- **Remembers across sessions.** Decisions and their reasons, your environment, your preferences,
  people and projects, corrections. Your agent searches the memory before answering and saves what
  lasts, so you stop repeating yourself.
- **One memory for all your agents and models.** Claude Code, Codex and opencode can share the same
  memory: what one saves, the others find. Tested with models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Meta.
- **Saves tokens.** Instead of pasting your notes or re-explaining context every session, the agent
  retrieves only what the question needs — typically 200–900 tokens, whether the memory holds 50
  entries or 50,000, because search walks a tree instead of reading everything.
  [Honest numbers](GUIDE.md#11-honest-numbers), including where it does *not* save.
- **Understands time.** When something changes ("I moved to Valencia", "staging is on PostgreSQL 17
  now"), the old memory is kept as history, flagged `OUTDATED`, and searches answer with the current
  one first. Where you live, where you work and your stack are tracked automatically; any other
  correction is linked when the agent saves it with `replaces`. When a question is ambiguous ("Luis"
  — which one?), it asks instead of guessing.
- **Portable.** Your memory is one folder of plain text files. Copy it to another computer, back it
  up, or put it under version control — it works wherever you put it.
- **Local, private and readable.** No cloud, no database, no account: IHMT stores everything on your
  disk and sends nothing anywhere. (The memories your agent retrieves reach its model like any other
  context.) Every memory is a text file you can open, and each person who installs IHMT starts with
  their own, empty memory.

> **Compatibility.** Officially supported: **Claude Co

evidence.heading: Let your AI agent install it
evidence.text:
Paste this into the AI agent you want to give a memory to — **Claude Code**, **Codex** and
**opencode** are tested; **GitHub Copilot**, **Antigravity**, **Cursor**, **Windsurf**, **Gemini CLI**,
**Claude Desktop** and other MCP clients should work too:

```
Install the IHMT memory MCP server for me from https://github.com/gonzaroman/IHMT-MEMORY — follow the instructions in its INSTALL.md.
```

The agent follows [`INSTALL.md`](INSTALL.md): it downloads IHMT to `~/IHMT-MEMORY`, keeps your
memory in `~/.ihmt`, registers the server **with itself only**, adds the usage instructions, and
tells you what it did. Then start a new session so the memory tools load.

**Using several agents?** Paste the same prompt in each one, whenever you want. If IHMT is already
installed — say you have used it with Claude for months and now want it in Codex — the agent finds
that installation, updates it if it safely can, and connects to the **same memory**, so it knows
what you told the others from day one.

It needs an agent that can run terminal commands or edit files; chat-only assistants in a browser
cannot install anything.


Manual install

Requirements: Python 3.10+, git, and your agent's CLI.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/gonzaroman/IHMT-MEMORY.git ~/IHMT-MEMORY
cd ~/IHMT-MEMORY
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-mcp.txt
mkdir -p ~/.ihmt
```

```bash

claude mcp list                     # ihmt-memory … ✔ Connected
```

The server name must come before `-e`. Then append
[`templates/memory-instructions.md`](templates/memory-instructions.md) to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`.

**Codex** — `codex mcp add ihmt-memory --env IHMT_HOME="$HOME/.ihm

evidence.heading: How it works
evidence.text:
A universal, domain-agnostic long-term memory for LLMs, stored as a recursive tree of plain files on
the local disk. No vector database, no server, **no third-party dependencies** — Python 3.10+ and the
standard library.

Instead of embedding everything into one flat index and scanning it, IHMT organizes knowledge into a
tree: raw text leaves at the bottom, recursive JSON summaries above them, and a single `root.json`
trunk at the top. A query walks that tree — root → branch → branch → leaf — so the number of files
opened grows with the *depth* of the tree (`≈ beam × log_B(n)`), not with the amount stored.

| | Flat RAG | IHMT |
|---|---|---|
| Retrieval cost | scan / ANN over all *n* chunks | `beam × log_B(n)` file reads |
| Structure | none — a bag of vectors | explicit hierarchy, inspectable |
| Chunking | fixed character windows | syntax-, scene- and date-aware |
| Stale facts | served silently | superseded, dated, and flagged |
| Ambiguity | returns a plausible guess | asks you for a clue |
| Storage | binary index | UTF-8 `.txt` + JSON you can read |

evidence.heading: Quick start
evidence.text:
```bash
python3 gui.py                       # graphical interface: set up, browse, inspect
python3 init_ihmt.py                 # or from the terminal: create ./ihmt_memory
python3 main.py demo                 # full walkthrough in ./demo_workspace
python3 -m unittest discover -v      # stdlib only; MCP tests skip without the SDK
```

Then use it on your own material:

```bash
python3 main.py ingest ~/notes ~/project/src/Main.java
python3 main.py consolidate --force
python3 main.py search "how did we handle stock reservations"
python3 main.py ask "Luis"                    # interactive clue loop
python3 main.py conflicts                     # what changed over time
```

As a library:

```python
from ihmt import IHMT

memory = IHMT.initialize("./workspace")
memory.ingest_file("examples/InventoryService.java")
memory.ingest_file("examples/journal_personal.txt")
memory.flush()                                # close the tree up to the root

answer = memory.search("reserveStock soft hold")
print(answer.best.content)                    # the leaf
print(answer.best.path)                       # ['root', 'N1-software.java-…', 'L-software.java-…']
print(answer.node_reads)                      # how many branch files were opened

for notice in memory.notices():
    print(notice)   # "On 2024-03-11 you said user location = 'Madrid', but on 2026-02-03 you updated to 'Valencia'."
```

evidence.heading: Use it from Claude Code (MCP)
evidence.text:
`mcp_server.py` exposes the tree to Claude Code as nine tools in three families: long-term memory,
project indexes and session scratch memory. The core stays dependency-free; the
SDK is an optional extra:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-mcp.txt        # mcp[cli]>=2.0
```

For a single project, copy `.mcp.json.example` to that project's `.mcp.json` and fill in the absolute
paths; Claude Code asks you to approve it on the next session there (`claude mcp list` shows it as
*Pending approval* until then):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ihmt-memory": {
      "command": "/absolute/path/to/IHMT-MEMORY/.venv/bin/python",
      "args": ["/absolute/path/to/IHMT-MEMORY/mcp_server.py"],
      "env": { "IHMT_HOME": "/absolute/path/to/IHMT-MEMORY" }
    }
  }
}
```

or in one command:

```bash
claude mcp add ihmt-memory --scope user \
  -e IHMT_HOME=/absolute/path/to/IHMT-MEMORY \
  -- /absolute/path/to/IHMT-MEMORY/.venv/bin/python /absolute/path/to/IHMT-MEMORY/mcp_server.py
```

`IHMT_HOME` selects the store (`$IHMT_HOME/ihmt_memory`), created on first use. Point every project at
one shared directory for a single cross-project memory, or give each project its own.

| Tool | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `search_memory(query, clue=None, detail="compact")` | Walks the tree. Compact output: the best memory with its date and `OUTDATED` notices, one line per other match; `detail="full"` adds ids, tree paths and excerpts. An ambiguous query returns an `AMBIGUOUS` block listing the candidates instead of guessing — call again with `clue`. A query that matches nothing says so, and so does one whose closest entry shares only a stray word with it (`NOT FOUND`). |
| `save_memory(content, domain="general", content_type="auto", replaces="")` | Classifies, splits a

evidence.heading: Design notes and limits
evidence.text:
* **Retrieval is a descent, not a scan.** That is the whole point, and it means a branch pruned at
  the trunk is not revisited. Domain-level pruning only happens when a query has actual signal at the
  trunk; if it has none, every domain stays in play and the beam applies one level down. The clue
  loop is the recovery mechanism when the descent goes wide.
* **Lexical, not semantic.** Matching is BM25 over accent-folded, CamelCase-split tokens: it works in
  any language and needs no model, but it will not match a synonym. Plugging an embedding re-ranker
  into `BM25Ranker` is the natural upgrade; the tree structure does not change.
* **Token counts are estimated** at ~4 characters per token. Budgets only need to be consistent, not
  exact.
* **Fact extraction is pattern-based.** The bundled rules cover common English/Spanish phrasings and
  clinical headers; `record_fact()` is the reliable path, and `add_pattern()` extends the rules.
* **Single-writer.** Writes are atomic (`tmp` + `os.replace`) and catalog rebuilds take a lock file,
  but the store assumes one writer at a time.
* `initialize(force=True)` discards *derived* state only — branches, catalog, timeline — and detaches
  the surviving leaves so the next consolidation rebuilds the hierarchy. Leaf content is never
  deleted.

```bash
curl --request POST --url https://api.apimart.ai/v1/images/generations \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $APIMART_API_KEY" --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-image-2-official","prompt":"A bamboo forest at sunrise, slow push-in","size":"1:1","resolution":"1K"}'

```python
import os, time, requests

BASE = "https://api.apimart.ai/v1"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['APIMART_API_KEY']}", "Content-Type": "application/json"}

created = requests.post(f"{BASE}/images/generations", headers=HEADERS, timeout=60, json={
    "model": "gpt-image-2-official", "prompt": "A bamboo forest at sunrise, slow push-in",
}).json()
task_id = created["data"]["id"]

while True:
    task = requests.get(f"{BASE}/tasks/{task_id}", headers=HEADERS, timeout=60).json()["data"]
    if task["status"] in ("completed", "failed"):
        break
    time.sleep(5)
print(task.get("cost"), task["result"]["images"][0]["url"])
```

evidence.text: Agent OpenTelemetry (otel) rules pack: enriches opentelemetry with agent telemetry, steps, access rights and policy to explain agent failure.

evidence.heading: Trustabl Agent OpenTelemetry Rules — v0.1
evidence.text:
A small Apache-2.0 OpenTelemetry process-metadata profile (`trustabl.*` span
attributes and events) plus a deterministic runtime rule format, published as
data so any observability backend can evaluate it against live agent trace data.

evidence.heading: What this is not
evidence.text:
- **Not loaded, parsed, or evaluated by `trustabl scan`.** The
  [`agent-reliability-analyzer`](https://github.com/trustabl/agent-reliability-analyzer)
  engine never imports or fetches anything from this repository. Nothing here
  is part of that engine's `ScanResult`, `RulesSkipped`, or
  `SupportedSchemaVersion` compatibility contract.
- **Not related to `agent-reliability-rules`**, the engine's own
  static-analysis rule pack repo. Those rules are pulled and evaluated
  *in-process* by the `trustabl` binary against source code it just parsed.
  The rules in this repository are evaluated by third-party observability
  backends (Grafana, Langfuse, Datadog, OpenLIT, …) against live OpenTelemetry trace
  data — the `trustabl` binary is never in that loop.

evidence.heading: Layout
evidence.text:
- [`attribute-profile.yaml`](attribute-profile.yaml) — the v0.1 `trustabl.*`
  span attribute and event reference.
- [`rule-ir-schema.yaml`](rule-ir-schema.yaml) — the rule YAML shape reference.
- [`rules/`](rules/) — all twelve v0.1 rules, each as a YAML file:
  `tool_loop`, `retry_storm`, `policy_absent`, `policy_drift`,
  `contract_drift`, `irreversible_unguarded`, `constraint_hit` (shadow),
  `false_idempotent`, `handoff_unbound`, `instrumentation_degraded`,
  plus two from the DSPM addendum: `dspm_unbound`, `denied_then_answered`.
- [`translations/`](translations/) — worked translations of the rules into
  vendor-native formats. Confidence varies by backend — see each subdirectory's
  own README for specifics:

    alerting-rule provisioning YAML, shaped for self-publish to Grafana's
    own catalog.
  - [`translations/langfuse/`](translations/langfuse/) — a score-config JSON.
    Apply against your own Langfuse project via their API.
  - [`translations/datadog/`](translations/datadog/) — a Monitor API JSON
    object. Apply against your own Datadog org.
  - [`translations/dunetrace/`](translations/dunetrace/) — a `detectors.yml`

  - [`translations/phoenix/`](translations/phoenix/) — a Python span evaluator
    function. **Speculative** — shape inferred from Phoenix's evaluator API.
  - [`translations/langsmith/`](translations/langsmith/) — a saved-filter
    query. **Most speculative of the seven** — LangSmith's filter grammar
    cannot fully express the sliding-window condition in one filter.
  - [`translations/openlit/`](translations/openlit/) — a Cl

evidence.heading: v0.1 rules
evidence.text:
All twelve rules are authored as YAML files in [`rules/`](rules/), each
following the shape defined in [`rule-ir-schema.yaml`](rule-ir-schema.yaml):

| Rule | Severity | Fix class | Shadow |
|------|----------|-----------|--------|
| [`tool_loop`](rules/tool_loop.yaml) | high | `policy.cap_tool` | no |
| [`retry_storm`](rules/retry_storm.yaml) | high | `policy.cap_retries` | no |
| [`policy_absent`](rules/policy_absent.yaml) | high | `policy.require_bundle` | no |
| [`policy_drift`](rules/policy_drift.yaml) | high | `policy.pin_bundle` | no |
| [`contract_drift`](rules/contract_drift.yaml) | high | `policy.pin_contract` | no |
| [`irreversible_unguarded`](rules/irreversible_unguarded.yaml) | critical | `policy.require_constraint` | no |
| [`constraint_hit`](rules/constraint_hit.yaml) | medium | `policy.review_constraint` | **yes** |
| [`false_idempotent`](rules/false_idempotent.yaml) | high | `policy.audit_tool` | no |
| [`handoff_unbound`](rules/handoff_unbound.yaml) | high | `policy.require_bundle_on_handoff` | no |
| [`instrumentation_degraded`](rules/instrumentation_degraded.yaml) | medium | `instrumentation.add_emitter` | no |
| [`dspm_unbound`](rules/dspm_unbound.yaml) | high | `policy.require_bundle` | no |
| [`denied_then_answered`](rules/denied_then_answered.yaml) | high | `policy.require_constraint` | no |

`constraint_hit` is shadow-only: constraint fires are expected behavior, not a
defect — the rule surfaces them for trend analysis without paging anyone.

The Grafana translation in [`translations/grafana/`](translations/grafana/) is
fully worked for `tool_loop`. The other eleven rules follow the same mapping;
translating them is the next translation-pack slice.

evidence.heading: Status
evidence.text:
v0.1, first slice. No translator tooling exists yet — every vendor translation
is hand-authored to prove (or, for the three speculative packs, sketch) the
rule-IR-to-vendor-format mapping, not generated. Licensed Apache-2.0.

evidence.heading: About this repo
evidence.text:
whatmodel is an open-source AI leaderboard database. The data, scoring and ranking engine,
and benchmark tools are available here. This README and [pages/](pages) are generated from the
same data and code with `npm run pages`.

An interactive version of the database can be found at [whatmodel.sh](https://whatmodel.sh). Every model has its own page showing
what it's good at, how each test result compares with other models, and how to run it:



| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `data/` | Models, benchmark results, prices, measured speeds and hardware. Every number links to its source. |
| `data/extracts/` | Share-alike source extracts, published separately as their licences require |
| `lib/` | The engine: scores (`score.ts`), memory fit and ranking (`fit.ts`), page data (`views.ts`), terminal output (`format.ts`), markdown pages (`markdown.ts`) |
| `pages/` | The other leaderboards, the method and one page per model, generated |
| `bench.sh`, `bench.py` | Interactive benchmark launcher and runner; see [BENCHMARKING.md](BENCHMARKING.md) |
| `scripts/` | Checks, import, export, page generation and measurement scripts |
| `licenses/` | Full licence notices for every source |
| `docs/` | Source audit, validation and coverage reports |

evidence.heading: From your terminal
evidence.text:
```sh
curl "whatmodel.sh/?ram=32&gpu=apple"
curl "whatmodel.sh/image?ram=64&gpu=card&vram=24&format=json"
```

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ram`, `vram` | GB, or raw bytes / kB / MiB as the OS reports them |
| `gpu` | `apple`, `card` (NVIDIA, AMD or Intel graphics card) or `none` |
| `mac` | bytes, optionally followed by a newline and the chip name; implies Apple Silicon |
| `nv` | `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,memory.total --format=csv,noheader` output |
| `hw` | exact chip or card id from `data/hardware.json` |
| `max` | highest price in the category's unit (LLMs: $ per 1M tokens, blended 3:1 in:out); `0` = local only |
| `sort`, `dir` | `score`, `where`, `speed`, `ram` or `context`; `asc` or `desc` |
| `set` | optional model-set filter; omitted = all sets, without changing the overall score scale |
| `score` | `set` uses only the selected set’s evaluations; omitted = overall scores, with uncalibrated scores/ranks reported as null |
| `all=1`, `n=20`, `format=json`, `color=1`, `chart=1` | show models that don't fit, row limit (text: 10, JSON: 40), JSON, ANSI colour, charts |
| `width=120`, `help=1` | wider terminal table (default: 80 columns), concise command help |

The same output runs from this repo, with no server:

```sh
npm install
npm run board -- "ram=32&gpu=apple"
npm run board -- image "ram=64&gpu=card&vram=24"
```

evidence.heading: How scores work
evidence.text:
Each category's score comes from a one-factor latent model fitted to the benchmark results, within sets
of models that share enough benchmarks to be compared. It lives in `lib/score.ts` and is explained in
[pages/method.md](pages/method.md). 50 is an average model, and ± is the uncertainty. `npm run check`
reports how well the fit predicts results it hasn't seen.

Sponsors never change rankings or scores. Sponsored spots on whatmodel.sh are always labelled, and you
can check the ranking against the code here.

evidence.heading: Use the data
evidence.text:
- Read the JSON in `data/` directly, or run `npm run export` to write cleaned snapshots, CSV tables
  (scores, models, results, speeds and bench runs) and a SHA-256 manifest to `dist/data/`. They're the same
  files whatmodel.sh serves at [whatmodel.sh/data/manifest.json](https://whatmodel.sh/data/manifest.json).
- The data is licensed [CC BY-SA 4.0](DATA-LICENSE.md): credit whatmodel.sh and share adaptations under
  the same licence. Each source's own licence also applies. `data/sources.json` lists them and
  `licenses/` has the full notices.

evidence.heading: The bench script
evidence.text:
The bench measures how fast models run on your machine. It finds the models and AI tools you have and
the whatmodel.sh models that fit your memory; you tick what to test, confirm the plan, then review the
measurements. It installs or downloads nothing without asking, and offers to set up Python if it's
missing. Works on macOS and Linux; on Windows, run it in WSL.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://whatmodel.sh/bench.sh | sh
```

Results stay local until you choose to open a prefilled GitHub issue. Review it and submit it yourself
in the browser. API and agent tests may incur provider charges. See [BENCHMARKING.md](BENCHMARKING.md)
for supported runners, measurement protocols and what the public report contains.

Submitted results are released under CC0 1.0 and reviewed before they're added.

evidence.heading: Contributing
evidence.text:
Corrections and new results are welcome, and you don't need to write code. See
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

evidence.heading: 仓库简介
evidence.text: Desktop app built on Claude Code agent harness with useful and fun features for proactive engineers.

evidence.heading: README
evidence.text:
**Workbench is a desktop app based on the Claude Code harness, built for proactive engineers.** It gives you a space to manage your project tasks and hand each one to an agent that works in its own git worktree, so your main branch stays untouched until you review and merge. Every task starts with a short triage run that efficiently picks the model and the thinking effort based on the task description, and decides whether the work needs planning, so a one-line fix doesn't burn an Opus run and a refactor across a dozen files doesn't get handed to Haiku. From there, the same session plans, implements, runs your project's checks, reviews its own diff with fresh eyes, and commits, while parallel tasks are told which files the other unmerged branches touch so they stay out of each other's way.


  
    
    
    
  


Workbench also improves over time by learning and retaining preferences from your sessions, enabling a built-in compounding engineering workflow. You become the manager/architect of your project, setting the direction and priorities while the agents do the work. Nothing lands until you have reviewed it, and you always know what the result costs.

evidence.heading: Motivation
evidence.text:
Every creative builder has a graveyard of ideas. Each idea wants an evening you don't have, and the ones you start stall where the interesting part ends, and the plumbing begins. The agent in your terminal can do that plumbing today, but you still sit with it one session at a time: one idea, one branch, one window, until the context runs out. Workbench closes that gap by turning your ideas into projects and your projects into a board of tasks the agents build in parallel, so they end up in review instead of buried.


  
    
    
    
  


Most tools in this space write their own agent harness, and none of them outperforms the one you already have installed. You see it in the results: a loop that plans worse, retries more, and spends more than Claude Code does on the same task. So why build another harness when one already works? Workbench runs on Claude Code rather than competing with it, using the same CLI with your own accounts, subagents, skills, and MCP servers, and spending its own effort on everything around the session instead.

evidence.heading: Contribute
evidence.text: Pull requests are temporarily not accepted, but every other kind of contribution is welcome. If something looks broken or missing, open an [issue](https://github.com/proactive-agent/workbench/issues) describing what you expected to happen instead. Ideas, questions, and features you would like to see belong in [discussions](https://github.com/proactive-agent/workbench/discussions), where they can be argued over before implementation.

evidence.heading: Introduction
evidence.text:
Collecting datasets from user-generated content communities is becoming an increasingly common approach to training models. Video platforms host a continuous stream of real-world content from diverse creators, offering opportunities to scale training data, broaden its distribution, and represent more people. Finding sources relevant to a specific domain within this growing collection has become an important part of dataset construction.

A common collection pipeline first identifies relevant accounts, then uses video models and human review to select individual videos suitable for training. Previous work has explored manually curated sources, automatic candidate retrieval, and channel-level sampling, yet source selection and content review still require human effort.   As the number of candidate accounts grows, the cost of browsing and judging them increases. Changes to category boundaries or collection goals can also require repeating part of that work. **Account screening has therefore become a bottleneck in domain dataset collection.**

An account's profile page already provides useful previews: titles describe video topics, thumbnails supply visual cues, and the account name and biography describe the creator's focus. These signals offer a basis for inexpensive source selection. Meanwhile, decision models can turn supplied evidence directly into category choices and relevance probabilities, answering several independent questions in a single request. This makes them suitable for large-scale, repeatable screening.

**To the best of our knowledge, Jev Account Filter is the first project to screen video-platform accounts without downloading or watching full videos.** It first selects candidates by title, then combines their thumbnails with account metadata to judge the

evidence.heading: Advantages
evidence.text: We screened **2,140 Douyin accounts** for sign-language content with **Jev 1.14**: **8 hours** of data collection and **1 hour** of API inference, at a total API cost of **$0.565** and **94.49%** accuracy.

evidence.heading: Application domains
evidence.text:
**Jev Account Filter can support both model-training dataset construction and sample selection and analysis for research, including news and communication studies.** The examples below include major datasets and representative studies whose papers and methods document human channel screening or curation of channel sources. The project could replace the manual channel-screening stage in these workflows. Sign language is the validated application; other domains can be explored through new category configurations.



- **Sign language account discovery:** find sign language channels and creators as sources for sign language translation datasets. OpenASL, YouTube-ASL, and YouTube-SL-25 illustrate the need to select relevant channel sources; our account-screening experiment evaluates this domain.
- **News and communication research:** screen news and current-affairs channels to build research samples for studying news creators, audience overlap, and cross-partisan discussions. Pew's YouTube studies illustrate this manual screening workload.
- **Instrument performance datasets:** identify piano and other instrument-performance channels before collecting music videos. PIAST illustrates the role of curated channel sources in music dataset construction.
- **Makeup tutorial datasets:** select beauty creators and makeup tutorial channels before collecting instructional videos. YouMakeup illustrates this source-selection stage.

The latter three are potential applications, requiring their own category rules and evaluation; they are not additional validated benchmarks.

Dataset papers: [OpenASL · §3](https://aclanthology.org/2022.emnlp-main.427.pdf#page=3) · [YouTube-ASL · §2.1, §3.2](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2023/file/5c61452daca5f0c260e683b317d13a3f-Paper-Datasets_and_Benchmar

evidence.text: Collection adapters and category rules are independent. Custom sources only need to follow the [data format](docs/data-format.md); a platform adapter is unnecessary.

evidence.heading: Visual analysis
evidence.text:
Screening produces more than an account list. The interactive analysis page brings together class composition, classification performance, score distributions, and feature clusters. Select a group in a chart to inspect individual accounts, candidate titles, thumbnails, and model scores. Adding a second-review CSV automatically updates the evaluation reference and enables a comparison of human annotation errors and model errors.

The statistical views below come from the latest complete **Jev 1.14 experiment on 2,140 Douyin accounts**; account-level evidence uses the explicitly published demo subset. The team's full account list and collected works remain private.

**Dataset composition and performance.** Class proportions describe the sample, while the reviewed comparison separates model errors from original annotation errors. Accuracy is a conditional estimate: the 198 previously reviewed accounts use second-review labels; the other 1,942 retain their original labels, assumed correct.



**Errors and score distributions.** The confusion matrix separates missed accounts from false inclusions. Normalized histograms compare account probabilities for human-error and model-error samples, helping identify score ranges that warrant closer review. The two error groups can overlap.



**Clusters of model outputs.** The predicted category and five candidate-video scores describe groups with different evidence profiles. The scatter plot shows a PCA projection; group panels report mean video scores and within-group error rates. Accounts missing any of the five scores are excluded without zero imputation. Clustering describes the results without changing the classification rules.

evidence.heading: 🚀 What is this project?
evidence.text:
This is a customized, enhanced fork of the original AnythingLLM Desktop application, specifically optimized and packaged as a **Portable Windows Application**. 

It transforms your desktop into a full-stack AI powerhouse, allowing you to interact with large language models (LLMs) and your own data securely. Because it's completely portable, you can run it from any folder or even a USB flash drive without touching your system registry or running complex installers.

evidence.heading: 🌟 Why this Fork?
evidence.text:
While the original AnythingLLM is fantastic, this fork was created to provide a lightweight, no-install experience for Windows users, along with several under-the-hood enhancements.

*(Note: Update these points with your actual specific changes)*
*   🧳 **True Portability:** No installers, no hidden AppData folders. Everything runs straight from the extracted folder.
*   ⚡ **Optimized Performance:** Faster document parsing and smoother UI rendering.
*   🎨 **UI/UX Refinements:** A cleaner, more intuitive interface tailored for power users.
*   🛠️ **Expanded Customization:** Deeper control over system prompts, chunking parameters, and RAG pipelines.

evidence.text:

*   🧠 **Bring Your Own LLM:** Seamlessly switch between Local LLMs, OpenAI, Anthropic, Groq, Mistral, and more.
